title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Recap and Roadmap
Last time: Dedekind & Cantor’s existential, set-theoretic style of mathematics — and Russell’s paradox, which broke Frege’s comprehension principle.
Today

paradoxes and consistency, predicativity, the axiom of choice
Brouwer’s intuitionism vs. Hilbert’s program

The question throughout: what is a legitimate mathematical object, definition, or proof?

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Comprehension Principle, Again
Recall the principle that broke under Russell’s paradox:
\[
\text{for any well-defined property } p,\ \text{there exists } \{x : p(x)\}
\]

This was the basis for the logicist understanding of set theory — “naive” set theory
Not just Russell’s paradox: two families of paradoxes emerged around 1900

set-theoretic paradoxes (Burali-Forti, Cantor, Russell/Zermelo)
semantic paradoxes (Richard, König, Grelling) — about truth and definability

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Set-Theoretic Paradoxes

Burali-Forti (1897; Cantor 1896): the set of all ordinals would itself be well-ordered, hence have an ordinal \(>\) every ordinal in it — contradiction
Cantor (1899): the set of all cardinals leads to the same kind of contradiction
Zermelo–Russell (1901–02): let \(p(x)\) be “\(x \notin x\)” and consider \(R = \{x : x \notin x\}\)

Comprehension is contradictory in the simplest possible way — no need for a theory of the transfinite to state it.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Hilbert and Existence
Hilbert abandoned logicism. He proposed working with axiom systems that comprise non-logical axioms.
This, however, requires a new kind of justification why the ojects we are trying to axiomatize exist.
Hilbert’s proposal:

A set of objects “exists” only if we can prove its defining axiom system consistent
concept \(\to\) set becomes consistency proof \(\to\) legitimate existence
Objects have a kind of ideal existence “in the realm of thought,” not independent metaphysical existence

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Predicativity — Poincaré’s Diagnosis
When Frege’s and Russell’s paradoxes became widely known (1903), Poincaré offered his own culprit: impredicative definitions.

A definition is impredicative when it refers to a totality that already contains the very element being defined.


Example: least upper bound – defining the supremum involves quantifying over “all upper bounds,” a set of real numbers, in order to pin down a particular real number. That real number is thus specified by reference to a totality it belongs to.
Poincaré: this kind of circularity is exactly what licenses the paradoxes

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Richard’s Paradox (a Semantic Paradox)

Only countably many reals are definable by a finite expression — list them \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots\) (lexicographic order)
Define \(r\): the \(n\)th decimal digit of \(r\) differs from the \(n\)th digit of \(a_n\)
\(r\) is not on the list — yet \(r\) was just defined, in finitely many words!

Poincaré’s diagnosis: \(r\)’s definition refers to the totality of all definable numbers, of which \(r\) is itself meant to be a member. Impredicative.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Two Responses to Impredicativity


Zermelo — unconvinced

Impredicative definitions are everywhere in classical analysis (e.g. least upper bound)
Harmless: the object isn’t created by the definition, only singled out from what already exists


Russell — convinced

Adopts Poincaré’s “vicious circle principle”
Builds a theory of types: objects stratified into levels; no set of “mixed” type
Result: Principia Mathematica (1910–13)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Where Predicativity Led

Russell’s ramified type theory needed extra ad hoc machinery (the axiom of reducibility) to recover ordinary mathematics
Weyl, in Das Kontinuum (1918), tried a leaner predicative foundation: accept classical logic and \(\mathbb{N}\), but build the reals predicatively

cost: \(\mathbb{R}\) is no longer complete — the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem fails

Predicative mathematics survives today as a serious middle ground between classical and constructive mathematics

title: The Foundational Crisis
section: Controversy on the Axiom of Choice
text:
Controversy on the Axiom of Choice
Zermelo (1904): \(\mathrm{AC} \implies\) every set — in particular \(\mathbb{R}\) — can be well-ordered.

\(\mathrm{AC}\): given any family of disjoint nonempty sets, a choice set exists containing one element from each
The proof gives no explicit construction of the well-ordering
Critics: \(\mathrm{AC}\) merely asserts the choice set exists, without a defining property for it

\(\Rightarrow\) a deep debate followed, cutting across the logicism/predicativism divide.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
From Controversy to Axiom System
The AC debate spurred Zermelo to work out his axiom system for set theory (1908) — a careful, mathematical (not logical) analysis of Cantor’s and Dedekind’s set theory.

Fraenkel & von Neumann (1920s) add: Replacement and Regularity
Weyl & Skolem: formalize within first-order logic — quantify only over sets, not over properties

\[
\rightsquigarrow \quad \mathrm{ZF(C)}
\]

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
What ZFC Codifies
ZFC settles the early-1900s controversies by simply building in the modern, anti-Kroneckerian traits:

impredicative definitions — allowed
arbitrary functions and subsets — allowed
purely existential proofs — allowed


The result: a working “Platonistic” view of mathematics — the objects a theory refers to are treated as if they exist independently of what a mathematician can explicitly define or construct.

By the 1920s, Russell’s (simplified) type theory and Zermelo’s set theory had largely converged on this same methodology.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Summary - Response to the Paradoxes
The paradoxes did not kill modern mathematics.

They forced a clarification: existence via consistency, not naive comprehension
Poincaré’s predicativism and Russell’s type theory tried to restrain the new methods
Zermelo’s set theory — soon ZFC — codified the new methods instead.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A New Kind of Critique
1921: Weyl publishes a paper in the Mathematische Zeitschrift — a disciple of Hilbert’s — openly siding with Brouwer, diagnosing a “crisis in the foundations.”

Weyl’s paper: deliberately a propaganda pamphlet, “to rouse the sleepers”
Hilbert’s reply, same year: Brouwer and Weyl are attempting a “putsch” — a “dictatorship à la Kronecker”

The foundational debate turns into open battle: Hilbert’s classical mathematics vs. Brouwer’s constructive “revolution.”

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
What is Brouwer’s “Revolution”?
Up to 1920, the debate concerned: real numbers, impredicativity, and the strong existential assumptions of set theory (esp. AC).
Brouwer went further: 

He put classical logic itself on trial: quantifiers over infinite domains, and the principle of excluded middle (PEM)
Poincaré, Klein, and others had said logic is not the whole of mathematics; Brouwer said mathematics is prior to and independent of logic and language altogether.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Intuitionism — First Principles

For Brouwer, mathematical objects are mental constructions; mathematics does not depend on language or logic to exist
Classical logic (including PEM) was abstracted from experience with finite sets — and wrongly extrapolated to infinite ones
PEM: \(p \vee \neg p\) — “either \(p\) or not \(p\)” — always holds, classically

Brouwer’s claim: this is not a law of thought, but an unjustified generalization.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Constructive Standard

Consequence: proof by contradiction is invalid.

Classically: assume \(\neg p\), derive a contradiction, conclude \(p\)
Constructively: this only shows \(\neg\neg p\) — not the same as a construction of \(p\)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A Different Notion of Truth
For a constructivist:

“\(p\) is true” means: we possess a proof of \(p\) by stringent constructive methods
“\(p\) is false” means: we possess a counterexample to \(p\)


To a constructivist, the statement “π is normal” currently has no truth value — not true, not false, not “unknown-but-determinate.” Truth is not timeless; it is made.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Rebuilding Analysis: Choice Sequences
Brouwer (1918) replaces Cantorian sets with constructive substitutes: spreads and species.

A choice sequence: a sequence of rationals not required to be fully specified in advance

may be generated by a fixed rule (e.g. Newton’s method for \(\sqrt 2\))
or by choices the mathematician makes freely, over time, subject to constraints


Intuitionistic mathematics is “mathematics in the making” — unlike the timeless, fully-determinate objects of classical analysis.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Spreads and a New Continuum

A spread is a law regulating which choice sequences are admissible — the basis for Brouwer’s reconstruction of \(\mathbb{R}\)
The continuum becomes a genuinely continuous domain, not a set of pre-existing points

an echo of Aristotle: the continuum is not made up of unextended points


A function on a spread must be determined from a finite initial segment of any choice sequence — this has a startling consequence.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Startling Consequence
Every intuitionistically total function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is (uniformly) continuous.

The classical step function \[
f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \leq 0 \\ 1 & x > 0 \end{cases}
\] is not a legitimate function for Brouwer
Reason: deciding \(x > 0\) vs. \(x \leq 0\) is not always possible — not decidable from a finite stage of the sequence

(Anticipates the later, independent discovery that all computable real functions are continuous — Turing and others.)

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
The Cost of Intuitionism
Rebuilding analysis this way is hard. Weyl, who once championed Brouwer’s program, wrote in 1925:

“The mathematician watches with pain the largest part of his towering theories dissolve into mist before his eyes.”

Brouwer himself, unfazed, replied (1933):

“The spheres of truth are less transparent than those of illusion.”

Weyl abandoned intuitionism shortly after. But Hilbert had another answer in mind.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Hilbert’s Program
Hilbert (1928): to “eliminate from the world once and for all the skeptical doubts” about classical mathematics.

Strategy: use Kroneckerian (finitary, constructive) means to justify anti-Kroneckerian (classical) methods
Key move: turn proofs into formal, syntactic objects — finite strings of symbols manipulated by explicit rules
A proof becomes something a finitary, combinatorial argument can reason about, from the outside — metamathematics

title: The Foundational Crisis
section: The Four Steps of the Program
text:
The Four Steps of the Program

Find suitable axioms and primitive concepts for a theory \(T\) (e.g. the real numbers)
Find axioms and rules for classical logic — syntactic rules turning propositions into new propositions
Formalize \(T\): propositions become strings of symbols, proofs become sequences of strings obeying formal rules
Give a finitary proof that no string expressing a contradiction can ever be the last line of a proof

If (iv) succeeds for \(T\): consistency is established by means even a strict finitist should accept.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Finitism: What Counts as “Given”
Hilbert’s answer to Poincaré’s 1905 circularity worry (a consistency proof for arithmetic would need induction):

What is genuinely, intuitively given: signs and formulas themselves, as concrete finite objects
Metamathematical reasoning about them needs only a very weak form of induction — much weaker than full arithmetical induction
Finitary mathematics needs no further justification — it is where justification bottoms out

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Progress and Limits (1920s)

Propositional logic: proved consistent and complete
First-order (predicate) logic: proved complete — Gödel’s dissertation, 1929
Ackermann, von Neumann: consistency results for subsystems of arithmetic (1928–1930)
By 1930 Hilbert believed full consistency of arithmetic was within reach

A crucial hidden assumption: that the axiomatic systems in question would also be complete.

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
“Formalism” — a Slightly Misleading Name

The label comes from Hilbert’s method: formalize a theory, study its formal proof-structure
But Hilbert did not think mathematics is a meaningless game with symbols

he consistently stressed the meaningfulness of informal mathematical statements

Unlike intuitionism, formalism was never a full philosophy of mathematics — it was a method for justifying the classical one

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
A Personal Crisis, Too
The dispute was not only intellectual.

Hilbert and Brouwer: strong-willed, brilliant, and deeply incompatible personalities
1928: Hilbert moves to remove Brouwer from the editorial board of Mathematische Annalen

Einstein: the move is “unwise” and wants no part of it
The board is dissolved and reconstituted without Brouwer — the journal loses Einstein and Carathéodory

Brouwer, disturbed, withdraws from the scene for years — as political tensions fade, so does the sense of “crisis”

title: The Foundational Crisis
text:
Looking Ahead
 
Hilbert’s program looked to be within reach by 1930 — one more push on the consistency of arithmetic.
 
Things turned out otherwise…

title: Relations and Functions
text: You have used relations (orderings) and functions all your life; the point here is to say what they are inside axiomatic set theory, and to notice where an extra axiom (Replacement) is needed to build them.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Relations
Definition (binary relation). \(R\) is a (binary) relation iff \(R\) is a set of ordered pairs:
\[
\forall u \in R\;\exists x, y\;\bigl(u = \langle x, y\rangle\bigr).
\]
Here \(\forall u \in R\,(\dots)\) is shorthand for \(\forall u\,(u \in R
\rightarrow \dots)\). We write
\[
x \mathbin{R} y \quad\text{for}\quad \langle x, y\rangle \in R,
\qquad\qquad
x \mathbin{\neg R} y \quad\text{for}\quad \langle x, y\rangle \notin R.
\]
The abbreviations \(x \mathbin{R} y\) and \(x \mathbin{\neg R} y\) are meaningful even when \(R\) is not a relation — we will use this later.

Usual terminology
Fix a set \(A\). The following say what it means for \(R\) to have a property on \(A\); each is just an abbreviation, obtained by plugging \(R\) into a formula.

transitive: \(x \mathbin{R} y \wedge y \mathbin{R} z \rightarrow x \mathbin{R} z\)
reflexive / irreflexive: \(\forall x \in A\;(x \mathbin{R} x)\) / \(\forall x \in A\;(x \mathbin{\neg R} x)\)
trichotomy: \(\forall x, y \in A\;\bigl(x \mathbin{R} y \vee y \mathbin{R} x \vee x = y\bigr)\)
symmetric: \(x \mathbin{R} y \leftrightarrow y \mathbin{R} x\)

and the three composite notions we care about:


\(R\) (strictly) partially orders \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive and irreflexive on \(A\).

\(R\) (strictly) totally orders \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive, irreflexive, and satisfies trichotomy on \(A\).

\(R\) is an equivalence relation on \(A\)

\(R\) is transitive, reflexive, and symmetric on \(A\).



We take the strict \(<\) as basic and read \(x \le y\) as \(x < y \vee x = y\). For example, \(<\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a strict total order; \(\le\) is not (it is not irreflexive).


Domain, range, restriction

\(\operatorname{dom}(R) := \{\,x : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\}\)
\(\operatorname{ran}(R) := \{\,y : \exists x\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\}\)
\(R \restriction A := \{\,\langle x, y\rangle \in R : x \in A\,\}\)

The definitions are stated for an arbitrary set \(R\), not only for relations. The restriction \(R \restriction A\) is used mostly for functions.
Justification (these classes are sets). Recall \(\langle x, y\rangle =
\bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\}\). So if \(\langle x, y\rangle \in R\), then \(\{x\}\) and \(\{x, y\}\) lie in \(\bigcup R\), and hence \(x, y \in \bigcup\bigcup R\). Comprehension then gives
\[
\operatorname{dom}(R) = \bigl\{\,x \in \textstyle\bigcup\bigcup R : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in R)\,\bigr\},
\]
and similarly for \(\operatorname{ran}(R)\).

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Functions
Definition (function). \(R\) is a function iff \(R\) is a relation and for every \(x \in \operatorname{dom}(R)\) there is a unique \(y\) with \(\langle x,
y\rangle \in R\); that unique \(y\) is written \(R(x)\).

\(F : A \to B\):   \(F\) is a function with \(\operatorname{dom}(F) = A\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(F) \subseteq B\).
\(F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{} B\):   \(F : A \to B\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(F) = B\) (a surjection).
\(F : A \xrightarrow{1\text{-}1} B\):   \(F : A \to B\) and \(\forall x, x' \in A\;\bigl(F(x) = F(x') \rightarrow x = x'\bigr)\) (an injection).
\(F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{1\text{-}1} B\):   both of the above (a bijection from \(A\) onto \(B\)).

Image of a set.
\[
F(A) \;=\; F{}''A \;=\; \operatorname{ran}(F \restriction A).
\]
The notation \(F(A)\) is standard but ambiguous when \(A\) happens to be both a member and a subset of \(\operatorname{dom}(F)\) — e.g. with \(\operatorname{dom}(F)
= 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\), is \(F(2)\) the value at \(2\) or the image of \(\{0, 1\}\)? Write \(F{}''A\) when this could be confused.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Building relations and functions
The axioms used so far (Extensionality, Comprehension, Pairing, Union) do not let us build many relations. The obvious source is the Cartesian product
\[
A \times B \;=\; \{\,\langle x, y\rangle : x \in A \wedge y \in B\,\},
\]
after which any relation between \(A\) and \(B\) is a subset of \(A \times B\), cut out by Comprehension. So everything reduces to: does \(A \times B\) exist?

First method: Power Set
If \(x \in A\) and \(y \in B\) then \(\{x\}, \{x, y\} \subseteq A \cup B\), so \(\langle x, y\rangle = \bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\} \in \mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)\bigr)\). Hence
\[
A \times B \;=\; \bigl\{\, w \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;(w = \langle x, y\rangle)\,\bigr\}
\]
exists by Power Set (twice) and Comprehension.
This works, but it is a little “wasteful” in terms of cardinality. The sets
\[
\{0\} \times \omega, \qquad
\operatorname{id}_\omega = \{\,\langle x, x\rangle : x \in \omega\,\}
\]
have the same “size” as \(\omega\), yet the justification above manufactures them as subsets of \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\omega))\) — a set of size \(2^{2^{\aleph_0}}\). We are invoking the existence of a huge set to produce a countable one.


Second method: Replacement

General method. Suppose \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\). Then Replacement gives a set \(B\) with \(\forall x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;\varphi(x,
y)\), and Comprehension trims it to \(\{\,y \in B : \exists x \in A\;\varphi(x,
y)\,\} = \{\,y : \exists x \in A\;\varphi(x, y)\,\}\). So the image of a set under a definable single-valued relation is a set.

Apply this to build \(A \times B\) without Power Set. Fix \(b \in B\) and let
\[
\varphi(x, y) \;\equiv\; y = \langle x, b\rangle .
\]
Then \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\), so by Replacement + Comprehension the set
\[
A \times \{b\} \;=\; \{\,\langle x, b\rangle : x \in A\,\}
\]
exists. Applying Replacement again — now over \(b \in B\) — gives
\[
S \;:=\; \bigl\{\, A \times \{b\} : b \in B\,\bigr\},
\]
and finally \(A \times B = \bigcup S\) by Union.

This argument never opened up \(\langle x, b\rangle\); it used only that \(\langle x, b\rangle\) is some set determined by \(x\) and \(b\). So it proves \(A \times B\) (and also \(\operatorname{dom}(R)\), \(\operatorname{ran}(R)\)) exist for any definition of the ordered pair.

Packaging the general method as a statement about functions:

Lemma. If \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\;\varphi(x, y)\), then there is a function \(f\) with \(\operatorname{dom}(f) = A\) such that for each \(x \in A\), \(f(x)\) is the unique \(y\) with \(\varphi(x, y)\).

Proof. Fix \(B\) from Replacement and set \(f = \{\,\langle x, y\rangle \in A
\times B : \varphi(x, y)\,\}\). \(\square\)

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Inverses, composition, isomorphism


\(R^{-1} := \{\,\langle y, x\rangle : \langle x, y\rangle \in R\,\}\)

a subset of \(\operatorname{ran}(R) \times \operatorname{dom}(R)\). If \(f\) is a function, \(f^{-1}\) is a function iff \(f\) is \(1\)-\(1\).

\(G \circ F := \{\,\langle x, z\rangle : \exists y\,(\langle x, y\rangle \in F \wedge \langle y, z\rangle \in G)\,\}\)

when \(F, G\) are functions with \(\operatorname{ran}(F) \subseteq
\operatorname{dom}(G)\), this is just \((G \circ F)(x) = G(F(x))\).



Isomorphism. Let \(R\) be a binary relation on \(A\) and \(S\) a binary relation on \(B\). Then \(F\) is an isomorphism from \((A, R)\) onto \((B, S)\) iff
\[
F : A \xrightarrow[\text{onto}]{1\text{-}1} B
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall x, y \in A\;\bigl[\,x \mathbin{R} y \leftrightarrow F(x) \mathbin{S} F(y)\,\bigr].
\]
We write \((A, R) \cong (B, S)\) when such an \(F\) exists. The definition makes sense for arbitrary relations; for now we use it for orderings.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Equivalence relations and quotients
Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(A\), and \(x \in A\). Define
\[
[x] \;:=\; \{\,y \in A : x \mathbin{R} y\,\}
\qquad\text{(Comprehension)},
\]
the equivalence class of \(x\), and
\[
A / R \;:=\; \bigl\{\, [x] : x \in A\,\bigr\}.
\]
To see \(A/R\) is a set, apply the general method with \(\varphi(x, y) \equiv y =
[x]\): by Lemma I.7.9 there is a function \(f\) with \(\operatorname{dom}(f) = A\) and \(f(x) = [x]\) — the quotient map \(x \mapsto [x]\) — and then \(A/R =
\operatorname{ran}(f)\).
This is the standard justification, in books on group theory and topology, for forming a quotient of a structure by an equivalence relation; the extra structure on \(A/R\) is defined separately.

title: Relations and Functions
text:
Object theory versus metatheory
The informal notions “relation” and “function” get two representations in set theory: as sets (objects of the formal theory ZFC), and as abbreviations in the metatheory.

As sets
A relation is a specific kind of set, handled inside ZFC. The defining property is a formula of the object theory — for example
\[
\operatorname{Rel}(R) \;:\equiv\; \forall u \in R\;\exists y, z\;\bigl(u = \langle y, z\rangle\bigr).
\]
We then prove facts about such sets as theorems of ZFC, e.g.
\[
\mathrm{ZFC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Rel}(R) \rightarrow \exists z\,\bigl(z = \operatorname{dom}(R)\bigr),
\]
using the justification given earlier. A concrete function such as \(f = \{\langle
1, 2\rangle, \langle 2, 2\rangle, \langle 3, 1\rangle\}\) is likewise a set formally defined in ZFC.


As abbreviations in the metatheory
By contrast, \(\in\), \(=\), \(\subseteq\) are informal relations — a different kind of animal. The “relation”
\[
S \;=\; \{\,p : \exists x, y\;(p = \langle x, y\rangle \wedge x \subseteq y)\,\}
\]
does not exist: it is a proper class, since \(\operatorname{dom}(S)\) would be the universe \(V\). We view \(x \subseteq y\) instead as an abbreviation in the metatheory for \(\forall z\,(z \in x \rightarrow z \in y)\); likewise \((A, R)
\cong (B, S)\) abbreviates a longer statement. Membership and equality, \(\in\) and \(=\), are already primitive symbols.
Many properties from the terminology list still make sense for such pseudorelations, by plugging them into the defining formula. For instance \(\in\) totally orders \(3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\) (i.e. \(\forall x, y, z \in 3\,[x \in y
\wedge y \in z \rightarrow x \in z]\), plus trichotomy), while \(\subseteq\) is transitive on all of \(V\) but not a total order of \(3\), and \(\in\) is not transitive on \(V\) (since \(0 \in \{0\} \in \{\{0\}\}\) but \(0 \notin \{\{0\}\}\)).
Similarly for functions: \(\bigcup : V \to V\) and \(\mathcal{P} : V \to V\) are pseudofunctions. There is no set of pairs \(\bigcup = \{\langle \mathcal{F},
\bigcup \mathcal{F}\rangle : \mathcal{F} \in V\}\); instead there is a formula \(\varphi(\mathcal{F}, Z)\) saying “\(Z\) is the union of the members of \(\mathcal{F}\)”, we prove \(\forall \mathcal{F}\;\exists! Z\;\varphi(\mathcal{F},
Z)\), and \(\bigcup \mathcal{F}\) denotes that \(Z\). Function properties still apply as abbreviations — e.g. “\(\bigcup\) is not \(1\)-\(1\)” is the formula
\[
\exists x_1, x_2, y\;\bigl[\varphi(x_1, y) \wedge \varphi(x_2, y) \wedge x_1 \neq x_2\bigr].
\]

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text: Reading: Lawvere–Rosebrugh, Sets for Mathematics, Chapter 5 (pp. 96–110). So far we have required of the category \(\mathcal{S}\) of abstract sets and mappings: a terminal object, finite limits (products, equalizers, pullbacks), and a truth-value object \(2\) that classifies parts. One axiom is missing before we can say what a topos is: the existence of mapping sets \(Y^B\). Today we add it, and we will see that the tools from last time — functors and natural transformations — are exactly the language in which this axiom is most naturally stated.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Where we are
The axioms on \(\mathcal{S}\) so far (L–R, Ch. 1–3):


\(\mathcal{S}\) is a category

Associative composition, identities.

Terminal set \(1\); initial set \(0\); \(1\) separates mappings

Elements of \(A\) are maps \(1 \to A\), and maps are determined by their values on elements.

Binary sums

\(A + B\) with injections, universal among pairs \(A \to Y\), \(B \to Y\).

Finite inverse limits

Products and equalizers (hence pullbacks and all finite limits).

Membership via truth values

Every part of \(A\) has a unique characteristic map \(A \to 2\), and every \(A \to 2\) is one.



Every one of these axioms has the same shape: an object is introduced together with a bijection between two kinds of maps. For products, maps into \(Y_0 \times Y_1\) correspond to pairs of maps; for sums, maps out of \(A + B\) correspond to pairs of maps; for \(2\), maps into \(2\) correspond to parts. Chapter 5 makes this shape explicit and then uses it for one more construction.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
section: The two-level pattern, illustrated by products
text:
The two-level pattern, illustrated by products
L–R write the defining property of the product as a “fraction” \[
\frac{\;X \longrightarrow Y_0 \times Y_1\;}{\;X \longrightarrow Y_0, \quad X \longrightarrow Y_1\;}
\] meaning: there is a natural process turning a map of the upper kind into one of the lower kind, a natural process in the other direction, and the two are mutually inverse.
Level 1 (crude): “there is such an invertible process, for all \(X, Y_0, Y_1\).”
Level 2 (refined): the process is carried out by a functorial construction plus composition with one specific map. And the specific map is obtained by bootstrapping: feed the crude process an identity map.

Downward. Take \(X = Y_0 \times Y_1\) and put \(1_{Y_0\times Y_1}\) above the bar. Below the bar we get two specific maps — the projections \(p_0, p_1\). The general downward process is then composition with them: \(f \mapsto (p_0 f, \, p_1 f)\).
Upward. Take \(Y_0 = Y_1 = X\) and put \((1_X, 1_X)\) below the bar. Above the bar we get a specific map, the diagonal \(\delta_X = \langle 1_X, 1_X\rangle : X \to X \times X\). Using the functoriality of \(\times\) on maps, \[
(f_0 \times f_1)\langle x_0, x_1\rangle = \langle f_0 x_0, f_1 x_1 \rangle,
\qquad (g_0 \times g_1)(f_0 \times f_1) = (g_0 f_0) \times (g_1 f_1),
\] the general upward process is \[
\langle f_0, f_1 \rangle = (f_0 \times f_1)\,\delta_X .
\] (Check it by composing both sides with \(p_0\) and \(p_1\).)


The pattern. Universal property \(=\) natural bijection of hom-sets. Applying the bijection to an identity produces a universal map (here \(p_0, p_1\) and \(\delta_X\)), and the general bijection is “apply the functor, then compose with the universal map.”

We now run exactly this program for a new construction.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Exponentiation

The crude idea
For sets \(B\), \(Y\) we want a set \(Y^B\) with \[
\frac{\;X \longrightarrow Y^B\;}{\;X \times B \longrightarrow Y\;}
\] natural in \(X\) (and \(Y\)). Bootstrap immediately with \(X = 1\): since \(1 \times B \cong B\), \[
\frac{\;1 \longrightarrow Y^B\;}{\;B \longrightarrow Y\;}
\] so the elements of \(Y^B\) must correspond exactly to the maps \(B \to Y\). This determines what \(Y^B\) “is,” just as the case \(X = 1\) of the product property told us that the elements of \(Y_0 \times Y_1\) are pairs of elements.


Families of maps, and naming schemes
A map \(f : X \times B \to Y\) (a “function of two variables”) is the same as a family of maps \(B \to Y\) parametrized by \(X\): for each element \(x : 1 \to X\) put \[
f_x : B \xrightarrow{\ \langle x \circ !_B,\, 1_B\rangle\ } X \times B \xrightarrow{\ f\ } Y,
\qquad f_x(b) = f(x, b).
\] Think of \(X\) as a set of names and of \(f\) as a naming scheme: \(x\) names \(f_x\). A naming scheme may or may not have the two properties

every map \(B \to Y\) has at least one name (\(x \mapsto f_x\) is onto), and
every nameable map has only one name (\(x \mapsto f_x\) is one-to-one).

A scheme with both properties is a universal naming scheme. We then write \(Y^B\) for the set of names, \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) for the scheme (“evaluation”), and \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\) for the unique name of \(f : B \to Y\): \[
\mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner, b) = f(b).
\]


The axiom
A universal scheme compares uniquely to every scheme, and that is what we take as the axiom.






NoteAxiom: Exponentiation



For any sets \(B, Y\) there is a set \(Y^B\) and a map \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) such that for every \(X\) and every \(f : X \times B \to Y\) there is a unique \(\ulcorner f \urcorner : X \to Y^B\) with \[
\mathrm{eval}\circ (\ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B) = f .
\] \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
Y^B \times B & \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{eval}\ } & Y \\[2pt]
{\scriptstyle \ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B}\Big\uparrow & \nearrow_{\scriptstyle f} & \\[2pt]
X \times B & &
\end{array}
\]


We call \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\) the transpose (or name, or curried form) of \(f\). Explicitly, \(\ulcorner f \urcorner(x) = \ulcorner f_x \urcorner\): the parametrized name of \(f\) assigns to \(x\) the name of \(f_x\).
Note the bootstrap again: \(\mathrm{eval}\) is the map corresponding to \(1_{Y^B}\), i.e. the unique \(f\) with \(\ulcorner f \urcorner = 1_{Y^B}\). It plays the role the projections played for products.






TipComparison with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)





In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) the set of functions \({}^B Y\) is constructed: it is carved out of \(\mathcal{P}(B \times Y)\) by Separation, so its existence is a consequence of Power Set. Here the direction is reversed: \(Y^B\) is primitive, characterized only by how maps into it behave, and the power set will appear below as the special case \(2^B\). Note also that the hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(B, Y)\) is a collection in the metatheory; the axiom says that it is internalized by an object of \(\mathcal{S}\), whose elements \(1 \to Y^B\) correspond to it.





Example: three descriptions of a motion
Let \(B\) be the particles of a cloud, \(E\) the points of space, \(T\) the instants of a time interval. A motion of the cloud can be given in three equivalent ways: \[
T \longrightarrow E^B, \qquad T \times B \longrightarrow E, \qquad B \longrightarrow E^T .
\] The first assigns to each instant a placement of the cloud; the middle one assigns to each instant and particle a position; the last assigns to each particle its path. The passage between the outer two uses the axiom twice and the twist \(B \times T \cong T \times B\) once.
Maps into a mapping set can always be “transformed down,” but maps out of a mapping set (operators, functionals) cannot. That is why the choice of description matters:

center of mass is a functional \(E^B \to E\), so to get the trajectory of the center of mass we need the motion in the form \(T \to E^B\) and compose: \(T \to E^B \to E\);
velocity is an operator \(E^T \to V^T\), so to get the velocity field we need \(B \to E^T\), compose to get \(B \to V^T\), and transpose twice to get \(T \to V^B\) (the velocity field at each instant).

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Functoriality and naturality

Exponentials are functorial in both variables







Proposition 1 (Covariance in the base (L–R 5.2)) 
Given \(\varphi : Y_1 \to Y_2\), there is a unique \(\varphi^B : Y_1^B \to Y_2^B\) with \[
\varphi^B \ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner \quad \text{for all } g : B \to Y_1 .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. To make a map into \(Y_2^B\), it suffices to make a map \(Y_1^B \times B \to Y_2\); take \(\varphi \circ \mathrm{eval}_1\) and set \(\varphi^B := \ulcorner \varphi\, \mathrm{eval}_1 \urcorner\), so \(\mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B \times 1_B) = \varphi\,\mathrm{eval}_1\). Then \[
\mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B)
= \mathrm{eval}_2(\varphi^B \times 1_B)(\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B)
= \varphi\, \mathrm{eval}_1(\ulcorner g \urcorner \times 1_B) = \varphi g
= \mathrm{eval}_2(\ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner \times 1_B),
\] and the uniqueness clause of the axiom gives \(\varphi^B\ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner\). The argument works verbatim for generalized elements \(g : X \times B \to Y_1\).











Proposition 2 (Contravariance in the exponent (L–R 5.4, 5.5)) 
Given \(\beta : B_2 \to B_1\), there is a unique \(Y^\beta : Y^{B_1} \to Y^{B_2}\) with \[
Y^\beta \ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner g \beta \urcorner, \qquad\text{namely}\qquad Y^\beta = \ulcorner \mathrm{eval}_1 \circ (1 \times \beta) \urcorner .
\] Moreover \(Y^{\beta\alpha} = Y^\alpha Y^\beta\) and \(Y^{1_B} = 1\).










NoteProof






Proof. The construction of \(Y^\beta\) is as in Proposition 1. For the composition law, evaluate both sides on a name: \(Y^\alpha Y^\beta \ulcorner g \urcorner = Y^\alpha\ulcorner g\beta \urcorner = \ulcorner (g\beta)\alpha \urcorner\) and \(Y^{\beta\alpha}\ulcorner g \urcorner = \ulcorner g(\beta\alpha) \urcorner\). These agree by associativity of composition — the proposition is “a higher expression of associativity.”




When \(\beta\) is a monomorphism, \(Y^\beta\) is restriction of maps to a part of the domain.
In the language of last time (cf. L–R Ex. 5.17):

\((-)^B : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{S}\), \(Y \mapsto Y^B\), \(\varphi \mapsto \varphi^B\) is a (covariant) functor,
\(Y^{(-)} : \mathcal{S}^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\), \(B \mapsto Y^B\), \(\beta \mapsto Y^\beta\) is a contravariant functor,
\(- \times B : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{S}\), \(X \mapsto X \times B\), \(\xi \mapsto \xi \times 1_B\) is a functor.



The transpose is a natural bijection
Fix \(B\). For each \(X\) and \(Y\) the axiom gives a bijection \[
\theta_{X,Y} : \mathcal{S}(X \times B,Y) \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \mathcal{S}(X,Y^B), \qquad f \mapsto \ulcorner f \urcorner.
\]







Proposition 3 (Naturality of transposition) 
For \(\xi : X' \to X\) and \(\varphi : Y \to Y'\), \[
\ulcorner f \circ (\xi \times 1_B) \urcorner = \ulcorner f \urcorner \circ \xi,
\qquad
\ulcorner \varphi \circ f \urcorner = \varphi^B \circ \ulcorner f \urcorner.
\] That is, \(\theta\) is a natural isomorphism between the functors \(\mathcal{S}(-\times B,-)\) and \(\mathcal{S}(-,(-)^B)\) from \(\mathcal{S}^{op}\times\mathcal{S}\) to sets.










NoteProof






Proof. The second identity is Proposition 1 for generalized elements. For the first, \(\mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner\xi \times 1_B) = \mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner f \urcorner \times 1_B)(\xi \times 1_B) = f(\xi \times 1_B)\), so \(\ulcorner f \urcorner\xi\) satisfies the defining equation of \(\ulcorner f(\xi\times 1_B) \urcorner\); apply uniqueness.




So the crude “bar” notation of L–R means precisely: a natural isomorphism of hom-functors. Two consequences are worth stating now.
1. Representability. For fixed \(B, Y\), the contravariant functor \(X \mapsto \mathcal{S}(X \times B,Y)\) is isomorphic to \(\mathcal{S}(-,Y^B)\); one says \(Y^B\) represents it. The axiom can be read as: “this functor is representable.” (We will see in a few weeks that this pins \(Y^B\) down up to unique isomorphism — the Yoneda lemma.)
2. Adjunction. Naturality in both variables says that \(-\times B\) is left adjoint to \((-)^B\), written \(- \times B \dashv (-)^B\). This is the formal definition we will meet next week; for now, compare the two universal maps with the product case:









product \(\;Y_0 \times Y_1\)
exponential \(\;Y^B\)




bijection
\(\dfrac{X \to Y_0 \times Y_1}{X \to Y_0,\; X \to Y_1}\)
\(\dfrac{X \to Y^B}{X \times B \to Y}\)


universal map from \(1\) above the bar
projections \(p_0, p_1\)
\(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\)


universal map from \(1\) below the bar
diagonal \(\delta_X\)
\(\eta_X = \ulcorner 1_{X\times B} \urcorner : X \to (X\times B)^B\)


downward process
\(f \mapsto (p_0 f, p_1 f)\)
\(g \mapsto \mathrm{eval}\circ (g \times 1_B)\)


upward process
\(\langle f_0, f_1\rangle = (f_0\times f_1)\,\delta_X\)
\(\ulcorner f \urcorner = f^B \circ \eta_X\)



The last entry is the second naturality identity applied to \(\varphi = f\) and the identity: \(\ulcorner f \urcorner = \ulcorner f \circ 1_{X\times B} \urcorner = f^B\ulcorner 1_{X \times B} \urcorner\). In elements, \(\eta_X(x) = \ulcorner b \mapsto \langle x, b\rangle \urcorner\). (\(\eta\) and \(\mathrm{eval}\) are the unit and counit of the adjunction.)






TipOptional: composition is itself a map (L–R 5.6)





Transposing \(Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1^B \times B \xrightarrow{1 \times \mathrm{eval}} Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{eval}} Y_2\) gives \[
c : Y_2^{Y_1} \times Y_1^B \to Y_2^B, \qquad c(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner, \ulcorner g \urcorner) = \ulcorner \varphi g \urcorner.
\] Transposing once more gives \(Y_2^{Y_1} \to (Y_2^B)^{(Y_1^B)}\), \(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner\mapsto \ulcorner \varphi^B \urcorner\): the functor \((-)^B\) is itself represented by an internal map. The operation that defines a category is internalized.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Power objects
Combine the truth-value axiom with the exponential axiom: \[
\frac{\;1 \longrightarrow 2^B\;}{\;B \longrightarrow 2\;}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\;B \longrightarrow 2\;}{\;\text{part of } B\;}.
\] So the elements of \(2^B\) are names of parts of \(B\) — \(2^B\) is the power set, now as a special case of mapping sets. The evaluation map is membership: if \(\varphi\) is the characteristic map of the part \(i\), then \[
[\, b \in i \,] := \mathrm{eval}(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner, b) = \varphi(b) \in 2 .
\] Contravariant functoriality has a familiar meaning:







Exercise 1 (L–R 5.7) For \(\beta : B_2 \to B_1\), the map \(2^\beta : 2^{B_1} \to 2^{B_2}\) represents taking inverse images along \(\beta\) of parts of \(B_1\). (Use: the inverse image of a part is a pullback, and the characteristic map of a pullback is a composite.)










TipTeaser: Cantor’s theorem without elements





Compare Cantor’s theorem in the cardinals notes. Lawvere’s fixed point theorem, which we will see later, shows: if \(g : B \times B \to Y\) is such that every map \(B \to Y\) is of the form \(g(b_0, -)\), then every \(\tau: Y \to Y\) has a fixed point. Since \(\neg : 2 \to 2\) has no fixed point, no \(B \to 2^B\) can be onto names. The diagonal argument is the bootstrap with \(\delta_B\).

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
The exponential laws
To justify the notation \(Y^B\) we want \(|Y^B| = |Y|^{|B|}\) for finite sets, and more generally the rules of exponent arithmetic as isomorphisms. L–R check each one by constructing explicit inverse maps and testing on elements. With naturality we can do all of them with one lemma.







Lemma 1 (Representability lemma) 
If there are bijections \(\theta_T : \mathcal{S}(T,A) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,A')\) natural in \(T\), then \(a := \theta_A(1_A) : A \to A'\) is an isomorphism (and \(\theta_T = a \circ -\)). The same holds with \(\mathcal{S}(A,T) \cong \mathcal{S}(A',T)\) natural in \(T\).










NoteProof






Proof. For \(h : T \to A\), naturality applied to \(h\) gives \(\theta_T(h) = \theta_T(1_A \circ h) = \theta_A(1_A) \circ h = a h\). Let \(a' := \theta_{A'}^{-1}(1_{A'}) : A' \to A\). Then \(a a' = \theta_{A'}(a') = 1_{A'}\), and \(\theta_A(a' a) = a a' a = a = \theta_A(1_A)\), so \(a'a = 1_A\) since \(\theta_A\) is injective. This is the bootstrap once more: everything is determined by where the identity goes.




So to prove \(A \cong A'\) it suffices to give a natural bijection between maps from an arbitrary \(T\) into \(A\) and into \(A'\) — i.e., to compare generalized elements.







Proposition 4 (Exponential laws (L–R 5.8–5.10)) 
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y^1 &\cong Y, & 1^B &\cong 1, & (Y_0 \times Y_1)^B &\cong Y_0^B \times Y_1^B,\\
Y^{X \times B} &\cong (Y^B)^X, & Y^0 &\cong 1, & Y^{A+B} &\cong Y^A \times Y^B .
\end{aligned}
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Each is a chain of natural bijections, followed by Lemma 1. For example: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{S}(T,(Y^B)^X) &\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times X,Y^B) \cong \mathcal{S}((T \times X) \times B,Y) \\
&\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times (X \times B),Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y^{X\times B}),
\end{aligned}
\] using the associativity isomorphism of products (natural in \(T\)) in the middle. Similarly \[
\mathcal{S}(T,(Y_0\times Y_1)^B) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y_0 \times Y_1)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T \times B,Y_0) \times \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y_1)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y_0^B \times Y_1^B).
\] \(Y^1 \cong Y\) and \(1^B \cong 1\) are the same kind of one-line computation.
The laws involving \(0\) and \(+\) need one more ingredient, which is interesting in its own right.











Theorem 1 (Exponentials force distributivity) 
In any category with finite products, finite sums, and exponentials, \[
T \times 0 \cong 0, \qquad (A + B) \times T \cong A \times T + B \times T .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Now we use the contravariant version of the lemma, natural in the codomain \(Y\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{S}((A+B) \times T,Y) &\cong \mathcal{S}(A+B,Y^T) \cong \mathcal{S}(A,Y^T) \times \mathcal{S}(B,Y^T) \\
&\cong \mathcal{S}(A \times T,Y) \times \mathcal{S}(B\times T,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(A \times T + B \times T,Y).
\end{aligned}
\] Likewise \(\mathcal{S}(0 \times T,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(0,Y^T)\) is a singleton for every \(Y\), so \(0 \times T\) is initial.




Distributivity does not mention exponentials, yet it follows from them (L–R return to this in §7.2): a left adjoint preserves sums, and \(-\times T\) is a left adjoint. With it, \[
\mathcal{S}(T,Y^{A+B}) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times(A+B),Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T\times A,Y) \times \mathcal{S}(T\times B,Y)
\cong \mathcal{S}(T,Y^A \times Y^B),
\] and \(\mathcal{S}(T,Y^0) \cong \mathcal{S}(T \times 0,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(0,Y) \cong \mathcal{S}(T,1)\). This finishes Proposition 4.
Counting. Writing a finite \(B\) as \(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1\) (\(n\) summands), the laws give \(Y^B \cong Y \times \cdots \times Y\), so \(|Y^B| = |Y|^n\). In particular \(|2^B| = 2^{|B|}\).






ImportantMethodological point



L–R verify these isomorphisms by checking on elements \(1 \to Y^B\). That is legitimate in \(\mathcal{S}\) because \(1\) separates mappings — but this axiom fails in most toposes. The argument with generalized elements \(T \to Y^B\) uses only the exponential axiom and therefore works in every cartesian closed category.

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Elementary toposes
We can now collect the axioms into a definition that no longer mentions \(\mathcal{S}\).






NoteDefinition: elementary topos



A category \(\mathcal{E}\) is an elementary topos if

\(\mathcal{E}\) has finite limits (a terminal object and pullbacks suffice);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has exponentials: for all \(B, Y\) an object \(Y^B\) with \(\mathrm{eval}: Y^B \times B \to Y\) as in the axiom (a category with 1 and 2 is called cartesian closed);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has a subobject classifier: an object \(\Omega\) and a map \(\mathrm{true} : 1 \to \Omega\) such that for every mono \(m : A' \rightarrowtail A\) there is a unique \(\chi_m : A \to \Omega\) making \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
A' & \longrightarrow & 1\\
{\scriptstyle m}\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow{\scriptstyle \mathrm{true}}\\
A & \xrightarrow[\ \chi_m\ ]{} & \Omega
\end{array}
\] a pullback.



In \(\mathcal{S}\), \(\Omega = 2\) and condition 3 is L–R’s axiom of membership via truth values, formulated with pullbacks. Conditions 2 and 3 together give power objects \(\Omega^B\), whose elements name parts of \(B\).
Remarkably, what we did not list follows: every elementary topos also has finite colimits (initial object, sums, coequalizers). This is a nontrivial theorem (due to Paré); the distributivity argument above gives a small taste of how much the exponentials carry.

What is special about \(\mathcal{S}\)
\(\mathcal{S}\) is a topos that satisfies further axioms:

\(1\) separates mappings (and \(0 \not\cong 1\)): \(\mathcal{S}\) is well-pointed;
\(\Omega = 2 = 1 + 1\): the topos is Boolean (internal logic is classical);
a natural numbers object (the categorical axiom of infinity);
the axiom of choice: every epimorphism has a section.

These, added to the topos axioms, make up Lawvere’s Elementary Theory of the Category of Sets (ETCS), which L–R summarize in Chapter 6. Comparing with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\): Power Set and Separation are replaced by \(\Omega^B\) and the subobject classifier, Infinity by the natural numbers object, Choice by split epis — and there is no counterpart of Replacement. We take up this comparison in Week 14.


Examples and non-examples

\(\mathcal{S}/X\) (L–R Ex. 5.12): an object is an \(X\)-indexed family \((A_x)_{x\in X}\); exponentials are computed fiberwise, \((Y^B)_x = Y_x^{B_x}\). A topos — “sets varying over a discrete parameter.”
\(G\)-sets for a group \(G\) (Ex. 5.13): \(Y^X\) is the set of all maps \(X \to Y\) with \((g\cdot f)(x) = g\, f(g^{-1}x)\); the inverse is essential. A topos, with \(\Omega = 2\) (trivial action).
\(M\)-sets for a monoid \(M\): the exponential is subtler, and \(\Omega\) is the set of left ideals of \(M\) — e.g. for \(M = (\mathbb{N}, +)\), “sets evolving in discrete time,” \(\Omega\) is infinite. A topos that is not Boolean: here condition 3 holds but \(\Omega \neq 1+1\).
Posets (Ex. 5.14): cartesian closed (\(Y^X\) = monotone maps, ordered pointwise), but not a topos: the identity map from a two-element discrete poset to a two-element chain is mono and epi but not iso, which cannot happen in a topos.
Finite-dimensional vector spaces with \(\times = \oplus\) (Ex. 5.11): not cartesian closed. If \(L(B,Y)\) were an exponential, then \(\dim \mathrm{Hom}(X \oplus B, Y) = (x + b)y\) would equal \(\dim \mathrm{Hom}(X, L(B,Y)) = xby\) for all dimensions. (The correct partner of \(L(B, Y)\) is \(\otimes\), not \(\oplus\).)

title: Mapping Sets and Exponentials
text:
Exercises







Exercise 2 L–R 5.3 and 5.16: functoriality of \((-)^B\), and the inverse maps for \(Y^{X\times B} \cong (Y^B)^X\), checked directly.











Exercise 3 L–R 5.17 (a)–(d): verify that \(\Delta\), \(-\times B\), \((-)^B\), and \(- \times -\) are functors. Then show that the diagonals \(\delta_X\) form a natural transformation from the identity functor to \((-\times-)\circ\Delta\), and that the \(\eta_X\) form one from the identity to \((-\times B)^B\).











Exercise 4 L–R 5.12 (\(\mathcal{S}/X\)) and 5.14 (posets): verify the universal property of the proposed exponentials.











Exercise 5 L–R 5.13 for a group \(G\). Bonus: for a monoid \(M\), show that \(Y^X := \{\)equivariant \(f : M \times X \to Y\}\) with \((m\cdot f)(n, x) = f(nm, x)\) is an exponential in \(M\)-sets.











Exercise 6 Using only arguments in the style of Lemma 1, show that in any cartesian closed category \(A \times (B + C) \cong A \times B + A \times C\) whenever the sums exist, and that any object admitting a map to \(0\) is itself initial.

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Recall two basic facts about cardinalities:

Finite unions of finite sets are finite.
Countable unions of countable sets are countable (using \(\mathsf{AC}\)).

This means it is “hard” to reach the cardinals \(\aleph_0\) and \(\aleph_1\) “from below”: you cannot obtain a set of size \(\aleph_0\) by putting together a few small pieces, and similarly for \(\aleph_1\). The notion of cofinality quantifies “how hard” it is to reach an ordinal from below.
Throughout this section, \({}\alpha\) denotes a limit ordinal (following Kunen, Def. I.13.10, we define cofinality only for limit ordinals).







Definition 1 
A set \(X \subseteq \alpha\) is cofinal in \({}\alpha\) if \[
    \forall \gamma < \alpha \; \exists \xi \in X \;\; \gamma < \xi.
\] Equivalently, \[
    \alpha = \bigcup_{\xi \in X} \xi = \sup X.
\]











Definition 2 
The cofinality of \({}\alpha\) is \[
    \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) = \text{least ordinal } \beta \text{ such that there exists } f: \beta \to \alpha \text{ with } \operatorname{ran}(f) \text{ cofinal in } \alpha.
\] We call such an \(f\) a cofinal map.




We can always assume that a cofinal map \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) is strictly increasing: if necessary, we can “thin it out”.







Lemma 1 
There exists a strictly increasing cofinal map \(g: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be cofinal. Define \(g\) by recursion: \[
    g(\eta) = \max\left\{ f(\eta), \; \sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} \right\}.
\] We have to check that \(g(\eta) < \alpha\). If \(\sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} = \alpha\), then \(g\mid_{\eta}\) would be a cofinal map from \(\eta < \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) into \({}\alpha\) (here we use that \({}\alpha\) is a limit), contradicting the minimality of \(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). By construction, \(g\) is strictly increasing, and \(g(\eta) \geq f(\eta)\) implies that \(g\) is cofinal.











Example 1 


\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega) = \omega\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega + n\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega\cdot\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega \cdot n\)












Proposition 1 
For any limit ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \leq \alpha\),
\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal,
\(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).











NoteProof






Proof. 

The identity map \(\alpha \to \alpha\) is cofinal.
Let \(\beta = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) and suppose \(|\beta| < \beta\). Let \(h: |\beta| \to \beta\) be a bijection and \(f: \beta \to \alpha\) cofinal. Then \(f \circ h: |\beta| \to \alpha\) has the same range as \(f\) and hence is cofinal, contradicting the minimality of \({}\beta\).
By (1), \(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) \leq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). For the other inequality, let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be strictly increasing and cofinal (Lemma 1), and let \(g: \delta \to \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) be cofinal. Then \(f \circ g: \delta \to \alpha\) is cofinal: given \(\gamma < \alpha\), pick \(\eta\) with \(f(\eta) > \gamma\), and \(\zeta < \delta\) with \(g(\zeta) > \eta\). Then \(f(g(\zeta)) > f(\eta) > \gamma\). Hence \(\delta \geq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).








Recall the enumeration of all infinite cardinals by means of the \(\aleph\)-sequence:
\[\begin{equation*}
\aleph_0 = \omega, \quad \aleph_{\alpha+1} = \aleph_\alpha^+, \quad  \aleph_\lambda = \sup \{ \aleph_\xi \colon \xi<\lambda\} \; \text{ for limit } \lambda.
\end{equation*}\]
Here \(\kappa^+\) is the least cardinal \(> \kappa\). Some cardinals are limits of short sequences of smaller cardinals – for example, \[\begin{equation*}
    \aleph_\omega = \lim_n \aleph_n
\end{equation*}\] is uncountable, but a limit of a countable sequence of smaller cardinals.







Definition 3 
Let \({}\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal. \({}\kappa\) is

regular if \(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) = \kappa\),
singular if \(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) < \kappa\).





In other words, a regular cardinal \({}\kappa\) cannot be reached by less than \({}\kappa\)-many steps: \[\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \iff \forall \alpha < \kappa \;  \forall f \;( f: \alpha \to \kappa \;  \to \; \sup_{\xi < \alpha} f(\xi) < \kappa).
\end{equation*}\]







Example 2 


\(\aleph_0\) is regular.
\(\aleph_1\) is regular.
\(\aleph_\omega\) is singular, with \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega) = \omega\), as witnessed by the cofinal sequence \(\aleph_0, \aleph_1, \aleph_2, \ldots \to \aleph_\omega\).





The regularity of \(\aleph_1\) is an instance of a general fact.







Proposition 2 
(\(\mathsf{AC}\)) Every infinite successor cardinal is regular.










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(\delta = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{\alpha+1}) < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\). Then there exists a cofinal \(f: \delta \to \aleph_{\alpha+1}\), so \[
    \aleph_{\alpha+1} = \bigcup_{\gamma < \delta} f(\gamma).
\] Now \(|\delta| < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\), and \(|f(\gamma)| < \aleph_{\alpha+1}\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\). Hence \(|\delta| \leq \aleph_\alpha\) and \(|f(\gamma)| \leq \aleph_\alpha\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\). This implies \[
    |\aleph_{\alpha+1}| = \left|\bigcup_{\gamma<\delta} f(\gamma)\right| \leq \aleph_\alpha \cdot \aleph_\alpha = \aleph_\alpha,
\] a consequence of Hessenberg’s Theorem (see the notes on Cardinals). This is a contradiction.




On the other hand, \[\begin{equation*}
\aleph_\omega,  \aleph_{\omega+\omega}, \aleph_{\aleph_{\omega}}, \aleph_{\aleph_{\aleph_\omega}}, \ldots
\end{equation*}\] are all singular. This follows from the following result, which reduces the cofinality of \(\aleph_\lambda\) to that of its index.







Proposition 3 
If \({}\lambda\) is a limit ordinal, then \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\lambda) = \operatorname{cf}(\lambda)\).










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\leq\)) Let \(f: \gamma \to \lambda\) be cofinal. Then \[
\hat{f}: \gamma \to \aleph_\lambda, \quad \beta \mapsto \aleph_{f(\beta)}
\] is cofinal in \(\aleph_\lambda\): If \(\eta < \aleph_\lambda\), then \(\eta < \aleph_\xi\) for some \(\xi < \lambda\). Pick \(\beta\) with \(f(\beta) > \xi\). Then \(\aleph_{f(\beta)} > \aleph_\xi > \eta\).
(\(\geq\)) Let \(f: \gamma \to \aleph_\lambda\) be cofinal. We turn \(f\) into a cofinal map \(g: \gamma \to \lambda\) by letting \[
    g(\beta) = \text{the } \alpha \text{ such that } |f(\beta)| = \aleph_\alpha
\] (and \(g(\beta) = 0\) if \(f(\beta)\) is finite). Since \(f(\beta) < \aleph_\lambda\), \(g(\beta) < \lambda\). If \(\xi < \lambda\), pick \(\beta\) with \(f(\beta) > \aleph_\xi\). Then \(|f(\beta)| \geq \aleph_\xi\), so \(g(\beta) \geq \xi\). Hence \(g\) is cofinal in \({}\lambda\).




For example, \(\operatorname{cf}(\aleph_{\omega+\omega}) = \operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\).


Cofinality also puts a restriction on the possible values of \(2^\kappa\). To prove this, we need a fundamental inequality between cardinal sums and products. For a family of cardinals \((\kappa_i)_{i\in I}\), let \[
    \sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i = \left|\bigcup_{i \in I} \{i\} \times \kappa_i \right|, \qquad \prod_{i \in I} \kappa_i = \left| \left\{ g \colon g \text{ function}, \; \operatorname{dom}(g) = I, \; \forall i \; g(i) \in \kappa_i \right\}\right|.
\]







Theorem 1 (König’s Theorem) 
(\(\mathsf{AC}\)) Let \((\kappa_i)_{i\in I}\) and \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\) be families of cardinals such that \(\kappa_i < \lambda_i\) for all \(i \in I\). Then \[
    \sum_{i \in I} \kappa_i < \prod_{i\in I} \lambda_i.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The map \((i,\xi) \mapsto g_{i,\xi}\), where \(g_{i,\xi}(i) = \xi+1\) and \(g_{i,\xi}(j) = 0\) for \(j \neq i\), is an injection, so \(\sum \kappa_i \leq \prod \lambda_i\).
Suppose \(f: \bigcup_{i} \{i\}\times \kappa_i \to \prod_i \lambda_i\). We show that \(f\) is not onto. For each \(i \in I\), the set \[
    \{ f(i,\xi)(i) \colon \xi < \kappa_i\} \subseteq \lambda_i
\] has cardinality \(\leq \kappa_i < \lambda_i\), so we can let \(y(i)\) be the least element of \(\lambda_i\) not in this set. Then \(y \in \prod_i \lambda_i\), but \(y \neq f(i,\xi)\) for all \(i, \xi\), since \(y\) and \(f(i,\xi)\) differ at coordinate \(i\).
(The Axiom of Choice is needed to ensure that the sets on both sides are well-orderable, so that their cardinalities are defined; for families of arbitrary sets, one uses \(\mathsf{AC}\) to choose the witnesses \(y(i)\).)











Proposition 4 
If \(\kappa \geq \aleph_0\), then \(\operatorname{cf}(2^\kappa) > \kappa\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(f: \delta \to 2^\kappa\) is cofinal with \(\delta \leq \kappa\), so that \[
    2^\kappa = \bigcup_{\gamma < \delta} f(\gamma).
\] Then \(|f(\gamma)| < 2^\kappa\) for all \(\gamma < \delta\), and by König’s Theorem, \[\begin{align*}
    2^\kappa = \left|\bigcup_{\gamma<\delta} f(\gamma)\right| & \leq \sum_{\gamma < \delta} |f(\gamma)| \\
    & < \prod_{\gamma < \delta} 2^\kappa = (2^\kappa)^\delta = 2^{\kappa \cdot \delta} = 2^\kappa,
\end{align*}\] where the last equality uses \(\delta \leq \kappa\). This is a contradiction.











Corollary 1 
\(2^{\aleph_0} \neq \aleph_\omega\).










NoteProof






Proof. \(\operatorname{cf}(2^{\aleph_0}) > \aleph_0 = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\omega)\).








We have seen that successor cardinals are regular, and that \(\aleph_\lambda\) for “small” limits \({}\lambda\) are singular. This suggests the question:






TipQuestion



Are there regular limit cardinals, i.e. regular cardinals of the form \(\aleph_\lambda\) with \(\lambda\) limit?


If \(\aleph_\lambda\) is a regular limit cardinal, then by Proposition 3 and Proposition 1, \[
    \aleph_\lambda = \operatorname{cf}(\aleph_\lambda) = \operatorname{cf}(\lambda) \leq \lambda,
\] and since always \(\lambda \leq \aleph_\lambda\), we must have \(\aleph_\lambda = \lambda\). So a regular limit cardinal must be very large: it is a fixed point of the \(\aleph\)-function.
This is captured by the notion of inaccessibility.







Definition 4 (Hausdorff 1908, Tarski, Zermelo 1930) 
An uncountable cardinal \(\kappa > \omega\) is

weakly inaccessible if \[\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \; &  \wedge \;  \exists \lambda (\operatorname{lim}(\lambda) \;  \wedge\;  \kappa = \aleph_\lambda)\\
                      (& \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \;  \wedge \;  \forall \alpha < \kappa \; \, \alpha^+ < \kappa)
\end{align*}\]
(strongly) inaccessible if \[\begin{equation*}
  \operatorname{reg}(\kappa) \;  \wedge \;  \forall \alpha < \kappa \;\; 2^{\alpha} < \kappa
\end{equation*}\]





Every strongly inaccessible cardinal is weakly inaccessible, since \(\alpha^+ \leq 2^\alpha\). Under the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis,
  \((\mathsf{GCH}) \quad \forall \alpha \;\;  2^{\aleph_\alpha} = \aleph_{\alpha}^+\)
weakly and strongly inaccessible cardinals coincide.
If \(\kappa\) is (weakly) inaccessible, then \(\kappa = \aleph_\kappa\), as shown above.


The cardinality of \(V_\alpha\) grows rather fast relative to \({}\alpha\). For example,
\[
    |V_{\omega+\alpha}| = \beth_\alpha
\]
where the beth function \(\beth_\alpha\) is defined as \[\begin{gather*}
    \beth_0 = \aleph_0 \\
    \beth_{\alpha+1} = 2^{\beth_\alpha} \\
    \beth_{\lambda} = \sup \{ \beth_\alpha \colon \alpha < \lambda\} \quad \text{ $\lambda$ limit}
\end{gather*}\]
The existence of inaccessible cardinals ensures that the von Neumann hierarchy is “long enough” for \({}\alpha\) to eventually “catch up” with the cardinality of \(V_\alpha\).







Proposition 5 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(|V_\kappa| = \kappa\).










NoteProof






Proof. Since \(\kappa \subseteq V_\kappa\), \(|V_\kappa| \geq \kappa\). For the other inequality, it suffices to show that \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\) for all \(\alpha < \kappa\), since then \(|V_\kappa| = |\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa} V_\alpha| \leq \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa\).
We show \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\) by induction on \(\alpha < \kappa\): if \(|V_\alpha| < \kappa\), then \(|V_{\alpha+1}| = 2^{|V_\alpha|} < \kappa\) since \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible. If \(\lambda < \kappa\) is a limit, then \(V_\lambda\) is a union of \(|\lambda| < \kappa\) many sets, each of size \(< \kappa\), so by regularity of \({}\kappa\), \(|V_\lambda| < \kappa\).




This in turn implies we can bound the cardinality of elements of \(V_\kappa\).







Proposition 6 
Suppose \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible and \(x\subseteq V_\kappa\). Then
\[
    x \in V_\kappa \; \Leftrightarrow \; |x| < \kappa.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x \in V_\kappa\), then \(x \in V_\alpha\) for some \(\alpha < \kappa\), and by transitivity \(x \subseteq V_\alpha\). By the proof of Proposition 5, \(|x| \leq |V_\alpha| < \kappa\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Since \(x \subseteq V_\kappa\), each \(y \in x\) has rank \(< \kappa\). Since \(|x| < \kappa\), by regularity of \({}\kappa\),
\[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{\operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x\} < \kappa
\]
which implies \(x \in V_\kappa\).




We have already seen that for limit \(\alpha > \omega\), \(V_\alpha\) is a model of all \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms except Replacement.







Theorem 2 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify that \(V_\kappa\) satisfies the axiom of Replacement. Suppose \(x \in V_\kappa\) and \(f:x \to V_\kappa\) is a function. Then \(f[x] \subseteq V_\kappa\), and by Proposition 6, \(|f[x]| \leq |x| < \kappa\). Applying the other direction of Proposition 6 to \(f[x]\), we obtain \(f[x] \in V_\kappa\), as desired.




Suppose an inaccessible cardinal exists, and let \({}\kappa\) be the least inaccessible.
It is not hard to verify that
\[
V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \text{``there does not exist an inaccessible cardinal''}.
\]
(You verify that being an inaccessible cardinal is absolute for \(V_\kappa\).) Therefore, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not provable from \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This fact also follows from Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.

title: Cofinality and Inaccessible Cardinals
text:
Recall two basic facts about cardinalities:

Finite unions of finite sets are finite.
Countable unions of countable sets are countable (using \(\mathsf{AC}\)).

This means it is “hard” to reach the cardinals \(\aleph_0\) and \(\aleph_1\) “from below”: you cannot obtain a set of size \(\aleph_0\) by putting together a few small pieces, and similarly for \(\aleph_1\). The notion of cofinality quantifies “how hard” it is to reach an ordinal from below.
Throughout this section, \({}\alpha\) denotes a limit ordinal (following Kunen, Def. I.13.10, we define cofinality only for limit ordinals).







Definition 1 
A set \(X \subseteq \alpha\) is cofinal in \({}\alpha\) if \[
    \forall \gamma < \alpha \; \exists \xi \in X \;\; \gamma < \xi.
\] Equivalently, \[
    \alpha = \bigcup_{\xi \in X} \xi = \sup X.
\]











Definition 2 
The cofinality of \({}\alpha\) is \[
    \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) = \text{least ordinal } \beta \text{ such that there exists } f: \beta \to \alpha \text{ with } \operatorname{ran}(f) \text{ cofinal in } \alpha.
\] We call such an \(f\) a cofinal map.




We can always assume that a cofinal map \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) is strictly increasing: if necessary, we can “thin it out”.







Lemma 1 
There exists a strictly increasing cofinal map \(g: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be cofinal. Define \(g\) by recursion: \[
    g(\eta) = \max\left\{ f(\eta), \; \sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} \right\}.
\] We have to check that \(g(\eta) < \alpha\). If \(\sup\{g(\zeta)+1 \colon \zeta < \eta\} = \alpha\), then \(g\mid_{\eta}\) would be a cofinal map from \(\eta < \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) into \({}\alpha\) (here we use that \({}\alpha\) is a limit), contradicting the minimality of \(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). By construction, \(g\) is strictly increasing, and \(g(\eta) \geq f(\eta)\) implies that \(g\) is cofinal.











Example 1 


\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega) = \omega\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega+\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega + n\)
\(\operatorname{cf}(\omega\cdot\omega) = \omega\), via \(n \mapsto \omega \cdot n\)












Proposition 1 
For any limit ordinal \({}\alpha\),

\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \leq \alpha\),
\(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) is a cardinal,
\(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).











NoteProof






Proof. 

The identity map \(\alpha \to \alpha\) is cofinal.
Let \(\beta = \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) and suppose \(|\beta| < \beta\). Let \(h: |\beta| \to \beta\) be a bijection and \(f: \beta \to \alpha\) cofinal. Then \(f \circ h: |\beta| \to \alpha\) has the same range as \(f\) and hence is cofinal, contradicting the minimality of \({}\beta\).
By (1), \(\operatorname{cf}(\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)) \leq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\). For the other inequality, let \(f: \operatorname{cf}(\alpha) \to \alpha\) be strictly increasing and cofinal (Lemma 1), and let \(g: \delta \to \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\) be cofinal. Then \(f \circ g: \delta \to \alpha\) is cofinal: given \(\gamma < \alpha\), pick \(\eta\) with \(f(\eta) > \gamma\), and \(\zeta < \delta\) with \(g(\zeta) > \eta\). Then \(f(g(\zeta)) > f(\eta) > \gamma\). Hence \(\delta \geq \operatorname{cf}(\alpha)\).
