\]










NoteProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x \in V_\kappa\), then \(x \in V_\alpha\) for some \(\alpha < \kappa\), and by transitivity \(x \subseteq V_\alpha\). By the proof of Proposition 5, \(|x| \leq |V_\alpha| < \kappa\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Since \(x \subseteq V_\kappa\), each \(y \in x\) has rank \(< \kappa\). Since \(|x| < \kappa\), by regularity of \({}\kappa\),
\[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{\operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x\} < \kappa
\]
which implies \(x \in V_\kappa\).




We have already seen that for limit \(\alpha > \omega\), \(V_\alpha\) is a model of all \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) axioms except Replacement.







Theorem 2 
If \({}\kappa\) is strongly inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. We verify that \(V_\kappa\) satisfies the axiom of Replacement. Suppose \(x \in V_\kappa\) and \(f:x \to V_\kappa\) is a function. Then \(f[x] \subseteq V_\kappa\), and by Proposition 6, \(|f[x]| \leq |x| < \kappa\). Applying the other direction of Proposition 6 to \(f[x]\), we obtain \(f[x] \in V_\kappa\), as desired.




Suppose an inaccessible cardinal exists, and let \({}\kappa\) be the least inaccessible.
It is not hard to verify that
\[
V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \text{``there does not exist an inaccessible cardinal''}.
\]
(You verify that being an inaccessible cardinal is absolute for \(V_\kappa\).) Therefore, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not provable from \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This fact also follows from Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text: These notes accompany Lecture 3. They expand the handwritten notes and follow Kunen, The Foundations of Mathematics, §0.4 and §I.1–I.6. Where Lecture 2 ended — Hilbert’s program — is where we begin.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
section: From Hilbert’s program to a working foundation
text:
From Hilbert’s program to a working foundation
Hilbert’s response to the foundational crisis was formalism: not the claim that mathematics is a meaningless game with symbols, but a method. Take a mathematical theory, write its axioms in a formal language, and study its formal proof-structure with modest, uncontroversial means. This method forces a distinction that will organize everything that follows.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
Metatheory and object theory
Formalism introduces a split between two levels of discourse.

The two levels








Object theory (formal theory)
Metatheory




Example
a theory of arithmetic, or ZFC itself
our reasoning about that theory


Status
a combinatorial object: sets of symbols, strings, rules
ordinary mathematical reasoning


Language
a fixed formal language, e.g. first-order logic
informal natural language


“Proof”
a finite symbolic derivation
an intuitively convincing argument




The object theory is formalized
To say the object theory is formalized means two things:

its axioms are expressed in a formal language (for us, first-order logic with ∈);
its theorems are deduced in a purely symbolic fashion — as Kleene put it, like a list of chess moves written in chess notation. Whether a string is a correct proof is decided by inspecting symbols, not by understanding meaning.

A consequence Hilbert exploited: once proofs are finite strings manipulated by explicit rules, the combinatorics of proof becomes essentially elementary arithmetic. Reasoning about proofs is reasoning about finite syntactic objects.


Reasoning in the metatheory
The metatheory is where we actually work when we prove things about the formal system. That reasoning is:

informal — carried out in natural language;
intuitively clear and convincing — it must persuade without itself being formalized;
finitistic — close to elementary number theory. We do not treat infinite totalities as completed wholes unless they can be clearly and explicitly specified. In flavour this is the intuitionist / constructivist standpoint: an existence claim should come with a construction.



A finitistic statement, and a non-statement
Consider the claim
\[
P \text{ and } \mathbb{N}\setminus P \text{ are both infinite,}
\qquad P = \{\text{primes}\}.
\]
This is a statement involving completed infinite sets (i.e. it is a statement about the natural numbers as a whole). But it can be rewritten finitistically:

For every natural number \(n > 1\) there is a composite number \(c\) with \(n < c \le 2n\), and a prime \(p\) with \(n < p \le n! + 1\).

Both witnesses are bounded (and even can be explicitely defined). This is the kind of fact the metatheory is entitled to assert.
Contrast this with
\[
|\mathbb{R}| = |\mathbb{C}|,
\]
which is meaningless in the metatheory — it is a statement about the cardinality of uncountable sets, with no finitistic content. It only makes sense inside an object theory such as ZFC.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
section: The foundational loop: formalizing the metatheory
text:
The foundational loop: formalizing the metatheory

For a foundational theory such as ZFC, the formal (object) theory should be strong enough to formalize its own metatheory. Otherwise the reasoning we use to study ZFC would sit outside the foundation ZFC claims to provide.

This motivates a thesis about ZFC — a property we would want a foundation to have:

Thesis. Every finitistic fact can be formalized and proved within ZFC.

Making this precise takes care, because most everyday mathematical statements are not literally in the language of ZFC. For instance
\[
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x^{3}\cdot x^{5} = x^{8}\bigr)
\]
uses \(\mathbb{R}\), multiplication, and exponentiation — none of which are primitive symbols of a language whose only non-logical symbol is ∈. Such statements enter ZFC through codings / representations.

Example: an arithmetic fact and its formal shadow
“\(2 + 8 = 10\)” is a fact of the metatheory. Inside ZFC we find:

a representation of each natural number as a specific set — write \(\ulcorner 2 \urcorner\), \(\ulcorner 8 \urcorner\), \(\ulcorner 10 \urcorner\);
a defined binary function symbol \(+\) for addition of such representations;

and then we can prove
\[
\mathrm{ZFC} \;\vdash\; \ulcorner 2 \urcorner + \ulcorner 8 \urcorner
= \ulcorner 10 \urcorner .
\]
The metatheoretic fact and its formal counterpart are different objects; the thesis says the second always tracks the first.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
ZFC as a foundational theory
The claim that ZFC founds mathematics rests on two theses:

All abstract mathematical concepts are set-theoretical.
All concrete mathematical objects are specific sets.

If one does not accept formalism, the “are” can be weakened to “have set-theoretical representations.”

Everything reduces to sets.


Example: what a function is
\[
\text{function} \;\cong\; \text{graph} \;\cong\;
\text{a set of ordered pairs } f \text{ with }
\forall x, y, z\,\bigl((x,y)\in f \wedge (x,z)\in f \rightarrow y = z\bigr).
\]
This pushes the question back to ordered pairs, which are themselves described as special kinds of sets — the standard choice being
\[
(x, y) := \bigl\{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\bigr\},
\]
for which one verifies \((x,y) = (x',y') \rightarrow (x = x' \wedge y = y')\).


The special nature of the ZFC axioms
Kunen distinguishes axioms used as statements of faith (obviously true facts, as the Greeks viewed Euclid’s postulates) from definitional axioms (merely delimiting a useful class of structures, as with the group axioms).
You can read the ZFC axioms in the first sense: To a Platonist, these might appear as obviously true facts. But we have seen that an all too careless treatment of the notion of set can lead to contradictions. However, one can, independent of the ontological status of the axioms, read ZFC as the theory of everything: one postulates the ZFC axioms once and for all, and every other axiom system — groups, rings, topological spaces — is defined inside it.


What we will do

The basic level. State the axioms and interpret them; work out what exactly the representations of \(3\) and of \(\mathbb{R}\) are. (Following von Neumann, \(0 = \varnothing\), \(1 = \{\varnothing\}\), \(2 = \{0,1\}\), \(3 = \{0,1,2\}\), …, \(\mathbb{N} = \omega\); and \(\mathbb{R}\) via Dedekind cuts.)
The advanced level. Draw out the consequences of the axioms for uncountable sets.

title: ZFC as a Foundational Theory
text:
The axioms of ZFC
The language is first-order logic with a single binary relation symbol ∈ (and equality). There is one sort of variable: everything ranges over sets. In the Union and Replacement axioms below, the capital letters \(A, Y,
\mathcal{F}, B\) are still just set variables — the capitals only aid reading.
Convention. Every axiom is understood to be universally quantified over its free variables (\(\forall x\,\forall y\,\dots\)).


Axiom 0 — Set Existence

\(\exists x\,(x = x)\)

Axiom 1 — Extensionality

\(\forall z\,(z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \;\rightarrow\; x = y\)


A set is determined by its members.

Axiom 2 — Foundation

\(\exists y\,(y \in x) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists y\,\bigl(y \in x \wedge \neg\exists z\,(z \in x \wedge z \in y)\bigr)\)


Every nonempty set has an ∈-minimal element; no infinite descending ∈-chains.

Axiom 3 — Comprehension (Separation) — scheme

For each formula \(\varphi\) with \(y\) not free: \(\exists y\,\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge
\varphi(x)\bigr)\)


Subsets are carved out of a set \(v\) that already exists — the restriction to \(x \in v\) is what defuses Russell’s paradox (there is no universal set). There is one axiom per formula, so this is infinitely many axioms; that is harmless in the metatheory, since “being a formula” is a finitistically decidable property.

Axiom 4 — Pairing

\(\exists z\,(x \in z \wedge y \in z)\)

Axiom 5 — Union

\(\exists A\,\forall Y\,\forall x\,
\bigl(x \in Y \wedge Y \in \mathcal{F} \;\rightarrow\; x \in A\bigr)\)

Axiom 6 — Replacement — scheme

For each formula \(\varphi\) with \(B\) not free: \(\forall x \in A\;\exists! y\,\varphi(x, y) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists B\,\forall x \in A\;\exists y \in B\;\varphi(x, y)\)


The image of a set under a definable class function is a set. Here \(\exists! y\,\varphi(x,y)\) abbreviates \(\exists y\,\bigl(\varphi(x,y) \wedge \forall z\,(\varphi(x,z) \rightarrow
y = z)\bigr)\). Again a scheme, and again finitistically unproblematic.




Some defined symbols
On the basis of Axioms 1, 3, 4, 5 we abbreviate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x \subseteq y \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \in x \rightarrow z \in y)\\[2pt]
x = \varnothing \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \notin x)\\[2pt]
y = S(x) \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow z \in x \vee z = x)
     \qquad\bigl(\,y = x \cup \{x\}\,\bigr)\\[2pt]
y = v \cap w \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge x \in w)\\[2pt]
\mathrm{SING}(x) \;&:\Longleftrightarrow\; \exists y \in x\;\forall z \in x\,(z = y)
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining axioms are easier to state with these in hand.


Axiom 7 — Infinity

\(\exists x\,\bigl(\varnothing \in x \wedge \forall y \in x\,(S(y) \in x)\bigr)\)


There is a set containing \(\varnothing\) and closed under \(y \mapsto y \cup
\{y\}\). Here “\(\varnothing \in x\)” abbreviates \(\exists y\,(y = \varnothing
\wedge y \in x)\), and “\(S(y) \in x\)” abbreviates \(\exists z\,(z = S(y) \wedge
z \in x)\).

Axiom 8 — Power Set

\(\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \subseteq x \rightarrow z \in y)\)

Axiom 9 — Choice (AC)

\(\varnothing \notin F \wedge \forall x \in F\;\forall y \in F\,
(x \neq y \rightarrow x \cap y = \varnothing) \;\rightarrow\;
\exists C\;\forall x \in F\;\mathrm{SING}(C \cap x)\)


For a family \(F\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty sets there is a set \(C\) meeting each member in exactly one point.





Named subsystems







System
Axioms




ZFC
1–9


ZF
1–8 (no Choice)


ZC
ZFC without Replacement (6)


Z
ZF without Replacement (6)



Other important subsystems:

\(X^{-}\) — drop Foundation (2);
\(X{-}\mathrm{P}\) — drop Power Set (8);
\(X{-}\mathrm{Inf}\) — drop Infinity (7).

Most of elementary mathematics can be carried out in \(\mathrm{ZC}^{-}\). A minimal working fragment is Basic Set Theory:
\[
\mathrm{BST} \;=\; \text{Axioms } 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \;+\; (6 \vee 8).
\]

title: Ordinals
text: We work in ZFC, but — as noted below — we deliberately avoid using Foundation, so that “being an ordinal” does real work.

title: Ordinals
text:
Why count past \(\mathbb{N}\)?
Cantor was led to the transfinite by a concrete problem. Given \(A \subseteq
\mathbb{R}\), its derivative is the set of its limit points,
\[
A' = \{\, x \in A : x \text{ is a limit point of } A \,\}.
\]
Iterating gives a descending chain \(A \supseteq A' \supseteq A'' \supseteq
\cdots\), and one can take a “limit” \(A^{(\infty)} = \bigcap_n A^{(n)}\). But \(A^{(\infty)}\) may still have isolated points, so the process continues: \(A^{(\infty)} \supsetneq (A^{(\infty)})' \supsetneq \cdots\). To index the stages we need numbers beyond the natural numbers:
\[
0, 1, 2, \dots, \omega, \omega+1, \omega+2, \dots, \omega+\omega, \dots,
\omega\cdot\omega, \dots
\]
Making “keep counting, even through limit stages” precise is exactly what the ordinals accomplish. The concept they rest on is the well-order.

title: Ordinals
text:
Well-founded relations
Throughout, \(R\) is a relation on a set \(A\), and for \(X \subseteq A\) we write \(R\restriction X = \{\langle x,y\rangle \in R : x, y \in X\}\).


\(y\) is \(R\)-minimal in \(X\):

\(y \in X\) and \(\neg\exists z\,(z \in X \wedge z \mathbin{R} y)\) — nothing in \(X\) is \(R\)-below \(y\).

\(R\) is well-founded on \(A\):

every nonempty \(X \subseteq A\) has an \(R\)-minimal element: \[
\forall X\,\bigl(\varnothing \neq X \subseteq A \;\rightarrow\;
\exists y \in X\;\forall z \in X\;\neg(z \mathbin{R} y)\bigr).
\]



Two basic facts:

The Axiom of Foundation says exactly that \(\in\) is well-founded on every set. We will not assume this below.
If \(A\) is finite, then \(R\) is well-founded on \(A\) iff \(R\) has no cycles \(a_0 \mathbin{R} a_1 \mathbin{R} \cdots \mathbin{R} a_n \mathbin{R} a_0\) on \(A\). (For infinite \(A\) this fails: the usual \(<\) on \(\mathbb{Q}\) is acyclic but not well-founded.)

Well-foundedness is the “no infinite descent” condition; it is what makes proof by induction and definition by recursion possible.

title: Ordinals
text:
Well-orders


Definition. \(R\) is a well-order (WO) on \(A\):

\(R\) totally orders \(A\) strictly and \(R\) is well-founded on \(A\).



Equivalently: a strict total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element. (In a total order an \(R\)-minimal element of \(X\) is automatically the \(R\)-least element of \(X\).)
Examples.

\((\mathbb{N}, <)\) is a well-order — this is the least number principle.
\(\bigl(\{\,1 - 2^{-n} : n \in \mathbb{N}\,\},\,<\bigr)\) is a well-order.
\(\bigl(\{\,m - 2^{-n} : m, n \geq 1\,\},\,<\bigr)\) is a well-order (a copy of \(\mathbb{N}\) followed by another copy, then another, …).
\((\mathbb{Q}, <)\), \((\mathbb{R}, <)\), \((\mathbb{Z}, <)\) are not WOs.


Well-orders are rigid
Orders are compared by embeddings: \(f : (A, <_A) \to (B, <_B)\) with \(x <_A y \leftrightarrow f(x) <_B f(y)\). An isomorphism is a bijective embedding; \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) have nontrivial automorphisms (\(z \mapsto
z+1\)). Well-orders do not.

Proposition. Let \((A, <)\) be a well-order and \(f : A \to A\) a self-embedding. Then \(x \leq f(x)\) for all \(x \in A\).

Proof. If \(\{x \in A : f(x) < x\} \neq \varnothing\), it has a least element \(z\). Then \(f(z) < z\), and applying the embedding \(f\bigl(f(z)\bigr) < f(z)\) — so \(f(z)\) is a smaller element of the set, contradicting minimality of \(z\). \(\square\)

Corollary. The only automorphism of a well-order is the identity.

Proof. If \(f\) is an automorphism, both \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are self-embeddings, so \(x \leq f(x)\) and \(x \leq f^{-1}(x)\); the latter gives \(f(x) \leq x\). \(\square\)
For \(b \in A\), the initial segment below \(b\) is
\[
A_{<b} \;:=\; \{\, a \in A : a < b \,\}.
\]

Corollary. No well-order is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself.

Proof. Suppose \(f : A \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } A_{<b}\). Then \(f(x) < b\) for every \(x\), in particular \(f(b) < b\) — contradicting the Proposition. \(\square\)

title: Ordinals
text:
Ordinal numbers
Cantor defined an ordinal as an isomorphism class of well-orders (an “order type”). von Neumann gave a canonical representative of each class: a specific set on which \(\in\) is the ordering. For instance
\[
3 = \bigl\{\, \varnothing,\ \{\varnothing\},\ \{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}
\,\bigr\}
\]
is a \(3\)-element set well-ordered by \(\in\).


Definition. A set \(A\) is transitive:

\(\forall x \in A\;(x \subseteq A)\) — every element is also a subset. (A transitive set cannot “hide” members inside its members.)

Definition (von Neumann). A set \(z\) is an ordinal, \(\operatorname{Ord}(z)\):

\(z\) is transitive and well-ordered by \(\in\).




We do not assume Foundation here. If we did, “well-ordered by \(\in\)” could be weakened to “linearly ordered by \(\in\)”, since well-foundedness would come for free. 



Proposition 1. If \(\operatorname{Ord}(\alpha)\) and \(x \in \alpha\), then \(\operatorname{Ord}(x)\). (Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal.)

Proof. Since \(\alpha\) is transitive, \(x \subseteq \alpha\), so \(\in\) well-orders \(x\) (a subset of a well-order is well-ordered). It remains to show \(x\) is a transitive set. Let \(y \in z \in x\). Then \(z \in \alpha\) (as \(x \subseteq
\alpha\)), so \(y \in \alpha\) (as \(z \subseteq \alpha\)). Now \(x, y \in \alpha\) and \(\in\) is a total order on \(\alpha\), so
\[
y \in x \quad\vee\quad x \in y \quad\vee\quad x = y.
\]
If \(x = y\) then \(x \in z \in x\); if \(x \in y\) then \(x \in y \in z \in x\) — both are \(\in\)-cycles in \(\alpha\), impossible since \(\in\) is well-founded on \(\alpha\). Hence \(y \in x\). \(\square\)
This suggests ordering ordinals by
\[
\alpha < \beta \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad \alpha \in \beta,
\]
and Proposition 1 gives, for every ordinal,
\[
\alpha \;=\; \{\, \beta : \beta < \alpha \,\}
\]
— an ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals.

title: Ordinals
text:
The well-ordering of the ordinals

Proposition 2. For ordinals \(\alpha, \beta\): \(\quad\alpha < \beta \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \alpha \subsetneq \beta\).

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) \(\alpha \in \beta\) and \(\beta\) transitive give \(\alpha
\subseteq \beta\); properly, since \(\alpha \notin \alpha\) (well-foundedness) while \(\alpha \in \beta\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) We prove the stronger statement
\[
\operatorname{trans}(a) \;\wedge\; a \subsetneq \beta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Ord}(a) \;\wedge\; a \in \beta.
\]
If \(a \subsetneq \beta\) then \(a\) is linearly ordered by \(\in\) (subset of \(\beta\)); being also transitive, \(a\) is an ordinal. For \(a \in \beta\): since \(\beta
\setminus a \neq \varnothing\), pick \(\gamma\) \(\in\)-minimal in \(\beta \setminus a\). We claim \(\gamma = a\).

\(\gamma \subseteq a\): if \(g \in \gamma\) then \(g \notin \beta \setminus a\) by minimality, and \(g \in \beta\) (transitivity of \(\beta\)), so \(g \in a\).
\(a \subseteq \gamma\): let \(x \in a\). Then \(x \in \beta\), so by trichotomy in \(\beta\), \(x \in \gamma \vee \gamma \in x \vee x = \gamma\). The last two force \(\gamma \in a\) (transitivity of \(a\), resp. directly), contradicting \(\gamma
\notin a\). So \(x \in \gamma\).

Hence \(a = \gamma \in \beta\). \(\square\)
Write \(ON = \{\, x : \operatorname{Ord}(x) \,\}\) for the collection of all ordinals.

Theorem. \(ON\) is well-ordered by \(<\) (\(=\in\)).
Since \(ON\) is not a set (next result), this is shorthand for a list of ZFC theorems: \(\in\) on the ordinals is (1) transitive, (2) irreflexive, (3) trichotomous, and (4) well-founded — every nonempty set of ordinals has an \(\in\)-least member.

Proof.

Transitive: \(\alpha < \beta < \gamma\) means \(\alpha \in \beta \in \gamma\); \(\gamma\) transitive gives \(\alpha \in \gamma\).
Irreflexive: \(\alpha \in \alpha\) would be an \(\in\)-cycle in \(\alpha\), contradicting well-foundedness of \(\in\) on \(\alpha\).
Trichotomy: first a lemma.

Lemma. \(\alpha \cap \beta\) is an ordinal.
It is transitive (an intersection of transitive sets is transitive) and well-ordered by \(\in\) (a subset of \(\alpha\)).

Let \(\gamma = \alpha \cap \beta\), so \(\gamma \subseteq \alpha\) and \(\gamma
\subseteq \beta\). By Proposition 2, \(\gamma \in \alpha\) or \(\gamma = \alpha\), and likewise for \(\beta\). If \(\gamma \in \alpha\) and \(\gamma \in \beta\) then \(\gamma \in \alpha \cap \beta = \gamma\), impossible. So \(\gamma = \alpha\) or \(\gamma = \beta\); that is \(\alpha \subseteq \beta\) or \(\beta \subseteq \alpha\), hence (Proposition 2) \(\alpha \leq \beta\) or \(\beta \leq \alpha\).
Well-founded: let \(A \neq \varnothing\) be a set of ordinals and \(\alpha \in
A\). If \(\alpha\) is \(\in\)-least, done. Otherwise \(\alpha \cap A = \{\beta \in A
: \beta < \alpha\}\) is a nonempty subset of \(\alpha\), so it has an \(\in\)-least element (since \(\in\) well-orders \(\alpha\)) — and that is \(\in\)-least in \(A\). \(\square\)


Burali-Forti. \(ON\) is a proper class: no set contains all the ordinals.

Proof. If every ordinal were in a set \(X\), then \(ON = \{y \in X :
\operatorname{Ord}(y)\}\) would be a set. It is transitive (Proposition 1) and well-ordered by \(\in\) (Theorem), hence an ordinal, hence \(ON \in ON\) — contradicting irreflexivity. (This needs no Foundation: ordinals are by definition strictly ordered by \(\in\).) \(\square\)
Working in Cantor’s naive set theory, Burali-Forti (1897) put together “the well-ordering of all well-orderings” to get a well-ordering strictly longer than every well-ordering, including itself.

title: Ordinals
text:
The natural numbers, again
Recall \(\omega\) was introduced (Axiom of Infinity) as the smallest inductive set — the smallest set containing \(\varnothing\) and closed under the successor
\[
S(x) = x \cup \{x\}.
\]

Proposition 3. If \(\operatorname{Ord}(\alpha)\) then \(\operatorname{Ord}\bigl(
S(\alpha)\bigr)\), and for every ordinal \(\gamma\), \(\quad\gamma < S(\alpha) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \gamma \leq \alpha\).

Proof (sketch). \(S(\alpha) = \alpha \cup \{\alpha\}\) is transitive: its members are the members of \(\alpha\) (each \(\subseteq \alpha \subseteq S(\alpha)\)) and \(\alpha\) itself (\(\subseteq S(\alpha)\)). It is well-ordered by \(\in\): it is \(\alpha\) with one new top element. The equivalence is then immediate from \(\gamma \in \alpha \cup \{\alpha\}\). \(\square\)


\(\alpha\) is a successor

\(\alpha = S(\beta)\) for some ordinal \(\beta\).

\(\alpha\) is a limit

\(\alpha \neq 0\) and \(\alpha\) is not a successor. Equivalently: \(\alpha \neq 0\) and \(\forall \beta < \alpha\;(S(\beta) < \alpha)\).

\(\alpha\) is finite (a natural number)

every \(\beta \leq \alpha\) is either \(0\) or a successor.




Proposition 4. If \(\alpha\) is finite, so is \(S(\alpha)\).

Now consider the class \(X = \{\, x : x \text{ is a finite ordinal} \,\}\). It contains \(0\) and is closed under \(S\) (Proposition 4) — it is inductive. Since \(\omega\) is the smallest inductive set, \(\omega \subseteq X\): every element of \(\omega\) is a finite ordinal.
Claim: there is no finite ordinal outside \(\omega\). Suppose \(n \in X
\setminus \omega\). (We cannot apply the least-element principle to \(X \setminus
\omega\) directly — it might be a proper class.) But \(S(n) \setminus \omega\) is a set (a subset of the ordinal \(S(n)\)), nonempty (\(n\) is in it), and consists of finite ordinals. So it has an \(\in\)-least element \(k\).

\(k \neq 0\), since \(0 \in \omega\).
So \(k\) is a successor, \(k = S(j)\). Then \(j \in k\), so by leastness \(j \notin
S(n) \setminus \omega\); but \(j \in S(n)\), so \(j \in \omega\). Since \(\omega\) is closed under \(S\), \(k = S(j) \in \omega\) — contradicting \(k \notin \omega\).

So \(X \setminus \omega = \varnothing\). \(\square\)

Proposition 5. Every set \(X\) that is an initial segment of \(ON\) — i.e. \(\forall \beta \in X\;\forall \alpha < \beta\;(\alpha \in X)\) — is an ordinal.

Proof. \(X\) is well-ordered by \(\in\) (Theorem). The initial-segment condition says \(\alpha \in \beta \in X \Rightarrow \alpha \in X\), i.e. \(X\) is transitive. \(\square\)

Corollary. \(\omega\) is an ordinal.

Proof. By the Claim, \(\omega\) is a set of ordinals; and it is an initial segment of \(ON\) (if \(\beta \in \omega\) and \(\alpha < \beta\) then \(\alpha\) is a finite ordinal, and \(\alpha \in \omega\) because every element of a finite ordinal is a finite ordinal, hence in \(\omega\)). Apply Proposition 5. \(\square\)

Corollary. \(\omega\) is the least limit ordinal.

Proof. \(\omega \neq 0\), and \(\omega\) is not a successor (if \(\omega = S(n)\) then \(n \in \omega\) and \(\omega = S(n) \in \omega\)). So \(\omega\) is a limit. Every smaller ordinal is a finite ordinal, hence \(0\) or a successor — not a limit. \(\square\)
We can keep going:
\[
\omega,\ \ S(\omega) = \omega+1,\ \ \omega+2,\ \dots,\ \
\underbrace{\omega+\omega}_{\omega\cdot 2},\ \dots,\ \omega\cdot\omega,\ \dots,\
\omega^{\omega},\ \dots,\ \omega^{\omega^{\omega}},\ \dots,\ \varepsilon_0,\ \dots
\]
(Ordinal \(+\), \(\cdot\), and exponentiation are defined by transfinite recursion later.) Every ordinal displayed here is still a countable set; the supremum of all countable ordinals is \(\omega_1\), the first uncountable ordinal.

title: Ordinals
text:
Representing well-orders as ordinals
The point of the von Neumann definition: each well-order should have exactly one ordinal representative.
We have already shown, for ordinals:

no ordinal is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself;
the only automorphism of an ordinal is the identity.

By trichotomy, (1) gives uniqueness: if \(\alpha \cong \beta\) then \(\alpha =
\beta\). (If \(\alpha < \beta\) then \(\alpha = \beta_{<\alpha}\) is a proper initial segment of \(\beta\), so \(\alpha \cong \beta\) would violate (1).)

Representation Theorem for WOs. If \(R\) well-orders \(A\), then there is a unique ordinal \(\alpha\) with \((A, R) \cong (\alpha, \in)\). The isomorphism is unique.
\(\alpha\) is called the order type of \((A, R)\), written \(\operatorname{type}
(A, R)\).

Proof. Uniqueness of \(\alpha\) is the remark above; uniqueness of the isomorphism follows from (2). For existence:
For \(a \in A\) put \(A_{<a} = \{x \in A : x \mathbin{R} a\}\); it is well-ordered by \(R\). Call \(a\) good if \((A_{<a}, R) \cong (\xi, \in)\) for some ordinal \(\xi\) — by uniqueness this \(\xi\) and the isomorphism \(h_a\) are then determined. Let
\[
G = \{\, a \in A : a \text{ is good} \,\}.
\]
By Replacement, \(f : G \to ON\), \(f(a) =\) the unique ordinal \(\cong (A_{<a}, R)\), is a function.
Observation. For \(a \in G\) and \(c \mathbin{R} a\): \(c \in G\), \(h_c = h_a
\restriction A_{<c}\), and \(f(c) = h_a(c)\). In particular \(G\) is an initial segment of \(A\), and \(f\) is order-preserving: \(a \mathbin{R} b \Rightarrow f(a) =
h_b(a) \in f(b)\), i.e. \(f(a) < f(b)\).
\(\operatorname{ran}(f)\) is an initial segment of \(ON\). If \(\xi = f(a) =
\operatorname{ran}(h_a)\) and \(\eta < \xi\), then \(\eta = h_a(b)\) for some \(b
\mathbin{R} a\), and \(h_a(b) = f(b)\), so \(\eta \in \operatorname{ran}(f)\).
By Proposition 5, \(\alpha := \operatorname{ran}(f)\) is an ordinal, and \(f : G
\xrightarrow{\cong} \alpha\).
Finally \(G = A\). If not, let \(a\) be \(R\)-minimal in \(A \setminus G\). Since \(G\) is an initial segment of \(A\), \(A_{<a} = G\), so \((A_{<a}, R) \cong (\alpha, \in)\) — making \(a\) good, a contradiction. \(\square\)

Looking ahead: transfinite induction
The existence proof quietly used a “least counterexample” argument on a well-order. Its systematic form, valid on \(ON\) itself:

Transfinite Induction. Let \(P\) be a property of ordinals. If

\(P(0)\);
\(P(\alpha) \Rightarrow P\bigl(S(\alpha)\bigr)\) for all \(\alpha\);
for every limit \(\lambda\): \(\bigl(\forall \beta < \lambda\; P(\beta)\bigr)
\Rightarrow P(\lambda)\);

then \(P(\alpha)\) for all ordinals \(\alpha\).

Informally: a least \(\alpha\) with \(\neg P(\alpha)\) would have to be \(0\), a successor, or a limit, and each case is excluded. Turning this — and the matching recursion principle — into theorems (given that \(ON\) is a proper class) is the next topic.

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
Last time we arrived at the definition of an elementary topos: a category with finite limits, exponentials, and a subobject classifier \(\true : 1 \to \Omega\). The category \(\mathcal{S}\) of abstract sets is one example. Today we look at many others. The guiding question is:

Which of the extra properties of \(\mathcal{S}\) survive in a given topos?

The answer shows that the topos axioms capture a very general notion of “set” — sets that vary, move, carry symmetry, or are only locally defined — and that the classical features of \(\mathcal{S}\) are genuinely additional axioms.

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
What is special about \(\mathcal{S}\) [≈ 5 min]
Recall the properties of \(\mathcal{S}\) that go beyond the topos axioms. For a topos \(\mathcal{E}\):


Well-pointed

\(0 \not\cong 1\), and \(1\) separates maps: if \(f \neq g : A \to B\), there is \(a : 1 \to A\) with \(fa \neq ga\).

Boolean

Every part has a complement; equivalently \([\true, \mathrm{false}] : 1 + 1 \to \Omega\) is an isomorphism.

Two-valued

\(\Omega\) has exactly two elements \(1 \to \Omega\) (equivalently, \(1\) has exactly two parts, \(0\) and \(1\)).

Natural numbers object

An object \(\mathbb{N}\) with \(0 : 1 \to \mathbb{N}\), \(s : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}\) such that for every \(x_0 : 1 \to X\), \(f : X \to X\) there is a unique \(h : \mathbb{N}\to X\) with \(h0 = x_0\) and \(hs = fh\).

Choice

Every epimorphism has a section.



“Two-valued” was not on our list last time. It is weaker than Boolean, and the examples below show that the two notions really differ.
In any topos, the parts of an object \(X\) form a lattice \(\Sub(X)\) (intersections are pullbacks, unions are images of sums). Each part \(A\) has a pseudo-complement \(\neg A\), the largest part disjoint from \(A\), and \(\Sub(X)\) is a Heyting algebra. Booleanness says \(A \vee \neg A = X\) for all parts \(A\), i.e. the internal logic satisfies excluded middle.
Two classical theorems connect the properties. We state them without proof (see Goldblatt, Topoi, or Mac Lane–Moerdijk).







Theorem 1 (Two roads to classical logic) 
Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a topos.

If \(\mathcal{E}\) is well-pointed, then \(\mathcal{E}\) is Boolean (and two-valued).
(Diaconescu) If every epimorphism in \(\mathcal{E}\) splits, then \(\mathcal{E}\) is Boolean.






Booleanness is the hinge. A topos that fails excluded middle fails both well-pointedness and choice. In \(\mathcal{S}\), the classicality of logic is not a separate assumption; it is forced by choice alone, and also by well-pointedness alone.

Part 2 is the categorical form of a fact you may know from set theory: over a constructive base theory, \(\mathsf{AC}\) implies the law of excluded middle.

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
The easy ones [≈ 7 min]

Finite sets
\(\FinSet\), the full subcategory of finite sets, is a topos: finite limits of finite sets are finite, \(Y^B\) is finite, and \(\Omega = 2\). It is well-pointed, Boolean, and satisfies choice (without any appeal to \(\mathsf{AC}\): a surjection between finite sets has a section by induction).
But it has no natural numbers object (Exercise 1). The axiom of infinity is not part of being a topos.


The trivial topos
The category \(\mathbf{1}\) with one object and one arrow is a topos: its single object is terminal, initial, \(\Omega\), and every exponential. Here \(0 \cong 1\). Every statement is “true” — which is why nondegeneracy \(0 \not\cong 1\) appears in the definition of well-pointedness.


Slices: sets over \(X\)
We met \(\mathcal{S}/X\) last time: an object is a map \(\alpha : A \to X\), i.e. an \(X\)-indexed family of sets \(A_x = \alpha^{-1}(x)\), and everything is computed fiberwise: \[
(A \times_X B)_x = A_x \times B_x, \qquad (Y^B)_x = Y_x^{B_x}, \qquad \Omega = (X \times 2 \to X), \quad \Omega_x = 2 .
\]

Terminal object: \(1_X : X \to X\), one point in every fiber.
Elements \(1 \to A\) are sections of \(\alpha\): a choice of one point in every fiber.
Not well-pointed (for \(|X| \ge 2\)): if one fiber of \(A\) is empty, \(A\) has no elements at all, yet if another fiber has two points, \(A\) has a non-identity automorphism (swap them).
Not two-valued: truth values \(1 \to \Omega\) are maps \(X \to 2\); there are \(2^{|X|}\) of them.
Boolean, with choice, and with a natural numbers object \(X \times \mathbb{N}\to X\): all fiberwise.

So: Boolean, but not well-pointed. “True” is now true at some indices and false at others.







Theorem 2 (Fundamental theorem of topos theory) 
If \(\mathcal{E}\) is a topos and \(X\) an object of \(\mathcal{E}\), then \(\mathcal{E}/X\) is a topos.










TipLooking ahead: dependent types





An object of \(\mathcal{E}/X\) is a “type depending on \(x : X\).” Pulling back along \(f : X' \to X\) is substitution, and it has a left adjoint \(\Sigma_f\) and a right adjoint \(\Pi_f\), which are exactly the dependent sum and dependent product of Martin-Löf type theory. This is the interpretation of type theory in locally cartesian closed categories that we return to in Week 14.

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
\(G\)-sets: Boolean without choice [≈ 6 min]
Let \(G\) be a group. An object of \(\mathcal{S}^G\) is a set with a \(G\)-action, a map is an equivariant map. Limits are computed on underlying sets with the induced action; the exponential \(Y^X\) is the set of all maps with \((g\cdot f)(x) = g\, f(g^{-1}x)\) (last time).

Subobject classifier. A part is a \(G\)-invariant subset. Since \(G\) is a group, the complement of an invariant subset is invariant. So \(\Omega = 2\) with the trivial action, and \(\mathcal{S}^G\) is Boolean and two-valued.
Not well-pointed. Elements \(1 \to X\) are fixed points. If \(G \neq 1\), the action of \(G\) on itself by translation has no fixed points but many automorphisms.
Choice fails. The unique map \(G \to 1\) is surjective, hence an epimorphism. A section \(1 \to G\) would be a fixed point. There is none.

So Diaconescu’s theorem has no converse: Boolean does not imply choice.






TipConnection to Week 5



The first independence proofs for \(\mathsf{AC}\) (Fraenkel, Mostowski) used permutation models: a universe of sets built over atoms, keeping only the sets that are fixed by “enough” permutations of the atoms. These models can be presented as toposes of \(G\)-sets for a group \(G\) of permutations of the atoms (with a topology on \(G\), and only actions with open stabilizers). What we just saw — no fixed point, hence no section — is the simplest instance of why choice fails there.

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
Presheaf toposes [≈ 17 min]
\(\mathcal{S}/X\) and \(\mathcal{S}^G\) are both special cases of one construction.






NoteDefinition: presheaves



Let \(C\) be a small category. A presheaf on \(C\) is a functor \(P : C^{op} \to \mathcal{S}\); for \(x \in P(c)\) and \(f : d \to c\) we write \(x \cdot f := P(f)(x) \in P(d)\) (“restriction of \(x\) along \(f\)”). Maps of presheaves are natural transformations. The category of presheaves is written \(\Psh{C}\).
For each object \(c\), the representable presheaf is \(\yon c := C(-, c)\).


Limits of presheaves are computed pointwise: \((P \times Q)(c) = P(c) \times Q(c)\), and so on. A map of presheaves is mono iff each component is injective, and epi iff each component is surjective. So a part of \(P\) is a family of subsets \(A(c) \subseteq P(c)\) closed under restriction.

Guessing \(\Omega\): let the axioms tell you
How could we find \(\Omega\)? Suppose it exists. We need one fact about representables.







Lemma 1 (Maps out of a representable) 
For every presheaf \(P\) and object \(c\), the map \(\NatT(\yon c, P) \to P(c)\), \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha_c(1_c)\), is a bijection.










NoteProof






Proof. Given \(\alpha\) and \(f : d \to c\), naturality of \(\alpha\) applied to \(f\) and the element \(1_c \in \yon c(c)\) gives \[
\alpha_d(f) = \alpha_d(1_c \circ f) = \alpha_c(1_c)\cdot f .
\] So \(\alpha\) is determined by \(x := \alpha_c(1_c)\). Conversely, for any \(x \in P(c)\), the formula \(\alpha_d(f) := x \cdot f\) defines a natural transformation (check naturality using that \(P\) is a functor). This is the bootstrap trick from last time — everything is determined by where the identity goes — and it is a special case of the Yoneda lemma, which we will meet properly soon.




Now combine the lemma with the subobject classifier axiom: \[
\Omega(c) \;\cong\; \NatT(\yon c, \Omega) \;\cong\; \Sub(\yon c).
\] So \(\Omega(c)\) must be the set of parts of \(\yon c\). A part of \(\yon c\) is a set \(S\) of arrows with codomain \(c\) that is closed under precomposition: if \(f \in S\) then \(f \circ g \in S\). Such a set is called a sieve on \(c\). Exactly the same reasoning determines the exponential: \((Y^X)(c) \cong \NatT(\yon c, Y^X) \cong \NatT(\yon c \times X, Y)\).







Theorem 3 (Presheaf toposes) 
For every small category \(C\), \(\Psh{C}\) is a topos, with

\(\Omega(c) = \{ S : S \text{ a sieve on } c\}\), and for \(f : d \to c\), \(S \cdot f = \{ g : f \circ g \in S\}\);
$_c = $ the maximal sieve (all arrows into \(c\));
for a part \(A \subseteq X\), the characteristic map \[
\chi_c(x) = \{\, f : d \to c \;:\; x \cdot f \in A(d) \,\};
\]
\((Y^X)(c) = \NatT(\yon c \times X, Y)\);
natural numbers object: the constant presheaf with value \(\mathbb{N}\).





The characteristic map has a nice reading: \(\chi(x)\) records all the ways in which \(x\) eventually ends up in \(A\). In \(\mathcal{S}\) there is only one “way” (\(1_c\)), so \(\chi(x)\) is just yes or no.






NoteFact: when is a presheaf topos Boolean?



\(\Psh{C}\) is Boolean if and only if \(C\) is a groupoid (every arrow invertible).




The recipe in action

(the Week 14 model of HoTT)



A few checks:

For a monoid \(M\) (one object, arrows \(= M\), composition \(=\) multiplication), a sieve is a subset \(S \subseteq M\) with \(S \cdot M \subseteq S\): a right ideal. (For left actions, as last time, one gets left ideals.) For a group, the only right ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(G\), recovering \(\Omega = 2\).
For \((\mathbb{N}, +)\) the ideals are \(\varnothing\) and \(k + \mathbb{N}\) for \(k \in \mathbb{N}\). Write \(\infty\) for \(\varnothing\) and \(k\) for \(k + \mathbb{N}\). Acting by \(1\) sends \(k + \mathbb{N}\) to \(\{n : 1 + n \in k + \mathbb{N}\} = (k-1)+\mathbb{N}\) (or \(\mathbb{N}\) if \(k = 0\)). This is the \(\Omega\) for sets with an endomap: \(\chi(x)\) is the time it takes \(x\) to enter \(A\).
For graphs, a presheaf \(X\) has a set of vertices \(X(V)\), a set of edges \(X(E)\), and source and target maps \(X(E) \to X(V)\). Arrows into \(V\): only \(1_V\), so there are two sieves on \(V\). Arrows into \(E\): \(1_E, s, t\), giving five sieves: \(\{1_E, s, t\}, \{s,t\}, \{s\}, \{t\}, \varnothing\). Read: the edge is in the subgraph; it is not, but both endpoints are; only the source is; only the target is; neither endpoint is.



The Sierpiński topos, by hand
The smallest non-Boolean example deserves a complete computation. Let \(C\) be the category with two objects \(0, 1\) and a single non-identity arrow \(u : 1 \to 0\). A presheaf on \(C\) is just a map \[
X_0 \xrightarrow{\ \xi\ } X_1 ,
\] and a morphism is a commuting square. Think of \(X_0\) as “what exists now,” \(X_1\) as “what exists later,” and \(\xi\) as “how things develop.” A part of \(X\) is a pair \(A_0 \subseteq X_0\), \(A_1 \subseteq X_1\) with \(\xi(A_0) \subseteq A_1\): once in \(A\), always in \(A\).
Truth values. Arrows into \(1\): only \(1_1\), so \(\Omega_1 = \{\top, \bot\}\). Arrows into \(0\): \(1_0\) and \(u\), and the sieves are \(\{1_0, u\}\), \(\{u\}\), \(\varnothing\). So \[
\Omega_0 = \{\top, \tfrac12, \bot\} \xrightarrow{\quad} \Omega_1 = \{\top, \bot\}, \qquad \top \mapsto \top,\ \ \tfrac12 \mapsto \top,\ \ \bot \mapsto \bot .
\] For a part \(A \subseteq X\) and \(a \in X_0\), \[
\chi_0(a) =
\begin{cases}
\top & a \in A_0 \quad (\text{true now}),\\
\tfrac12 & a \notin A_0 \text{ but } \xi(a) \in A_1 \quad (\text{not yet, but later}),\\
\bot & \xi(a) \notin A_1 \quad (\text{never}).
\end{cases}
\] You can verify directly that this classifies parts (Exercise 2).
Excluded middle fails. Take \(X = 1 = (1 \to 1)\) and the part \(A = (\varnothing, 1)\): the proposition “it is not true now, but it will be.” The pseudo-complement \(\neg A\) must be disjoint from \(A\), so \((\neg A)_1 = \varnothing\), hence \((\neg A)_0 = \varnothing\) as well. Therefore \[
\neg A = 0, \qquad A \vee \neg A = A \neq 1, \qquad \neg\neg A = 1 \neq A .
\] \(A\) is not false (it is not refuted), and yet not true. Its characteristic map is the truth value \((\tfrac12, \top) : 1 \to \Omega\).
The rest of the profile:

Three global truth values \((\top,\top), (\tfrac12, \top), (\bot, \bot)\): not two-valued.
Not well-pointed. An element \(1 \to X\) is just an \(a \in X_0\). The object \(\varnothing \to 2\) has no elements, but two different automorphisms.
Choice fails, by Diaconescu — or directly (Exercise 2).







TipKripke models





This is exactly the semantics of intuitionistic logic by Kripke models with two worlds. Functors \(P \to \mathcal{S}\) on a poset \(P\) (i.e. presheaves on \(P^{op}\)) are Kripke models over \(P\): a statement is “true at stage \(p\)” if it holds at \(p\) and at all later stages, and \(\neg\varphi\) is true at \(p\) if \(\varphi\) fails at every later stage. Presheaves on \((\mathbb{N},\le)^{op}\) are “sets through discrete time.”

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
Sheaves on a space [≈ 10 min]
Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) its poset of open sets, viewed as a category (\(V \to U\) iff \(V \subseteq U\)). A presheaf on \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) assigns to each open \(U\) a set \(F(U)\) (“sections over \(U\)”) with restriction maps \(s \mapsto s|_V\) for \(V \subseteq U\). Example: \(F(U) = C(U, \mathbb{R})\).






NoteDefinition: sheaf



A presheaf \(F\) on \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is a sheaf if whenever \(U = \bigcup_i U_i\) and \(s_i \in F(U_i)\) agree on overlaps (\(s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j} = s_j|_{U_i \cap U_j}\)), there is a unique \(s \in F(U)\) with \(s|_{U_i} = s_i\) for all \(i\).


Continuous functions form a sheaf (“continuity is local”); bounded functions do not. The category \(\Sh(X)\) of sheaves is a topos, with \[
\Omega(U) = \{ V : V \subseteq U \text{ open}\}, \qquad V|_W = V \cap W, \qquad \true_U = U,
\] and for a subsheaf \(A \subseteq F\) and \(s \in F(U)\), \[
\chi_U(s) = \bigcup\{ W \subseteq U \text{ open} : s|_W \in A(W) \} :
\] the truth value of “\(s \in A\)” is the largest open set on which it holds.
Global truth values are the open sets of \(X\), and the logic of truth values is the Heyting algebra \(\mathcal{O}(X)\): \[
U \wedge V = U \cap V, \qquad U \vee V = U \cup V, \qquad \neg U = \operatorname{int}(X \setminus U).
\] In \(\mathbb{R}\), with \(U = (0, \infty)\): \(\neg U = (-\infty, 0)\), so \(U \vee \neg U = \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} \neq \mathbb{R}\).

The real numbers in \(\Sh(\mathbb{R})\)
\(\Sh(X)\) has a real numbers object (constructed by Dedekind cuts internally), and it turns out to be the sheaf of continuous real-valued functions, \(U \mapsto C(U, \mathbb{R})\). So an “internal real number” over \(\mathbb{R}\) is a continuous function, e.g. the identity \(x : \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\). Compute truth values: \[
[\![x < 0]\!] = (-\infty, 0), \qquad [\![x = 0]\!] = \operatorname{int}\{0\} = \varnothing, \qquad [\![x > 0]\!] = (0, \infty).
\] Hence \[
[\![\,x < 0 \;\vee\; x = 0 \;\vee\; x > 0\,]\!] = \mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\} \neq \mathbb{R}.
\] Trichotomy fails for the internal reals. This is not a pathology but a feature: it is the internal reflection of the fact that a continuous function cannot be split, continuously, into “negative,” “zero,” and “positive” cases. Constructive analysis is the mathematics that is valid in all such toposes.

Grothendieck toposes. Replacing \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) by a category with a suitable notion of “covering” (a site) gives the Grothendieck toposes, the setting of modern algebraic geometry. \(\mathcal{S}\), \(\mathcal{S}/X\), \(G\)-sets, all presheaf toposes and all \(\Sh(X)\) are Grothendieck toposes. In fact the Sierpiński topos is \(\Sh\) of the Sierpiński space (Exercise 3), and \(\mathcal{S}/X\) is \(\Sh\) of the discrete space \(X\).

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
Toposes from logic [≈ 8 min]
The last two examples are only surveyed: their constructions take more than a lecture each.

Forcing as sheaves
Cohen’s proof that \(\mathsf{CH}\) is independent of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) (Week 5) can be redone in topos theory (Tierney; Mac Lane–Moerdijk, Ch. VI). Take the poset \(P\) of Cohen’s forcing conditions and form the topos \(\Sh_{\neg\neg}(P)\) of sheaves for the “dense” covering relation. This Cohen topos is Boolean, has a natural numbers object, and internally there is an object strictly between \(\mathbb{N}\) and \(\Omega^{\mathbb{N}}\) in size: \(\mathsf{CH}\) fails. Similarly, Boolean-valued models \(V^{\mathbb{B}}\) correspond to sheaves on a complete Boolean algebra \(\mathbb{B}\). Forcing is “sets varying over conditions.”


Realizability: the effective topos
Hyland’s effective topos \(\Eff\) is built from Kleene’s realizability: a statement is true when some program (an index of a computable function) “realizes” it. In \(\Eff\):

the natural numbers object is the ordinary \(\mathbb{N}\), but every function \(\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}\) is computable (internally, “Church’s thesis” holds);
it is two-valued but not Boolean: excluded middle would require deciding the halting problem;
it is not a Grothendieck topos: it does not arise from sheaves on any site.

Realizability is the ancestor of the “proofs as programs” reading of logic we meet in Week 10: a proof of \(\forall n\, \exists m\, \varphi(n,m)\) in \(\Eff\) comes with an algorithm computing \(m\) from \(n\).

title: A Gallery of Toposes
text:
Non-examples [≈ 4 min]
Topos theory gives quick tests for showing a category is not a topos. In a topos, every map that is both mono and epi is an isomorphism, the initial object is strict, and \(- \times B\) preserves colimits (it is a left adjoint).

\(\mathbf{Pos}\): cartesian closed, but the identity map from the 2-element discrete poset to the 2-element chain is mono and epi without being an iso.
\(\mathbf{Top}\): not even cartesian closed. Not every \(- \times B\) preserves quotients (e.g. \(B = \mathbb{Q}\)).
\(\mathbf{Grp}\): no subobject classifier. If \(\true : 1 \to \Omega\) existed, every subgroup would be the pullback of \(\true\) along a homomorphism, i.e. a kernel, hence normal. But \(S_3\) has non-normal subgroups.
\(\mathcal{S}^{op}\): has finite limits and colimits, but its initial object (the set \(1\)) is not strict.
