Note that since for any \(\beta\), \(F(\beta,\beta) \geq \beta\), we must have \(F(\aleph_\alpha, \aleph_\alpha) > \aleph_\alpha\).
Since \(F\) is a bijection, there exist ordinals \(\beta, \gamma < \aleph_\alpha\) such that \(F(\beta, \gamma) = \aleph_\alpha\). If we put \(\delta = \max\{\beta,\gamma\}+1\), we have \(\omega \leq \delta < \aleph_\alpha\) (since \(\aleph_\alpha\) has to be a limit ordinal).
Since \((\beta, \gamma) <_g (\delta, \delta)\), it follows that \(F(\delta \times \delta) > \aleph_\alpha\) and thus \(F(\delta\times \delta) \supseteq \aleph_\alpha\). The latter implies \(|\delta \times \delta| \geq \aleph_\alpha\). But \(|\delta\times\delta| = |\delta|\cdot |\delta|\) and by minimality of \(\alpha\), \(|\delta|\cdot |\delta| = |\delta| < \aleph_\alpha\), contradiction.











Corollary 1 
If \(\kappa, \lambda\) are infinite cardinals, then \[\begin{equation*}
\kappa  + \lambda = \kappa \cdot \lambda = \max\{\kappa, \lambda\}.
\end{equation*}\]










NoteProof






Proof. If \(\kappa\) is infinite, we have, by simple monotonicity arguments, \[\begin{equation*}
\kappa \le \kappa  + \kappa \le \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa, \quad  \text{hence}  \; \kappa  + \kappa = \kappa \cdot \kappa = \kappa.
\end{equation*}\]
If, say, \(0< \kappa \leq \lambda\) with \(\lambda\) infinite, the above implies \[\begin{align}
\lambda \le \kappa  + \lambda \le \lambda + \lambda = \lambda, & \quad \text{ and thus }  \;\kappa  + \lambda= \lambda = \max\{\kappa,\lambda\},\\
\lambda \le \kappa  \cdot \lambda \le \lambda \cdot \lambda = \lambda, & \quad  \text{ and thus }  \; \kappa  \cdot \lambda = \lambda = \max\{\kappa,\lambda\}.
\end{align}\]

title: Cardinals
text:
While, as we just saw, addition and multiplication are trivial for infinite cardinals, determining the simplest transfinite power, \(2^{\aleph_0}\), already leads to unsolvable problems. \(2^{\aleph_0}\) plays an important role since it is the cardinality of the continuum.







Proposition 2 
\[|\mathbb{R}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})| = 2^{\aleph_0}.\]










TipHint





Use, for example:

Dedekind cuts
every real number has an infinite binary expansion
subsets can be identified with their characteristic function

The Theorem 1 makes life easier here.



We can draw some conclusions:

With \(|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{ \aleph_0}\) we also get \(|\mathbb{R}^n |\) = \((2^{ \aleph_0})^n = 2^{\aleph_0},\) by Hessenberg’s Theorem. It even holds that (exercise!) \[\begin{equation*}
|\{s \colon \mathbb{N}\to  \mathbb{R}\}|  =  (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0} = 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\] That is, there are as many countable sequences of real numbers as there are real numbers.
Since every continuous real-valued function on \(\mathbb{R}\) is determined by its values on \(\mathbb{Q}\), we have \[
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\text{ continuous } \}| = |\{f:\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = (2^{ \aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} =  2^{ \aleph_0}.
\]
We obtain a higher cardinality by passing to the power set of the real numbers or to the set of all real-valued functions on \(\mathbb{R}\): \[\begin{equation*}
|\{f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\}| = |\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})| =  2^{2^{ \aleph_0}} > 2^{ \aleph_0}.
\end{equation*}\]







ImportantContinuum Hypothesis (\(\mathsf{CH}\) – cardinal version)



\[
2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1
\]


\(\mathsf{CH}\) asserts that the cardinality of \(\mathbb{R}\) is the next biggest cardinal after \(\omega = \aleph_0\) (the cardinality of all countably infinite sets).

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text: We take the axioms of ZFC as given and start deriving things — beginning with Axioms 1, 3, 4, 5 (Extensionality, Comprehension, Pairing, Union).
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Extensionality and Comprehension
Axiom 1 (Extensionality). A set is completely determined by its elements:
\[
\forall z\,(z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \;\rightarrow\; x = y .
\]
This does more than it seems. It also fixes what our universe contains. If we allowed an object with no members that is not the empty set — a duck \(D\) and a badger \(B\), say — then \(\forall z\,(z \in B \leftrightarrow z \in D)\) would hold vacuously, forcing \(B = D = \varnothing\). So every object in our universe is a set, and hereditarily so: its members, their members, and so on are all sets. The universe of hereditary sets is informally called \(V\).
Axiom 3 (Comprehension / Separation). For each formula \(\varphi\) (with \(y\) not free),
\[
\forall v\;\exists y\;\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in v \wedge
\varphi(x)\bigr).
\]
Subsets are separated out of a set that already exists. This restriction is the whole point, as the next section shows.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
How Comprehension avoids Russell’s paradox
Naive comprehension — “for every property \(Q\), the set \(\{x : Q(x)\}\) exists” — is inconsistent. With \(Q(x) \equiv x \notin x\) we get Russell’s set \(R\) and the contradiction \(R \in R \leftrightarrow R \notin R\).
Under Axiom 3 we may only form, relative to a set \(v\),
\[
R_v \;=\; \{\,x \in v : x \notin x\,\}.
\]
Run Russell’s argument on this. If \(R_v \in v\), then \(R_v \in R_v
\leftrightarrow R_v \notin R_v\) — still a contradiction. The escape is that we are no longer forced into it: we simply conclude
\[
R_v \notin v .
\]
Since \(v\) was arbitrary, every set omits some object, and there is no set of all sets:

Theorem (no universal set). \(\;\forall v\;\exists R\;(R \notin v).\)

Whether this is a desirable feature is a fair question — a foundation in which “the collection of all sets” is not itself an object can feel like a defect. It is better read as the price of consistency: the same restriction that blocks Russell blocks the universal set.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
section: Formal definitions versus their metatheoretic meaning
text:
Formal definitions versus their metatheoretic meaning
A defined symbol is introduced by a purely symbolic clause. For intersection:
\[
\mathrm{int}(a, b, y) \;:\Longleftrightarrow\;
\forall x\,\bigl(x \in y \leftrightarrow (x \in a \wedge x \in b)\bigr).
\]
Informally we read \(y = a \cap b\), but that reading lives in the metatheory. Before we are entitled to write the term \(a \cap b\), we must check that it names exactly one set:

Lemma. \(\;\forall a, b\;\exists! y\;\mathrm{int}(a, b, y).\)

Existence is Comprehension applied to \(v = a\) with \(\varphi(x) \equiv x \in a
\wedge x \in b\). Uniqueness is Extensionality: if \(\mathrm{int}(a,b,y)\) and \(\mathrm{int}(a,b,z)\), then \(\forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \in z)\), hence \(y = z\).
This is the standard pattern. We name an operation (or a constant) only after proving that the defining formula is satisfied by exactly one set — just as one proves \(\sqrt{2}\) is the unique \(y > 0\) with \(y^2 = 2\) before using the notation.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Classes and the class-builder notation
Let \(\varphi(x)\) be any formula. Informally \(\{x : \varphi(x)\}\) is a class — this is just notation.

If there is a set \(A\) with \(\forall x\,(x \in A \leftrightarrow
\varphi(x))\), then \(A\) is unique by Extensionality; we write \(A = \{x :
\varphi(x)\}\) and say the class exists (is a set).
Otherwise \(\{x : \varphi(x)\}\) is a proper class — a figure of speech, not an object.

Two examples:
\[
\varphi(x) \equiv x \notin x
\qquad\rightsquigarrow\qquad
\mathrm{ZFC} \vdash \neg\exists y\,\forall x\,(x \in y \leftrightarrow x \notin
x),
\]
so Russell’s class is proper;
\[
\varphi(x) \equiv x = x
\qquad\rightsquigarrow\qquad
\neg\exists A\,\forall x\,(x \in A),
\]
so the universal class \(V = \{x : x = x\}\) is proper. Saying “\(V\) does not exist” is just another way of writing \(\neg\exists A\,\forall x\,(x \in A)\); there is no more of a puzzle here than in “trolls do not exist.”
Finally, \(\{x \in z : \varphi(x)\}\) abbreviates \(\{x : x \in z \wedge
\varphi(x)\}\), and Comprehension says these always exist.
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms
text:
Building sets from nothing

The empty set


\(\varnothing\)

the unique \(y\) with \(\forall z\,(z \notin y)\).



Existence: take any set (Axiom 0) and apply Comprehension with an always-false \(\varphi\), e.g. \(x \neq x\). Uniqueness: Extensionality. At this point \(\varnothing\) is the only specific set we have proved to exist.


Pairs
Pairing gives \(\exists z\,(x \in z \wedge y \in z)\); the \(z\) may have other elements, so trim it with Comprehension to \(\{w \in z : w = x \vee w = y\}\). This licenses:

\(\{x, y\} := \{w : w = x \vee w = y\}\)
\(\{x\} := \{x, x\}\)
\(\langle x, y \rangle = (x, y) := \bigl\{\{x\},\, \{x, y\}\bigr\}\)

The one property the ordered pair must have is
\[
\langle x, y \rangle = \langle x', y' \rangle \;\rightarrow\;
x = x' \wedge y = y'
\]
(prove it by splitting into the cases \(x = y\) and \(x \neq y\)). Any other definition with this property would serve equally well; the bracket notation \(\langle\,\cdot\,,\cdot\,\rangle\) marks that we mean this one.
We can now start counting:
\[
0 = \varnothing, \qquad
1 = \{0\} = \{\varnothing\}, \qquad
2 = \{0, 1\} = \bigl\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\bigr\}.
\]
The axioms so far generate infinitely many different sets — for example, \(\varnothing\), \(\{\varnothing\}\), \(\{\{\varnothing\}\}\), … — but none with more than two elements.


Union: getting bigger sets


Axiom 5 — Union

\(\forall \mathcal{F}\;\exists A\;\forall Y\;\forall x\,
\bigl(x \in Y \wedge Y \in \mathcal{F} \;\rightarrow\; x \in A\bigr)\)


\(\bigcup \mathcal{F} := \{x : \exists Y \in \mathcal{F}\;(x \in Y)\}\) — the members of members of \(\mathcal{F}\).
It exists: take \(A\) from the axiom and separate \(\{x \in A : \exists Y \in \mathcal{F}\,(x \in Y)\}\).
\(u \cup v :=  \bigcup \{u, v\}\)

The axiom is stated for arbitrary families so that it covers infinite unions too, not just \(u \cup v\).
Worked example: the number 3. We have \(0, 1, 2\). Then:

\(\{0, 1\}\) by Pairing;
\(\{2\} = \{2, 2\}\) by Pairing;
\(\mathcal{F} = \bigl\{\{0,1\},\, \{2\}\bigr\}\) by Pairing;
\(\bigcup \mathcal{F} = \{0, 1, 2\} =: 3\).

Equivalently \(3 = 2 \cup \{2\}\). In general the successor is
\[
S(x) = x \cup \{x\}, \qquad
3 = S(2),\quad 4 = S(3),\quad \dots
\]
crumbs: 4 · First Consequences of the ZFC Axioms

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Reading. Lawvere–Rosebrugh, Sets for Mathematics (L–R), §§2.3–2.5; Riehl, Category Theory in Context, §§1.2–1.4 and §2.1.
Goal. We first finish L–R’s treatment of parts by introducing the inverse image of a part along a map. We then restate everything we know about elements, parts, and characteristic functions in the language of modern category theory: hom-sets, functors, natural transformations, and representable functors. The punchline is a single sentence:

The axiom of §2.4 says that the functor \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is represented by the object \(2\), with universal element \(\mathrm{true}\).

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Where we are
Throughout, \(\mathcal{S}\) denotes the category of abstract sets and mappings of L–R. So far we have the following axioms: \(\mathcal{S}\) is a category (L–R §1.4); it has a terminal object \(1\) (§1.2) and an initial object \(0\) (§1.5); it has binary sums (§2.1); \(1\) separates mappings (§1.5); and the axiom of §2.4, recalled below.

Elements and parts







Definition 1 An element of \(X\) is a map \(x\colon 1\to X\).










NoteAxiom: \(1\) separates mappings (L–R §1.5)



If \(f,g\colon X\to Y\) satisfy \(fx=gx\) for every element \(x\) of \(X\), then \(f=g\).









Definition 2 (L–R §§2.2–2.3, Def. 2.24) 
Let \(X\) be a set.

A part of \(X\) is a monomorphism \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\).
For parts \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\) and \(j\colon B\rightarrowtail X\), we say \(i\) is included in \(j\), written \(i\subseteq_X j\), if there is a map \(k\colon A\to B\) with \(jk=i\). (Such a \(k\) is unique, since \(j\) is monic.)
Parts \(i\) and \(j\) are equivalent, written \(i\equiv_X j\), if \(i\subseteq_X j\) and \(j\subseteq_X i\).
An element \(x\) of \(X\) is a member of the part \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\), written \(x\in_X i\), if \(x=ia\) for some element \(a\) of \(A\). (Such an \(a\) is unique.)

We often drop the subscript \(X\).




Equivalent parts have the same members: if \(i=jk\) and \(x=ia\), then \(x=j(ka)\).







Lemma 1 
Every element \(x\colon 1\to X\) is a part of \(X\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(xa=xb\) for \(a,b\colon T\to 1\), then \(a=b\) because \(1\) is terminal. So \(x\) is monic.










ImportantConvention: elements, not generalized elements



L–R define membership for generalized elements \(x\colon T\to X\) with arbitrary domain \(T\), and their Definition 2.20 of characteristic function quantifies over all of these. For abstract sets it makes no difference whether we use all generalized elements or only elements \(1\to X\), by Proposition 1. In these notes we work with elements only.









Proposition 1 (Elements suffice; L–R pp. 36–37) 
Let \(i\) and \(j\) be parts of \(X\). If every element of \(X\) that is a member of \(i\) is also a member of \(j\), then \(i\subseteq_X j\). Consequently, two parts with the same members are equivalent.




L–R justify this informally by the “arbitrariness of mappings” and promise a more explicit argument. One such argument uses the axiom of §2.4 together with the separator axiom; see Exercise 2.


Characteristic functions
Fix the set \(2\) with its element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\to 2\).







Definition 3 (L–R Def. 2.20) 
A map \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is a characteristic function of a part \(i\) of \(X\) if for every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff \varphi x=\mathrm{true}.
\]










NoteAxiom: Membership representation via truth values (L–R §2.4)




Every map \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is the characteristic function of some part of \(X\).
Every part \(i\) of \(X\) has exactly one characteristic function, denoted \(\chi_i\).



Exercise 3 shows that our definition of characteristic function agrees with L–R’s version for generalized elements.







Proposition 2 (L–R Prop. 2.22) 
Parts \(i\) and \(j\) of \(X\) are equivalent if and only if \(\chi_i=\chi_j\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(i\equiv j\), then \(i\) and \(j\) have the same members, so \(\chi_i\) is also a characteristic function of \(j\). By uniqueness, \(\chi_i=\chi_j\). Conversely, if \(\chi_i=\chi_j\), then for every element \(x\), \(x\in i \iff \chi_i x=\mathrm{true}\iff \chi_j x=\mathrm{true}\iff x\in j\). By Proposition 1, \(i\equiv j\).











Example 1 (L–R Ex. 2.21) 
By Lemma 1, \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail 2\) is a part of \(2\). Its characteristic function is \(1_2\). Indeed, since the only map \(1\to 1\) is \(1_1\), an element \(y\) of \(2\) is a member of \(\mathrm{true}\) exactly when \(y=\mathrm{true}\), that is, when \(1_2\,y=\mathrm{true}\).











Remark 1. L–R point out right after the axiom that it is special to \(\mathcal{S}\) and to the so-called Boolean toposes. In a general topos there is still an object of truth values, usually written \(\Omega\) with an element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\to\Omega\), satisfying (1) and (2); but \(\Omega\) need not have just two elements. L–R §6.2 gives an example with three truth values.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Inverse image of a part
In naive set theory, the preimage of \(B\subseteq Y\) under \(f\colon X\to Y\) is \(\{x\in X : f(x)\in B\}\). The categorical version is defined by the same membership condition. This operation goes under many names: inverse image, preimage, substitution, pullback.







Definition 4 (L–R §2.5) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and let \(j\) be a part of \(Y\). A part \(i\) of \(X\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\) if for every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff fx\in j .
\]











Proposition 3 
Any two inverse images of \(j\) along \(f\) are equivalent.










NoteProof






Proof. They have the same members, so this follows from Proposition 1.




We may therefore speak of the inverse image and write it \(f^{-1}(j)\), as L–R do (Ex. 2.39), keeping in mind that it is determined only up to equivalence.
L–R simply assert at the start of §2.5 that inverse images exist. In fact, existence is a consequence of the axiom of §2.4, and the proof yields L–R’s Theorem 2.33 at the same time.







Theorem 1 (Existence of inverse images; L–R Thm. 2.33) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and let \(j\) be a part of \(Y\). The part of \(X\) whose characteristic function is \(\chi_j\circ f\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\). In particular, inverse images always exist, and \[
\chi_{f^{-1}(j)}=\chi_j\circ f .
\]










NoteProof






Proof. By part (1) of the axiom, \(\chi_j\circ f\colon X\to 2\) is the characteristic function of some part \(i\) of \(X\). For every element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in i \iff \chi_j(fx)=\mathrm{true}\iff fx\in j ,
\] using the definition of characteristic function first for \(i\), then for \(j\). So \(i\) is an inverse image of \(j\) along \(f\), and its characteristic function is \(\chi_j\circ f\).











Remark 2 (Comparison with ZFC). Part (1) of the axiom is a comprehension principle: for every “predicate” \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) there is a part of \(X\) consisting of the elements where \(\varphi\) is true, \(\{x\in X: \varphi x=\mathrm{true}\}\). Compare the Comprehension (Separation) axiom of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). There is an important difference: \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) separates by arbitrary formulas, while here we may separate only by predicates that are already given as maps \(X\to 2\). Richer forms of comprehension become available later, once we have exponentials and quantifiers.











Proposition 4 (L–R Prop. 2.31) 
For any \(\psi\colon Y\to 2\), the map \(\psi\) is a characteristic function of \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\). Consequently, \(\psi=\chi_j\) if and only if \(j\equiv\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\).










NoteProof






Proof. By Example 1, \(y\in\mathrm{true}\) iff \(y=\mathrm{true}\). Hence \(x\in\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\) iff \(\psi x\in\mathrm{true}\) iff \(\psi x=\mathrm{true}\), which proves the first claim. If \(j\equiv\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), then \(j\) has the same members as \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), so \(\psi\) is a characteristic function of \(j\). Conversely, if \(\psi=\chi_j\), then \(j\) and \(\psi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\) have the same characteristic function, so they are equivalent by Proposition 2.











Proposition 5 (Functoriality of inverse image; L–R Ex. 2.30) 
Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\), and let \(j,j'\) be parts of \(Y\) and \(k\) a part of \(Z\).

\(1_Y^{-1}(j)\equiv j\).
\((g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\equiv f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k))\).
If \(j\subseteq j'\), then \(f^{-1}(j)\subseteq f^{-1}(j')\). In particular, if \(j\equiv j'\), then \(f^{-1}(j)\equiv f^{-1}(j')\).











NoteProof






Proof. Each statement is proved by comparing members and applying Proposition 1. (a) \(x\in1_Y^{-1}(j)\) iff \(x\in j\). (b) For an element \(x\) of \(X\), \[
x\in(gf)^{-1}(k) \iff g(fx)\in k \iff fx\in g^{-1}(k) \iff x\in f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k)) .
\] (c) If \(j=j'k'\) and \(x\in f^{-1}(j)\), then \(fx\in j\), so \(fx\in j'\), so \(x\in f^{-1}(j')\).




Note the reversal of order in (b): pulling back along \(g\circ f\) is pulling back along \(g\) first, then along \(f\). L–R call this the contravariant functoriality of inverse image. The section on functors explains the terminology.







Remark 3. L–R prove Theorem 1 differently: by Proposition 4 and Proposition 5, \[
(\chi_j f)^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\equiv f^{-1}(\chi_j^{-1}(\mathrm{true}))\equiv f^{-1}(j),
\] so \(\chi_j f\) is the characteristic function of \(f^{-1}(j)\). This argument only works once we know that \(f^{-1}(j)\) exists, which is why we proved existence first. The section on representability explains what lies behind L–R’s argument.




The next proposition anticipates the notion of pullback, which we study in L–R §3.5.







Proposition 6 (L–R Ex. 2.29) 
Let \(j\colon B\rightarrowtail Y\) be a part of \(Y\), let \(f\colon X\to Y\), and let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\) be \(f^{-1}(j)\).

There is a unique \(f'\colon A\to B\) with \(jf'=fi\); that is, \(f\) restricted to \(i\) lands in \(j\).
If \(m\) is any part of \(X\) such that \(fm=jg\) for some \(g\), then \(m\subseteq i\).

Thus \(f^{-1}(j)\) is the largest part of \(X\) on which \(f\) lands in \(j\).




Part (b) follows from Proposition 1: if \(x=mc\) is a member of \(m\), then \(fx=j(gc)\in j\), so \(x\in i\). Part (a) is Exercise 4.







Definition 5 (L–R Def. 2.36) 
A part \(m\) of \(Y\) is an intersection of parts \(i\) and \(j\) of \(Y\), written \(m=i\cap j\), if for every element \(y\) of \(Y\), \(y\in m\) iff (\(y\in i\) and \(y\in j\)).











Proposition 7 (L–R Ex. 2.35, Rem. 2.37) 
Let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail Y\) and \(j\) be parts of \(Y\), and let \(k=i^{-1}(j)\). Then \(i\circ k\) is an intersection \(i\cap j\).










NoteProof






Proof. A composite of monos is monic, so \(ik\) is a part. If \(y=i(ka)\), then \(y\in i\), and \(y\in j\) because \(ka\in i^{-1}(j)\). Conversely, if \(y\in i\) and \(y\in j\), write \(y=ia\); then \(ia\in j\), so \(a\in i^{-1}(j)\), say \(a=kb\), and \(y=ikb\in ik\).

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
section: Hom-sets and the category of sets
text:
Hom-sets and the category of sets

Two kinds of sets
From now on we must keep two levels apart.

\(\mathcal{S}\) is the category of abstract sets that we are axiomatizing. Its objects are the things we study.
\(\mathsf{Set}\) is the category of sets of our metatheory (for instance, sets in the sense of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\)), with functions between them. These are the sets we use to talk about \(\mathcal{S}\).

In this section the collections we attach to an object of \(\mathcal{S}\) (its elements, its parts, its characteristic functions) are objects of \(\mathsf{Set}\), not of \(\mathcal{S}\).







Definition 6 (Hom-sets) 
For objects \(X\), \(Y\) of a category \(\mathsf{C}\), write \(\mathsf{C}(X,Y)\) for the set of morphisms \(X\to Y\). (A common alternative notation is \(\operatorname{Hom}_\mathsf{C}(X,Y)\).)











Remark 4. Chapter 5 of L–R constructs, for sets \(X\) and \(Y\), an object \(Y^X\) of \(\mathcal{S}\) whose elements correspond to maps \(X\to Y\): an internal version of the external hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(X,Y)\). Do not confuse the two. In particular, we do not write \(Y^X\) for the hom-set.






Restating what we know







Definition 7 
For a set \(X\), let \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) be the set of equivalence classes of parts of \(X\), partially ordered by inclusion.1 L–R say “part”; the standard term is subobject, hence the notation. We usually write \(j\) for the equivalence class of \(j\).




In this notation:

The elements of \(X\) form the hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\).
The separator axiom says: if \(f,g\in\mathcal{S}(X,Y)\) agree on every \(x\in\mathcal{S}(1,X)\), then \(f=g\).
Proposition 1 says: the function \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}(1,X))\) sending a part to its set of members is injective.
The axiom of §2.4 says the following.








Proposition 8 
For every set \(X\), the assignment \(j\mapsto\chi_j\) is a well-defined bijection \[
\chi_X\colon \operatorname{Sub}(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal{S}(X,2).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Part (2) of the axiom gives the assignment on parts, and Proposition 2 (\(\Rightarrow\)) shows it is well defined on equivalence classes. It is injective by Proposition 2 (\(\Leftarrow\)) and surjective by part (1) of the axiom.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Functors

Moving things along a map
Given \(f\colon X\to Y\) in \(\mathcal{S}\), how do the collections attached to \(X\) relate to those attached to \(Y\)?








Collection
How \(f\) moves it
Direction




Elements
\(x\mapsto f\circ x\), \(\;\mathcal{S}(1,X)\to\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\)
forward


Characteristic functions
\(\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ f\), \(\;\mathcal{S}(Y,2)\to\mathcal{S}(X,2)\)
backward


Parts
\(j\mapsto f^{-1}(j)\), \(\;\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\to\operatorname{Sub}(X)\)
backward



Maps out of a fixed object (elements) are pushed forward by composing after \(f\). Maps into a fixed object (characteristic functions) are pulled back by composing before \(f\).
In each case two laws hold. The identity map moves nothing: \[
1_X\circ x=x,\qquad \varphi\circ 1_X=\varphi,\qquad 1_X^{-1}(j)\equiv j.
\] Moving along a composite is moving in two steps, with the order preserved or reversed: \[
(g\circ f)\circ x=g\circ(f\circ x),\qquad
\varphi\circ(g\circ f)=(\varphi\circ g)\circ f,\qquad
(g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\equiv f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k)) .
\] For elements and characteristic functions these are just the identity and associativity laws of a category; for parts, it is Proposition 5. A rule for moving things along maps that obeys these two laws is called a functor.


Functors and variance







Definition 8 (Riehl §1.3) 
Let \(\mathsf{C}\) and \(\mathsf{D}\) be categories. A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) consists of

an object \(Fc\) of \(\mathsf{D}\) for each object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\), and
a morphism \(Ff\colon Fc\to Fc'\) of \(\mathsf{D}\) for each morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) of \(\mathsf{C}\),

such that \[
F(1_c)=1_{Fc}\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff
\] for every object \(c\) and every composable pair \(f\), \(g\).











Example 2 \(\mathsf{Set}\) is a category, as is \(\mathsf{Pos}\), the category of partially ordered sets and order-preserving maps. Every category has an identity functor.




Some of the rules in the table reverse the direction of maps. These are handled by reversing the arrows of the domain category.







Definition 9 (Riehl §1.2) 
The opposite category \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) has the same objects as \(\mathsf{C}\), and a morphism \(f^\mathrm{op}\colon c'\to c\) in \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) for each morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) in \(\mathsf{C}\). Composition is defined by \(f^\mathrm{op}\circ g^\mathrm{op}=(g\circ f)^\mathrm{op}\), and identities are \(1_c^\mathrm{op}\).




Exercise 1 asks you to check that \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) is a category.







Definition 10 (Variance) 
A contravariant functor from \(\mathsf{C}\) to \(\mathsf{D}\) is a functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{D}\). Unwinding the definitions, it sends each \(f\colon c\to c'\) to a morphism \(Ff\colon Fc'\to Fc\) in the opposite direction, with \[
F(1_c)=1_{Fc}\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(g\circ f)=Ff\circ Fg .
\] A functor \(\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) is called covariant when we want to stress the contrast. The variance of a functor says whether it preserves or reverses the direction of morphisms.











Proposition 9 (Hom-functors) 
Let \(c\) be an object of a category \(\mathsf{C}\) whose hom-sets are sets.

There is a functor \(\mathsf{C}(c,-)\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(x\) to \(\mathsf{C}(c,x)\) and \(f\colon x\to y\) to \[
f_*\colon\mathsf{C}(c,x)\to\mathsf{C}(c,y),\qquad h\mapsto f\circ h .
\]
There is a functor \(\mathsf{C}(-,c)\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(x\) to \(\mathsf{C}(x,c)\) and \(f\colon x\to y\) to \[
f^*\colon\mathsf{C}(y,c)\to\mathsf{C}(x,c),\qquad h\mapsto h\circ f .
\]











NoteProof






Proof. 

\((1_x)_*h=1_x\circ h=h\) and \((g\circ f)_*h=(g\circ f)\circ h=g\circ(f\circ h)=g_*f_*h\).
\((1_x)^*h=h\) and \((g\circ f)^*h=h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f=f^*g^*h\).





So the functor laws for hom-functors are the identity and associativity axioms of a category. Two special cases are the first two rows of the table:

\(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\colon\mathcal{S}\to\mathsf{Set}\), the elements functor (covariant);
\(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\colon\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\), the characteristic functions functor (contravariant).

The third row is also a functor.







Theorem 2 
There is a functor \(\operatorname{Sub}\colon\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) sending \(X\) to \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\) and \(f\colon X\to Y\) to \[
f^{-1}(-)\colon\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\to\operatorname{Sub}(X),\qquad j\mapsto f^{-1}(j).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The function \(f^{-1}(-)\) is well defined on equivalence classes by Proposition 5 (c). The functor laws are Proposition 5 (a) and (b).











Remark 5 (Why equivalence classes?). At the level of individual monos, inverse image is not a function: its defining membership condition determines \(f^{-1}(j)\) only up to equivalence. The functor laws also hold only up to equivalence: \((g\circ f)^{-1}(k)\) and \(f^{-1}(g^{-1}(k))\) are equivalent parts, not literally the same mono. Passing to equivalence classes makes \(f^{-1}(-)\) a genuine function and turns these equivalences into the equalities the definition of a functor requires.











Remark 6. By Proposition 5 (c), each \(f^{-1}(-)\) preserves inclusion, so \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is in fact a functor \(\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Pos}\).











Remark 7 (Notation). Riehl writes \(f^*\) for precomposition with \(f\). Many authors also write \(f^*\) for inverse image along \(f\). Theorem 3 below shows that the two operations correspond under \(\chi\), so the clash is harmless. In these notes, inverse image is written \(f^{-1}(-)\).






Faithfulness and the separator axiom







Definition 11 
A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) is faithful if for all objects \(c,c'\), the function \(\mathsf{C}(c,c')\to\mathsf{D}(Fc,Fc')\), \(f\mapsto Ff\), is injective.











Proposition 10 
The axiom that \(1\) separates mappings holds if and only if the elements functor \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\colon\mathcal{S}\to\mathsf{Set}\) is faithful.










NoteProof






Proof. For \(f,g\colon X\to Y\) we have \(f_*=g_*\) as functions \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\to\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\) exactly when \(fx=gx\) for every element \(x\). Faithfulness says that this forces \(f=g\), which is the separator axiom.




A category whose terminal object separates mappings is called well-pointed. In the categories of variable sets we will meet later (L–R §6.2), \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\) is still a functor but is no longer faithful: distinct maps can agree on all elements. This is why L–R use generalized elements \(T\to X\) in their definitions.







Remark 8 (Mixed variance). Letting both arguments vary gives a functor of two variables, \(\mathsf{C}(-,-)\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\times\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{Set}\), contravariant in the first argument and covariant in the second. The exponential \(Y^X\) of L–R Chapter 5 behaves the same way.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Natural transformations
We now have two contravariant functors \(\operatorname{Sub}\) and \(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\), and for each \(X\) a bijection \(\chi_X\colon\operatorname{Sub}(X)\to\mathcal{S}(X,2)\) between their values. The question is whether this comparison respects the way both functors move along maps. Is “transport, then compare” the same as “compare, then transport”?







Definition 12 (Riehl §1.4) 
Let \(F,G\colon\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{D}\) be functors. A natural transformation \(\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow G\) consists of a morphism \(\alpha_c\colon Fc\to Gc\) in \(\mathsf{D}\) for each object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) (the components of \(\alpha\)), such that for every morphism \(f\colon c\to c'\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) the following square commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
Fc @>{\alpha_c}>> Gc \\
@V{Ff}VV @VV{Gf}V \\
Fc' @>>{\alpha_{c'}}> Gc'
\end{CD}
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad Gf\circ\alpha_c=\alpha_{c'}\circ Ff .
\] A natural isomorphism is a natural transformation all of whose components are isomorphisms. We write \(F\cong G\).




For contravariant functors \(F,G\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) and a morphism \(f\colon x\to y\) of \(\mathsf{C}\), the naturality square reads \[
\begin{CD}
Fy @>{\alpha_y}>> Gy \\
@V{Ff}VV @VV{Gf}V \\
Fx @>>{\alpha_x}> Gx
\end{CD}
\] Naturality only makes sense for two functors of the same variance; otherwise there is no square to check.







Example 3 
Let \(u\colon Z\to Z'\) be a morphism of \(\mathsf{C}\). Postcomposition with \(u\) gives, for each \(x\), a function \(u_*\colon\mathsf{C}(x,Z)\to\mathsf{C}(x,Z')\). These form a natural transformation \(u_*\colon\mathsf{C}(-,Z)\Rightarrow\mathsf{C}(-,Z')\): for \(f\colon x\to y\) the square \[
\begin{CD}
\mathsf{C}(y,Z) @>{u_*}>> \mathsf{C}(y,Z') \\
@V{f^*}VV @VV{f^*}V \\
\mathsf{C}(x,Z) @>>{u_*}> \mathsf{C}(x,Z')
\end{CD}
\] commutes because \(u\circ(h\circ f)=(u\circ h)\circ f\). Once again, naturality is associativity.




Now the main case.







Theorem 3 
The bijections \(\chi_X\) form a natural isomorphism \[
\chi\colon\operatorname{Sub}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Each component is a bijection by Proposition 8. Naturality means that for every \(f\colon X\to Y\) the square \[
\begin{CD}
\operatorname{Sub}(Y) @>{\chi_Y}>> \mathcal{S}(Y,2) \\
@V{f^{-1}(-)}VV @VV{f^*}V \\
\operatorname{Sub}(X) @>>{\chi_X}> \mathcal{S}(X,2)
\end{CD}
\] commutes, that is, \(\chi_{f^{-1}(j)}=\chi_j\circ f\) for every part \(j\) of \(Y\). This is Theorem 1.




In words: parts of \(X\) are the same thing as maps \(X\to 2\), compatibly with every map \(f\). The axiom of §2.4 supplies the bijections, and L–R’s Theorem 2.33 says that they are compatible with inverse images.







Remark 9 (What “natural” means). Informally, a natural comparison is one that is defined uniformly in \(X\), without choosing anything specific to \(X\). Bijections that depend on choices, such as a chosen listing of the elements of \(X\), are typically not natural.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Representability and the universal element
Theorem 3 says that the functor \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is isomorphic to a hom-functor. This situation has a name.







Definition 13 (Riehl §2.1) 
A functor \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) is representable if there is an object \(c\) of \(\mathsf{C}\) and a natural isomorphism \(\mathsf{C}(-,c)\cong F\). We then say that \(c\) represents \(F\).




So \(\operatorname{Sub}\) is represented by \(2\). The next lemma shows that a natural transformation out of a hom-functor can be built from a single element.







Lemma 2 
Let \(F\colon\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}\) be a functor, \(c\) an object of \(\mathsf{C}\), and \(u\in Fc\). Then the functions \[
\theta_x\colon\mathsf{C}(x,c)\to Fx,\qquad \varphi\mapsto(F\varphi)(u),
\] form a natural transformation \(\theta\colon\mathsf{C}(-,c)\Rightarrow F\).










NoteProof






Proof. For \(f\colon x'\to x\) and \(\varphi\colon x\to c\), functoriality of \(F\) gives \[
\theta_{x'}(f^*\varphi)=F(\varphi\circ f)(u)=(Ff\circ F\varphi)(u)=Ff\big(\theta_x(\varphi)\big),
\] which is the naturality condition.











Definition 14 
An element \(u\in Fc\) is a universal element of \(F\) if the natural transformation \(\theta\) of Lemma 2 is a natural isomorphism. Equivalently: for every object \(x\) and every \(a\in Fx\) there is exactly one \(\varphi\colon x\to c\) with \((F\varphi)(u)=a\).











Theorem 4 
The part \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail 2\) is a universal element of \(\operatorname{Sub}\). Explicitly, for every set \(X\) and every part \(j\) of \(X\), there is exactly one \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) with \(j\equiv\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), and the resulting isomorphism \(\theta\) is the inverse of \(\chi\).










NoteProof






Proof. Here \(\theta_X(\varphi)=\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\). By Proposition 4, this is the part whose characteristic function is \(\varphi\), so \(\chi_X(\theta_X(\varphi))=\varphi\). Also by Proposition 4, \(\theta_X(\chi_X(j))=\chi_j^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\equiv j\). So \(\theta_X=\chi_X^{-1}\) is a bijection for every \(X\).




Note that the naturality of \(\theta\) came for free, from functoriality of \(\operatorname{Sub}\) alone (Lemma 2). The content of the axiom of §2.4 is that this particular \(\theta\), built from \(\mathrm{true}\), has bijective components. This is the idea behind L–R’s proof of Theorem 2.33.







Remark 10 (Preview: the Yoneda lemma). In the situation of Lemma 2, the identity \(1_c\in\mathsf{C}(c,c)\) is sent to \(\theta_c(1_c)=(F1_c)(u)=u\). The Yoneda lemma (Riehl §2.2) says that this is the general pattern: every natural transformation \(\alpha\colon\mathsf{C}(-,c)\Rightarrow F\) equals the \(\theta\) built from the element \(u=\alpha_c(1_c)\). In our case, \(\chi^{-1}\) is determined by \(\chi_2^{-1}(1_2)=\mathrm{true}\) (Example 1). So the entire correspondence between parts and characteristic functions is encoded in one piece of data: the part \(\mathrm{true}\) of \(2\).











Corollary 1 
The truth-value object is unique up to unique isomorphism: if \(v\colon 1\rightarrowtail V\) is also a universal element of \(\operatorname{Sub}\), there is exactly one isomorphism \(\psi\colon 2\to V\) with \(\psi\circ\mathrm{true}=v\).




The proof is Exercise 8. It is a special case of a general fact: an object representing a functor is unique up to unique isomorphism.







Remark 11. In topos theory, the axiom “there is an object \(\Omega\) with a universal element \(\mathrm{true}\colon 1\rightarrowtail\Omega\) of \(\operatorname{Sub}\)” is called the existence of a subobject classifier. Its usual formulation uses pullbacks, which we introduce in L–R §3.5; Proposition 6 is a preview.

title: Parts, Characteristic Functions, and Inverse Images
text:
Exercises







Exercise 1 
Verify that \(\mathsf{C}^\mathrm{op}\) satisfies the axioms of a category.











Exercise 2 
Prove Proposition 1, using L–R’s Definition 2.20, which quantifies over generalized elements \(T\to X\), and the axiom that \(1\) separates mappings.










TipHint





Let \(i\colon A\rightarrowtail X\). Compare \(\chi_j\circ i\) with \(\mathrm{true}_A=\mathrm{true}\circ !_A\) on elements of \(A\), then apply Definition 2.20 to the generalized element \(i\).










Exercise 3 
Using Proposition 1, show that \(\varphi\colon X\to 2\) is a characteristic function of a part \(i\) in our sense (testing elements only) if and only if it is one in the sense of L–R’s Definition 2.20 (testing all generalized elements).











Exercise 4 
Prove Proposition 6 (a).










TipHint





Use the separator axiom to show \(\chi_j\circ f\circ i=\mathrm{true}_A\), then use Exercise 3.










Exercise 5 
For \(f\colon X\to Y\), show that \(f^{-1}(1_Y)\equiv 1_X\) and that \(f^{-1}(j_1\cap j_2)\equiv f^{-1}(j_1)\cap f^{-1}(j_2)\) (L–R Ex. 2.39).











Exercise 6 
Show that the inverses of the components of a natural isomorphism form a natural transformation.











Exercise 7 
Show that every functor sends isomorphisms to isomorphisms. Conclude that if \(X\cong Y\) in \(\mathcal{S}\), then \(\operatorname{Sub}(X)\cong\operatorname{Sub}(Y)\) in \(\mathsf{Set}\).











Exercise 8 
Prove Corollary 1.










TipHint





Let \(\varphi\colon V\to 2\) satisfy \(v\equiv\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{true})\), and \(\psi\colon 2\to V\) satisfy \(\mathrm{true}\equiv\psi^{-1}(v)\). Use Proposition 5 and the uniqueness in Theorem 4 to show \(\varphi\psi=1_2\), and similarly \(\psi\varphi=1_V\).










Exercise 9 
By Lemma 1, \(x\mapsto x\) sends \(\mathcal{S}(1,X)\) to parts of \(X\). Explain why it makes no sense to ask whether this is a natural transformation \(\mathcal{S}(1,-)\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sub}\).











Exercise 10 
Granting that \(2\) has exactly two elements, \(\mathrm{true}\) and \(\mathrm{false}\), there are exactly four maps \(u\colon 2\to 2\). By Example 3, each gives a natural transformation \(u_*\colon\mathcal{S}(-,2)\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2)\). Using \(\chi\), describe what each one does to parts. (The Yoneda lemma will show that these are all the natural transformations \(\mathcal{S}(-,2)\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}(-,2)\).)











Exercise 11 
Show that the elements functor preserves products in the following sense: if \(X\xleftarrow{p}P\xrightarrow{q}Y\) is a product diagram in \(\mathcal{S}\) (L–R §3.3), then \(x\mapsto(px,qx)\) is a bijection \(\mathcal{S}(1,P)\to\mathcal{S}(1,X)\times\mathcal{S}(1,Y)\).

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
We asked of a foundational theory that it be strong enough to formalize its own metatheory. \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) meets this demand: formulas, proofs, and the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) itself are finite syntactic objects, and \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can represent and reason about them, just as it represents “\(2 + 8 = 10\)” by a formal shadow \(\ulcorner 2 \urcorner + \ulcorner 8 \urcorner = \ulcorner 10 \urcorner\).
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems show that this strength comes at a price. A theory that can talk about its own proofs cannot prove its own consistency. Rather than a defect, this turns out to be a measuring device: it lets us compare theories by how much consistency they can certify. Large cardinal axioms will serve as the scale.
Our guiding question:






TipQuestion



Can we prove that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) + “there is an inaccessible cardinal” is consistent, assuming that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent?


We already know that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of an inaccessible cardinal (if \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent). The answer to the question above will be a much stronger no.





Throughout this section, \({}T\) is a first-order theory satisfying the following conditions.

\({}T\) is recursively axiomatized: there is an algorithm that decides whether a given formula is an axiom of \({}T\).
\({}T\) interprets enough arithmetic: the axioms of Robinson’s arithmetic \(\mathsf{Q}\) (a weak, finitely axiomatized fragment of Peano arithmetic \(\mathsf{PA}\)) are provable in \({}T\), possibly after translating the language of arithmetic into the language of \({}T\).

\(\mathsf{ZFC}\) satisfies both conditions. It has infinitely many axioms because of the Comprehension and Replacement schemes, but it is decidable whether a formula is an instance of one of them. Arithmetic is interpreted via \({}\omega\) with ordinal addition and multiplication.
The first step is to turn syntax into arithmetic. Fix an effective coding of symbols, formulas, and finite sequences of formulas by natural numbers. Write \(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner\) for the code (Gödel number) of \({}\varphi\), and also for the numeral representing it in the language of arithmetic. Inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), one can just as well code syntax by hereditarily finite sets.
Since \({}T\) is recursively axiomatized, the relation
\[
    \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x) \; :\iff \; p \text{ codes a $T$-proof of the formula coded by } x
\]
is decidable: one only needs to check that every step of the finite sequence coded by \(p\) is an axiom or follows from earlier steps by a rule of inference. Decidable relations can be expressed in arithmetic by formulas with only bounded quantifiers \(\forall y < t\), \(\exists y < t\) (more precisely, by formulas that \({}T\) proves equivalent to such formulas on all numerals). We call such formulas \(\Delta^0_0\). Note the analogy with the set-theoretic \(\Delta_0\) formulas from Models of Set Theory.
A formula is \(\Sigma^0_1\) if it has the form \(\exists y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\), and \(\Pi^0_1\) if it has the form \(\forall y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\).







Definition 1 
The provability predicate of \({}T\) is the \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \[
    \operatorname{Prov}_T(x) \;:\equiv\; \exists p \; \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x),
\] and the consistency statement of \({}T\) is the \(\Pi^0_1\) sentence \[
    \operatorname{Con}(T) \;:\equiv\; \neg\, \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner 0 = 1 \urcorner).
\]





\(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is a sentence of arithmetic. It says “no natural number codes a \(T\)-proof of \(0 = 1\).” It is a statement about \(\mathbb{N}\) and nothing more, and it can be checked instance by instance: each single number either codes such a proof or it does not.

Observe the two levels at work. “\({}T\) is consistent” is a statement of the metatheory. \(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is its formal shadow, a sentence that \({}T\) itself can attempt to prove.
The key bridge between true arithmetic facts and provability is the following.







Lemma 1 (\(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness) 
If \({}\sigma\) is a \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence that is true in \(\mathbb{N}\), then \(\mathsf{Q}\vdash \sigma\), and hence \(T \vdash \sigma\).




In particular, if \(T \vdash \varphi\), then the statement \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\) is a true \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence (a proof exists), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).



The second ingredient is a way to construct self-referential sentences.







Lemma 2 (Diagonal lemma) 
For every formula \(\psi(x)\) with one free variable, there is a sentence \({}\sigma\) such that \[
    T \vdash \sigma \leftrightarrow \psi(\ulcorner \sigma \urcorner).
\]








Apply Lemma 2 to \(\psi(x) :\equiv \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(x)\). We obtain a sentence \({}G\), the Gödel sentence of \({}T\), such that
\[
    T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner).
\]
Informally, \({}G\) says “I am not provable in \({}T\).”







Theorem 1 (Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash G\). If \({}T\) is moreover \(\omega\)-consistent, then also \(T \nvdash \neg G\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(T \vdash G\). By \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). But from \(G\) and the defining property of \({}G\), also \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). Hence \({}T\) is inconsistent.
Now suppose \(T \vdash \neg G\), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), that is, \(T \vdash \exists p\, \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\). By the first part, \(T \nvdash G\), so no number \(n\) codes a proof of \({}G\), and by \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prf}_T(\underline{n}, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\) for every \(n\). This is exactly what \(\omega\)-consistency rules out.




The assumption of \(\omega\)-consistency can be weakened to plain consistency by a cleverer choice of self-referential sentence (Rosser’s trick). We will not need this.







Corollary 1 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \({}G\) is true in \(\mathbb{N}\) but not provable in \({}T\).










NoteProof






Proof. \({}G\) is equivalent to \(\neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), which states exactly what Theorem 1 established.








The proof of the first part of Theorem 1 was finitistic: it used nothing but elementary reasoning about finite syntactic objects. By the thesis that every finitistic argument can be formalized, \({}T\) should be able to carry it out internally. Making this precise is laborious, and the standard route goes through three properties of \(\operatorname{Prov}_T\), the Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions. For all sentences \({}\varphi, \psi\):

(D1) If \(T \vdash \varphi\), then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).
(D2) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi\to \psi \urcorner) \to \big(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \psi \urcorner)\big)\).
(D3) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \urcorner)\).

(D1) is Lemma 1. (D2) formalizes modus ponens. (D3) is (D1) formalized inside \({}T\): it is a formalized version of \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, and its verification is where the real work lies. We take (D1)–(D3) for granted.







Theorem 2 (Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).










NoteProof






Proof. We show \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\). Then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\) would imply \(T \vdash G\), contradicting Theorem 1.
Write \(P(\varphi)\) for \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\). Since \(T \vdash G \to \neg P(G)\), (D1) and (D2) give \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(\neg P(G)).
\] By (D3), \(T \vdash P(G) \to P(P(G))\). Using (D1) and (D2) once more, applied to the tautology \(P(G) \to (\neg P(G) \to 0 = 1)\), we can combine the two: \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(0 = 1).
\] Contraposing, \(T \vdash \neg P(0=1) \to \neg P(G)\), that is, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \neg P(G)\). Since \(T \vdash \neg P(G) \to G\), we obtain \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\).




This settles Hilbert’s program in the negative: finitistic metamathematics can be formalized in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), so if it could establish the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) would prove \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\).



For set theory, the most useful form of \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) is semantic. In Models of Set Theory we used Gödel’s completeness theorem in the metatheory: if \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then it has a model. Both the soundness and completeness theorems are themselves theorems of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), when the satisfaction relation \(M \models \varphi\) for set-sized structures \(M\) is defined inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This gives:







Proposition 1 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \leftrightarrow \exists M\, (M \models \mathsf{ZFC}).
\]




Combining this with Theorem 2:







Corollary 2 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent, then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove that there exists a set model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). In particular, \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of a transitive model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), or of an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(V_\alpha \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).








Let \(\mathsf{IC}\) denote the axiom “there exists a (strongly) inaccessible cardinal.” Recall from Large Cardinals that if \({}\kappa\) is inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\). With Proposition 1, this yields:







Proposition 2 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Argue in \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\). Let \({}\kappa\) be inaccessible. Then \(V_\kappa\) is a set and \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\), so \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) holds by Proposition 1.











Corollary 3 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent, then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\nvdash \mathsf{IC}\).










NoteProof






Proof. If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \mathsf{IC}\), then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) by Proposition 2, contradicting Theorem 2.




We had seen a second proof of Corollary 3 in Large Cardinals: if \({}\kappa\) is the least inaccessible, then \(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{IC}\), since being inaccessible is absolute for \(V_\kappa\). Formalized, this argument shows
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg \mathsf{IC}).
\]
So the absoluteness argument tells us that \(\neg\mathsf{IC}\) is consistent relative to \(\mathsf{IC}\). The second incompleteness theorem tells us much more: we cannot even show that \(\mathsf{IC}\) is consistent relative to \(\mathsf{ZFC}\).







Theorem 3 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) is consistent, then \[
    \mathsf{ZFC}\nvdash \; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \to \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}).
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(\mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \to \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC})\). Then the same implication is provable in the stronger theory \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\). By Proposition 2, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \vdash \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\). Combining the two, \[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}),
\] and by Theorem 2, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) is inconsistent.




In other words, the existence of an inaccessible cardinal is not merely unprovable in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). It is a genuinely stronger assumption: accepting it commits us to new arithmetic truths, such as \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\), that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) cannot reach.


Compare this with the Continuum Hypothesis. By Gödel’s constructible universe \({}L\) and Cohen’s method of forcing (which we will study later),
\[
    \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \iff \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{CH}) \iff \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{CH}),
\]
and these equivalences are provable in a weak base theory. So both \(\mathsf{CH}\) and \(\mathsf{IC}\) are independent of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), but in different ways.

\(\mathsf{CH}\) is equiconsistent independent: adding \(\mathsf{CH}\) or its negation costs nothing in terms of consistency.
\(\mathsf{IC}\) is strength-increasing independent: adding it proves new \(\Pi^0_1\) sentences.





The phenomenon of the previous section can be organized into an ordering of theories. We fix a weak base theory \({}B\), say \(\mathsf{PA}\), or \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) when we compare extensions of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), and consider recursively axiomatized theories extending \({}B\).







Definition 2 (Consistency strength) 
Let \({}T\) and \({}S\) be theories. Define \[
    T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S \;:\iff\; B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S) \to \operatorname{Con}(T).
\] We say \({}T\) and \({}S\) are equiconsistent, \(T \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\). We write \(T <_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).




The relation \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is reflexive and transitive. The notation \(<_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is justified by the following generalization of Theorem 3.







Proposition 3 
Suppose \({}S\) is consistent and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\). Then \(S \not\le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \operatorname{Con}(S)\). Since \({}S\) extends \({}B\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\), we get \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S)\), contradicting Theorem 2.











Example 1 
The following relations hold.








Relation
Method





\(\mathsf{ZF}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{GCH}\)
the inner model \({}L\)
Gödel 1938


\(\mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{CH}\)
forcing
Cohen 1963


\(\mathsf{PA} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\)
\({}\omega\) is a model of \(\mathsf{PA}\)



\(\mathsf{ZFC}<_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
\(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\)
Proposition 2


\(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}+ \text{``every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable''} \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
forcing / the inner model \({}L\)
Solovay 1970, Shelah 1984







The last line connects to the measure problem: in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) there are non-measurable sets of reals, but if we drop full Choice and keep only Dependent Choice, “every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable” is consistent, at exactly the cost of an inaccessible cardinal.


How does one establish such equiconsistencies? There are two directions.

Upper bounds: build a model. To show \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), one assumes a model of \({}S\) and builds from it a model of \({}T\). The models \(V_\kappa\) and forcing extensions are of this kind. Solovay’s half of the last example starts with an inaccessible and builds, by forcing, a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}\) in which every set of reals is measurable.
Lower bounds: find the large cardinal in an inner model. To show \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\), one assumes \({}T\) and shows that some inner model, such as \({}L\), satisfies \({}S\). Shelah’s half of the example shows that if all (\(\Sigma^1_3\)) sets of reals are measurable, then \(\omega_1\) is an inaccessible cardinal in \({}L\).

A remarkable empirical fact: all “natural” theories studied so far line up linearly under \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\), and large cardinal axioms provide a scale against which they can be measured. There is no known explanation for this phenomenon, and one can construct artificial theories (using self-reference) that are incomparable.




To see that the consistency hierarchy continues above inaccessibles, we return to the partition properties from Large Cardinals. Recall that \(\kappa \to (\lambda)^2_2\) means that every partition \(F : [\kappa]^2 \to \{0, 1\}\) has a homogeneous set of size \({}\lambda\), and that Ramsey’s theorem gives \(\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_2\).







Definition 3 
An uncountable cardinal \({}\kappa\) is weakly compact if \(\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2\).




Write \(\mathsf{WC}\) for the axiom “there exists a weakly compact cardinal.”









Proposition 4 
Every weakly compact cardinal is regular.





For the strong limit property, we compare well-orders with the lexicographic order on \(2^\lambda\), the set of functions \(f: \lambda \to \{0, 1\}\): \[
    f <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}} g \;:\iff\; f(\xi) < g(\xi), \text{ where $\xi$ is least with } f(\xi) \neq g(\xi).
\] This is a linear order. Its key property is that it contains no long well-ordered sequences.







Lemma 3 (Sierpiński) 
For every infinite cardinal \({}\lambda\), \((2^\lambda, <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}})\) has no strictly increasing and no strictly decreasing sequence of length \(\lambda^+\).











Exercise 1 Prove Lemma 3.
Hint: Suppose \((f_\alpha)_{\alpha < \lambda^+}\) is strictly increasing. First let \(\gamma \leq \lambda\) be least such that the restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\gamma}\) take \(\lambda^+\) many values, and pass to a subsequence to reduce to the case where all restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\xi}\), \(\xi < \gamma\), take at most \({}\lambda\) values in total. Then let \(\xi_\alpha\) be least where \(f_\alpha\) and \(f_{\alpha+1}\) differ and show that \(\alpha \mapsto f_\alpha \mid_{\xi_\alpha}\) is injective.











Proposition 5 
Every weakly compact cardinal is inaccessible.










Weakly compact cardinals are much larger than the first inaccessible.









Proposition 6 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}),
\] and hence, if \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\) is consistent, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\).









We have climbed two rungs of a much longer ladder.
\[
\begin{align}
    \mathsf{ZFC}\;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{inaccessible} & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{weakly compact} \\
    & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{Ramsey} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{measurable} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \cdots
\end{align}
\]


The rungs are genuinely separated. For example, if \({}\kappa\) is measurable, then the set of weakly compact cardinals below \({}\kappa\) belongs to every normal ultrafilter on \({}\kappa\), so \({}\kappa\) is the \(\kappa\)-th weakly compact cardinal.
The ladder continues far beyond measurables, through strong, Woodin, and supercompact cardinals, all the way up to axioms that assert the existence of nontrivial elementary embeddings \(j : V_\lambda \to V_\lambda\).
There is a ceiling. Kunen’s inconsistency theorem shows, in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), that there is no nontrivial elementary embedding \(j : V \to V\). Large cardinal axioms are therefore not arbitrary: the most naive strengthening is outright inconsistent.



Theorem 3 shows that the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) can never be established on the basis of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) alone. So why do set theorists regard large cardinal axioms as legitimate, or even as true? Several kinds of reasons are commonly offered.

Reflection and the iterative conception. The universe \(V\) is built in stages \(V_\alpha\), and it should be “too large” to be fully described from within. An inaccessible \({}\kappa\) is a stage \(V_\kappa\) that already looks like the whole universe as far as \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can tell. Indescribable cardinals strengthen this: no property of a given complexity can distinguish \(V_\kappa\) from \(V\).
Fruitfulness and convergence. Large cardinals settle questions about sets of reals that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) leaves open, and very different approaches lead to the same large cardinal hypotheses, as with the measurability example above.
Track record. Decades of intensive study have not produced a contradiction from the axioms below Kunen’s bound.

Whatever one makes of these, the incompleteness theorems give large cardinals a precise arithmetic meaning. Each rung of the ladder proves new \(\Pi^0_1\) theorems, namely the consistency of the rungs below it. In this sense, accepting a stronger large cardinal is a commitment about the natural numbers: that certain searches for contradictions will never succeed.






K. Kunen, The Foundations of Mathematics and Set Theory (2011): incompleteness, models of set theory, and inaccessible cardinals.
T. Jech, Set Theory (3rd millennium ed.): weakly compact and indescribable cardinals, and Sierpiński’s lemma.
A. Kanamori, The Higher Infinite: the large cardinal hierarchy and its history.
R. M. Solovay, “A model of set theory in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable,” Annals of Mathematics 92 (1970).
S. Shelah, “Can you take Solovay’s inaccessible away?” Israel Journal of Mathematics 48 (1984).

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
We asked of a foundational theory that it be strong enough to formalize its own metatheory. \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) meets this demand: formulas, proofs, and the axioms of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) itself are finite syntactic objects, and \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can represent and reason about them, just as it represents “\(2 + 8 = 10\)” by a formal shadow \(\ulcorner 2 \urcorner + \ulcorner 8 \urcorner = \ulcorner 10 \urcorner\).
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems show that this strength comes at a price. A theory that can talk about its own proofs cannot prove its own consistency. Rather than a defect, this turns out to be a measuring device: it lets us compare theories by how much consistency they can certify. Large cardinal axioms will serve as the scale.
Our guiding question:






TipQuestion



Can we prove that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) + “there is an inaccessible cardinal” is consistent, assuming that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent?


We already know that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of an inaccessible cardinal (if \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent). The answer to the question above will be a much stronger no.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
Throughout this section, \({}T\) is a first-order theory satisfying the following conditions.

\({}T\) is recursively axiomatized: there is an algorithm that decides whether a given formula is an axiom of \({}T\).
\({}T\) interprets enough arithmetic: the axioms of Robinson’s arithmetic \(\mathsf{Q}\) (a weak, finitely axiomatized fragment of Peano arithmetic \(\mathsf{PA}\)) are provable in \({}T\), possibly after translating the language of arithmetic into the language of \({}T\).

\(\mathsf{ZFC}\) satisfies both conditions. It has infinitely many axioms because of the Comprehension and Replacement schemes, but it is decidable whether a formula is an instance of one of them. Arithmetic is interpreted via \({}\omega\) with ordinal addition and multiplication.
The first step is to turn syntax into arithmetic. Fix an effective coding of symbols, formulas, and finite sequences of formulas by natural numbers. Write \(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner\) for the code (Gödel number) of \({}\varphi\), and also for the numeral representing it in the language of arithmetic. Inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), one can just as well code syntax by hereditarily finite sets.
Since \({}T\) is recursively axiomatized, the relation
\[
    \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x) \; :\iff \; p \text{ codes a $T$-proof of the formula coded by } x
\]
is decidable: one only needs to check that every step of the finite sequence coded by \(p\) is an axiom or follows from earlier steps by a rule of inference. Decidable relations can be expressed in arithmetic by formulas with only bounded quantifiers \(\forall y < t\), \(\exists y < t\) (more precisely, by formulas that \({}T\) proves equivalent to such formulas on all numerals). We call such formulas \(\Delta^0_0\). Note the analogy with the set-theoretic \(\Delta_0\) formulas from Models of Set Theory.
A formula is \(\Sigma^0_1\) if it has the form \(\exists y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\), and \(\Pi^0_1\) if it has the form \(\forall y\, \theta\) with \(\theta\) in \(\Delta^0_0\).







Definition 1 
The provability predicate of \({}T\) is the \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \[
    \operatorname{Prov}_T(x) \;:\equiv\; \exists p \; \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, x),
\] and the consistency statement of \({}T\) is the \(\Pi^0_1\) sentence \[
    \operatorname{Con}(T) \;:\equiv\; \neg\, \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner 0 = 1 \urcorner).
\]





\(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is a sentence of arithmetic. It says “no natural number codes a \(T\)-proof of \(0 = 1\).” It is a statement about \(\mathbb{N}\) and nothing more, and it can be checked instance by instance: each single number either codes such a proof or it does not.

Observe the two levels at work. “\({}T\) is consistent” is a statement of the metatheory. \(\operatorname{Con}(T)\) is its formal shadow, a sentence that \({}T\) itself can attempt to prove.
The key bridge between true arithmetic facts and provability is the following.







Lemma 1 (\(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness) 
If \({}\sigma\) is a \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence that is true in \(\mathbb{N}\), then \(\mathsf{Q}\vdash \sigma\), and hence \(T \vdash \sigma\).




In particular, if \(T \vdash \varphi\), then the statement \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\) is a true \(\Sigma^0_1\) sentence (a proof exists), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).



The second ingredient is a way to construct self-referential sentences.







Lemma 2 (Diagonal lemma) 
For every formula \(\psi(x)\) with one free variable, there is a sentence \({}\sigma\) such that \[
    T \vdash \sigma \leftrightarrow \psi(\ulcorner \sigma \urcorner).
\]








Apply Lemma 2 to \(\psi(x) :\equiv \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(x)\). We obtain a sentence \({}G\), the Gödel sentence of \({}T\), such that
\[
    T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner).
\]
Informally, \({}G\) says “I am not provable in \({}T\).”







Theorem 1 (Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash G\). If \({}T\) is moreover \(\omega\)-consistent, then also \(T \nvdash \neg G\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(T \vdash G\). By \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). But from \(G\) and the defining property of \({}G\), also \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\). Hence \({}T\) is inconsistent.
Now suppose \(T \vdash \neg G\), so \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), that is, \(T \vdash \exists p\, \operatorname{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\). By the first part, \(T \nvdash G\), so no number \(n\) codes a proof of \({}G\), and by \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness \(T \vdash \neg \operatorname{Prf}_T(\underline{n}, \ulcorner G \urcorner)\) for every \(n\). This is exactly what \(\omega\)-consistency rules out.




The assumption of \(\omega\)-consistency can be weakened to plain consistency by a cleverer choice of self-referential sentence (Rosser’s trick). We will not need this.







Corollary 1 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \({}G\) is true in \(\mathbb{N}\) but not provable in \({}T\).










NoteProof






Proof. \({}G\) is equivalent to \(\neg \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)\), which states exactly what Theorem 1 established.








The proof of the first part of Theorem 1 was finitistic: it used nothing but elementary reasoning about finite syntactic objects. By the thesis that every finitistic argument can be formalized, \({}T\) should be able to carry it out internally. Making this precise is laborious, and the standard route goes through three properties of \(\operatorname{Prov}_T\), the Hilbert–Bernays–Löb derivability conditions. For all sentences \({}\varphi, \psi\):

(D1) If \(T \vdash \varphi\), then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\).
(D2) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi\to \psi \urcorner) \to \big(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \psi \urcorner)\big)\).
(D3) \(T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \to \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \urcorner)\).

(D1) is Lemma 1. (D2) formalizes modus ponens. (D3) is (D1) formalized inside \({}T\): it is a formalized version of \(\Sigma^0_1\)-completeness, and its verification is where the real work lies. We take (D1)–(D3) for granted.







Theorem 2 (Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem) 
If \({}T\) is consistent, then \(T \nvdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).










NoteProof






Proof. We show \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\). Then \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\) would imply \(T \vdash G\), contradicting Theorem 1.
Write \(P(\varphi)\) for \(\operatorname{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner)\). Since \(T \vdash G \to \neg P(G)\), (D1) and (D2) give \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(\neg P(G)).
\] By (D3), \(T \vdash P(G) \to P(P(G))\). Using (D1) and (D2) once more, applied to the tautology \(P(G) \to (\neg P(G) \to 0 = 1)\), we can combine the two: \[
    T \vdash P(G) \to P(0 = 1).
\] Contraposing, \(T \vdash \neg P(0=1) \to \neg P(G)\), that is, \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \neg P(G)\). Since \(T \vdash \neg P(G) \to G\), we obtain \(T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G\).




This settles Hilbert’s program in the negative: finitistic metamathematics can be formalized in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), so if it could establish the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) would prove \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\).



For set theory, the most useful form of \(\operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC})\) is semantic. In Models of Set Theory we used Gödel’s completeness theorem in the metatheory: if \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is consistent, then it has a model. Both the soundness and completeness theorems are themselves theorems of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), when the satisfaction relation \(M \models \varphi\) for set-sized structures \(M\) is defined inside \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). This gives:







Proposition 1 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}\vdash \; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}) \leftrightarrow \exists M\, (M \models \mathsf{ZFC}).
\]




Combining this with Theorem 2:







Corollary 2 
If \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) is consistent, then \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove that there exists a set model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). In particular, \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) does not prove the existence of a transitive model of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), or of an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(V_\alpha \models \mathsf{ZFC}\).

text:

\[

\]
