title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
The phenomenon of the previous section can be organized into an ordering of theories. We fix a weak base theory \({}B\), say \(\mathsf{PA}\), or \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) when we compare extensions of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), and consider recursively axiomatized theories extending \({}B\).







Definition 2 (Consistency strength) 
Let \({}T\) and \({}S\) be theories. Define \[
    T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S \;:\iff\; B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S) \to \operatorname{Con}(T).
\] We say \({}T\) and \({}S\) are equiconsistent, \(T \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\). We write \(T <_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) if \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\).




The relation \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is reflexive and transitive. The notation \(<_{\operatorname{Con}}\) is justified by the following generalization of Theorem 3.







Proposition 3 
Suppose \({}S\) is consistent and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\). Then \(S \not\le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\).










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(B \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to \operatorname{Con}(S)\). Since \({}S\) extends \({}B\) and \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T)\), we get \(S \vdash \operatorname{Con}(S)\), contradicting Theorem 2.











Example 1 
The following relations hold.








Relation
Method





\(\mathsf{ZF}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{GCH}\)
the inner model \({}L\)
Gödel 1938


\(\mathsf{ZFC}\equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \neg\mathsf{CH}\)
forcing
Cohen 1963


\(\mathsf{PA} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}\)
\({}\omega\) is a model of \(\mathsf{PA}\)



\(\mathsf{ZFC}<_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
\(V_\kappa \models \mathsf{ZFC}\)
Proposition 2


\(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}+ \text{``every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable''} \equiv_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\)
forcing / the inner model \({}L\)
Solovay 1970, Shelah 1984







The last line connects to the measure problem: in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) there are non-measurable sets of reals, but if we drop full Choice and keep only Dependent Choice, “every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable” is consistent, at exactly the cost of an inaccessible cardinal.


How does one establish such equiconsistencies? There are two directions.

Upper bounds: build a model. To show \(T \le_{\operatorname{Con}} S\), one assumes a model of \({}S\) and builds from it a model of \({}T\). The models \(V_\kappa\) and forcing extensions are of this kind. Solovay’s half of the last example starts with an inaccessible and builds, by forcing, a model of \(\mathsf{ZF}+ \mathsf{DC}\) in which every set of reals is measurable.
Lower bounds: find the large cardinal in an inner model. To show \(S \le_{\operatorname{Con}} T\), one assumes \({}T\) and shows that some inner model, such as \({}L\), satisfies \({}S\). Shelah’s half of the example shows that if all (\(\Sigma^1_3\)) sets of reals are measurable, then \(\omega_1\) is an inaccessible cardinal in \({}L\).

A remarkable empirical fact: all “natural” theories studied so far line up linearly under \(\le_{\operatorname{Con}}\), and large cardinal axioms provide a scale against which they can be measured. There is no known explanation for this phenomenon, and one can construct artificial theories (using self-reference) that are incomparable.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
To see that the consistency hierarchy continues above inaccessibles, we return to the partition properties from Large Cardinals. Recall that \(\kappa \to (\lambda)^2_2\) means that every partition \(F : [\kappa]^2 \to \{0, 1\}\) has a homogeneous set of size \({}\lambda\), and that Ramsey’s theorem gives \(\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_2\).







Definition 3 
An uncountable cardinal \({}\kappa\) is weakly compact if \(\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2\).




Write \(\mathsf{WC}\) for the axiom “there exists a weakly compact cardinal.”









Proposition 4 
Every weakly compact cardinal is regular.





For the strong limit property, we compare well-orders with the lexicographic order on \(2^\lambda\), the set of functions \(f: \lambda \to \{0, 1\}\): \[
    f <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}} g \;:\iff\; f(\xi) < g(\xi), \text{ where $\xi$ is least with } f(\xi) \neq g(\xi).
\] This is a linear order. Its key property is that it contains no long well-ordered sequences.







Lemma 3 (Sierpiński) 
For every infinite cardinal \({}\lambda\), \((2^\lambda, <_{\mathop{\mathrm{lex}}})\) has no strictly increasing and no strictly decreasing sequence of length \(\lambda^+\).











Exercise 1 Prove Lemma 3.
Hint: Suppose \((f_\alpha)_{\alpha < \lambda^+}\) is strictly increasing. First let \(\gamma \leq \lambda\) be least such that the restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\gamma}\) take \(\lambda^+\) many values, and pass to a subsequence to reduce to the case where all restrictions \(f_\alpha \mid_{\xi}\), \(\xi < \gamma\), take at most \({}\lambda\) values in total. Then let \(\xi_\alpha\) be least where \(f_\alpha\) and \(f_{\alpha+1}\) differ and show that \(\alpha \mapsto f_\alpha \mid_{\xi_\alpha}\) is injective.











Proposition 5 
Every weakly compact cardinal is inaccessible.










Weakly compact cardinals are much larger than the first inaccessible.









Proposition 6 
\[
    \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC} \;\vdash\; \operatorname{Con}(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}),
\] and hence, if \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\) is consistent, \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC} <_{\operatorname{Con}} \mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{WC}\).

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
We have climbed two rungs of a much longer ladder.
\[
\begin{align}
    \mathsf{ZFC}\;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{inaccessible} & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{weakly compact} \\
    & \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{Ramsey} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \text{measurable} \;<_{\operatorname{Con}}\; \cdots
\end{align}
\]


The rungs are genuinely separated. For example, if \({}\kappa\) is measurable, then the set of weakly compact cardinals below \({}\kappa\) belongs to every normal ultrafilter on \({}\kappa\), so \({}\kappa\) is the \(\kappa\)-th weakly compact cardinal.
The ladder continues far beyond measurables, through strong, Woodin, and supercompact cardinals, all the way up to axioms that assert the existence of nontrivial elementary embeddings \(j : V_\lambda \to V_\lambda\).
There is a ceiling. Kunen’s inconsistency theorem shows, in \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), that there is no nontrivial elementary embedding \(j : V \to V\). Large cardinal axioms are therefore not arbitrary: the most naive strengthening is outright inconsistent.



Theorem 3 shows that the consistency of \(\mathsf{ZFC}+ \mathsf{IC}\) can never be established on the basis of \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) alone. So why do set theorists regard large cardinal axioms as legitimate, or even as true? Several kinds of reasons are commonly offered.

Reflection and the iterative conception. The universe \(V\) is built in stages \(V_\alpha\), and it should be “too large” to be fully described from within. An inaccessible \({}\kappa\) is a stage \(V_\kappa\) that already looks like the whole universe as far as \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) can tell. Indescribable cardinals strengthen this: no property of a given complexity can distinguish \(V_\kappa\) from \(V\).
Fruitfulness and convergence. Large cardinals settle questions about sets of reals that \(\mathsf{ZFC}\) leaves open, and very different approaches lead to the same large cardinal hypotheses, as with the measurability example above.
Track record. Decades of intensive study have not produced a contradiction from the axioms below Kunen’s bound.

Whatever one makes of these, the incompleteness theorems give large cardinals a precise arithmetic meaning. Each rung of the ladder proves new \(\Pi^0_1\) theorems, namely the consistency of the rungs below it. In this sense, accepting a stronger large cardinal is a commitment about the natural numbers: that certain searches for contradictions will never succeed.

title: Incompleteness and Consistency Strength
text:
K. Kunen, The Foundations of Mathematics and Set Theory (2011): incompleteness, models of set theory, and inaccessible cardinals.
T. Jech, Set Theory (3rd millennium ed.): weakly compact and indescribable cardinals, and Sierpiński’s lemma.
A. Kanamori, The Higher Infinite: the large cardinal hierarchy and its history.
R. M. Solovay, “A model of set theory in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable,” Annals of Mathematics 92 (1970).
S. Shelah, “Can you take Solovay’s inaccessible away?” Israel Journal of Mathematics 48 (1984).

title: The Axiom of Choice
text:
The Axiom of Choice
Can every set be well-ordered? This property is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice and therefore has a somewhat controversial ontological status among mathematicians.
Let \(X\) be a set of non-empty sets. A choice function for \(X\) is a function \(f\) that assigns every set \(Y \in X\) an element \(y \in Y\).






NoteAxiom of Choice (\(\mathsf{AC}\))



Every set \(X\) of non-empty sets has a choice function.


The Axiom of Choice allows for enumerating a (non-empty) set \(A\) by using a choice function for all non-empty subsets of \(A\). If the set of elements of \(A\) not yet enumerated is non-empty, the choice function applied to this set will give us the next element to be enumerated (thereby well-ordering \(A\)). On the other hand, if \(A\) is well-ordered, we can obtain a choice function by mapping a non-empty subset of \(A\) to its least element under the well-ordering.
It follows that the Axiom of Choice is equivalent to Zermelo’s Well-Ordering Principle:






NoteWell-Ordering Principle (\(\mathsf{WO}\))



Every set can be well-ordered


Besides \(\mathsf{WO}\), \(\mathsf{AC}\) has applications in pretty much any branch of mathematics, with many equivalent principles (such as Zorn’s Lemma, that every vector space has a basis, and Tychonoff’s theorem), but also some strange consequences (such as the Banach–Tarski paradox).
The foundational issue with the Axiom of Choice lies primarily in the fact that it postulates the existence of a function without giving any hint at how such a function might be defined. For some sets (e.g., the rationals) we can explicitly describe a well-ordering (by identifying \(\mathbb{Q}\) with a subset of \(\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}\) and then well-ordering that). But \(\mathsf{AC}\) also guarantees a well-order of the reals, and if you try to ‘write down’ such a well-order, you will quickly run into difficulties.







Remark 1 (Further reading). For more on the history and the controversy surrounding the Axiom of Choice, see G.H. Moore: Zermelo’s Axiom of Choice, Springer. 1982.




We will need the Axiom of Choice in many places. In the next section, we will use it to develop the theory of cardinal numbers. Some axioms that are considered in descriptive set theory (such as the Axiom of Determinacy, \(\mathsf{AD}\)) contradict \(\mathsf{AC}\). It is therefore important to keep track of where exactly we use the Axiom of Choice.
For some applications, it suffices to use weaker forms of \(\mathsf{AC}\).






NoteAxiom of Countable Choice (\(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\))



\[
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; A_n \ne \emptyset \quad \Rightarrow \quad  \exists f \; \forall n \in \omega \;  f(n) \in A_n
\]








NoteAxiom of Dependent Choice (\(\mathsf{DC}\))



If \(R\) is a binary relation on a set \(A\), \(a_0 \in A\), and \(\forall x \in A \exists y \in A \; xRy\), then \[
\exists f : \mathbb{N}\longrightarrow A  \text{ with }  \; f(0) = a_0  \; \wedge  \;\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\; f(n) R f(n+1).
\]









Proposition 1 
\(\mathsf{AC}\) implies \(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{DC}\) implies \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\).




Both implications are strict, in the sense that there are mathematical universes in which the weaker axiom holds and the stronger fails.
The axiom \(\mathsf{AC}_{\omega}\) is sufficient to prove, for example, the following:

Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset.
A countable union of countable sets is countable.

\(\mathsf{DC}\) and \(\mathsf{AC}_\omega\) therefore play an important role in the foundations of analysis and measure theory.

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
While the class \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\) of all ordinals is not a set, it is still transitive and well-ordered by \(\in\). Regarding the associated order \(\leq\), every set of ordinals \(a\) has a supremum \(\bigcup a = \bigcup_{\xi \in a} \xi\) and (if \(a \ne \emptyset\)) an infimum \(\bigcap a = \bigcap_{\xi \in a} \xi\), which is the smallest element of \(a\). Such a smallest element exists actually for every (non-empty) class \(A\) (since if \(\xi \in A\), we only need to find the infimum of the set of ordinals \(\le \xi\).) This allows us to prove properties about all ordinals by induction.







Proposition 1 (Induction for ordinals, I) 
For every property \(\varphi\), \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall \alpha \; [ \forall \xi < \alpha \; \varphi(\xi) \to \varphi(\alpha)] \to \forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha).
\end{equation*}\]




We have repeatedly used induction already for ordinals \(< \omega_1\), the first uncountable ordinal.
To prove this principle simply observe that if \(\forall \alpha \, \varphi(\alpha)\) failed there would have to be a smallest \({}\alpha\) with \(\neg \varphi(\alpha)\), contradicting the induction hypothesis.
Since every ordinal is either \(0\), a successor, or a limit ordinal, we have the following variant of induction.







Proposition 2 (Induction for ordinals, II) 
For every property \({}\varphi\), if

(i) \(\varphi(0)\),
(ii) \(\forall \alpha (\varphi(\alpha) \to \varphi(\alpha+1))\), and
(iii) \((\forall \xi < \lambda \; \varphi(\xi)) \to \varphi(\lambda))\) for all limit \(\lambda\),

then \(\forall \alpha \;  \varphi(\alpha)\).




(i) and (ii) coincide with the usual induction scheme for natural numbers. To cover all ordinals we need to add (iii).



The induction principle can be used to define functions by recursion. For example, addition on the natural numbers is given by
\[\begin{align*}
    x+0 \quad & =  x\\
    x+ (y+1) & =  (x + y)+1.
\end{align*}\]
In the case of ordinals, we have to consider the limit case, too.







Theorem 1 (Recursion on ordinals) 
If \(G : \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is a function, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that for all \(\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\),
\[
F(\alpha) = G(F\mid_{\alpha})
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The uniqueness of the function \(F\) follows by induction.
To show the existence of \(F\), we define the following:

Call \(h\) tame if \[\begin{equation*}
\exists \alpha \, (h: \alpha \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\wedge \forall \xi \in \alpha \; h(\xi) = G(h \mid_{\xi}))
\end{equation*}\]
Say \(h\) is compatible with \(g\) if \[\begin{equation*}
  \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom}(h) \cap \operatorname{Dom}(g) \; h(x) = g(x)
\end{equation*}\]

It follows by induction that any two tame functions are compatible.
This lets us define the desired \(F\) as
\[
F := \bigcup \{h \colon h\, \text{ tame}\}
\]
Then \(F\) is a function (otherwise there would be two incompatible tame functions), its domain is transitive, and satisfies the recursion condition (since it is the union of tame functions).
It remains to show that \(F\) is defined on all of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\). If \(D = \operatorname{Dom}(F) \neq \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), then we would have \(D = \alpha\) for some ordinal \({}\alpha\). In particular \(D\) is a set therefore \(F = f\) is a set, for some tame \(f\). This \(f\) could be extended to a tame \(h = f \cup \{(\alpha,G(f \mid_{\alpha}))\}\), contradiction.




Note that we defined \(F\) explicitly as a union of all partial solutions to the recursion equation. (Of course, since \(F\) is a proper class, one has the translate the informal definition of \(F\) above into a formal expression.)
As with induction, we have the following variant of the recursion principle.







Proposition 3 (Recursion on ordinals, variant) 
If \(G, H: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) are functions and \(a\) is a set, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{align*}
    F(0) \quad & =  a\\
    F(\alpha+1) & =  G(\alpha,F(\alpha)) \\    
    F(\lambda) \quad & =  H(\lambda, \{F(\xi) \colon \xi<\lambda \}) \quad \text{for } \operatorname{Lim}(\lambda).
\end{align*}\]




We can establish a similar principle for a well-ordering \(<\) on a class \(A\). In case of a proper class, though, we have to require that for every \(a \in A\), the class of all predecessors of \(a\) \[\begin{equation*}
S(a,<): = \{x \in A\colon x < a \},
\end{equation*}\] is a set (if \(A\) is a set, this follows automatically by Separation). If this is the case, the recursion principle yields a function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F\mid_{S(a,<)}).
\end{equation*}\]



More generally, we can define induction and recursion on well-founded relations. We already encountered those in a previous chapter.







Definition 1 
A relation \(R\) on a class \(A\) is well-founded if it satisfies the minimality condition \[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Min}_R) \qquad  \emptyset \neq b \subset A \to \exists x \in b \; \forall y \in b \, (  \neg y R x)
\end{equation*}\] and the set condition \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall x \in A \; S(a,R):= \{x \colon x R a\} \text{ is a set}
\end{equation*}\]




If \(A\) is a set, the minimality condition is again automatically satisfied by Separation.
The set condition allows for taking the \(R\)-transitive closure of a set \(a \in A\): the smallest superset \(\operatorname{TC}_R(a)\) of \(a\) that is \(R\)-transitive:
\[ \forall x \in \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\; S(x,R) \subseteq  \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\]
This is done by recursion over the natural numbers. The following is an important example.







Example 1 (Transitive closure of a set) 
By the axiom of Foundation, \(\in\) is a well-founded relation on \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\). (The set condition is satisfied since \(S(a,\in)=a\).)
We can form the transitive closure, the smallest transitive superset, of a set \(a\) as
\[\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{TC}(a):&= a \cup \bigcup a \cup \bigcup \bigcup a \ldots
= \bigcup_{n< \omega} U^n(a), \quad \text{ where} \\
&U^0(a) = a, U^{n+1}(a) = \bigcup U^n(a).
\end{align*}\]
This is an example of definition by recursion along \(\mathbb{N}\).




We can use the existence of \(\operatorname{TC}_R\) as a set to strengthen the minimality condition to subclasses, similar to the case of the well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\):







Lemma 1 
For every non-empty class \(B \subseteq A\), there exists \(x \in B\) such that
\[
    \forall y \in B \;  \neg y R x
\]




To prove this lemma, simply pick any \(x \in B\), take its transitive \(R\)-closure, and intersect it with \(B\):
\[
    C = \operatorname{TC}_R(x) \cap B.
\]
\(C\) is a set, and by the minimality condition \((\operatorname{Min}_R)\) has an \(R\)-minimal element \(a\). \(a\) has to be minimal for \(B\), too, since otherwise there exists \(b \in B\) with \(b R a\). Since \(a \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), \(b \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), and therefore \(b \in C\), contradicting the minimality of \(a\).
The lemma implies a corresponding induction principle for well-founded relations:
\[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Ind}_R) \qquad  \forall x \in A [ \forall y ( yRx \, \to \varphi(y)) \to \varphi(x)] \to \forall x \in A \, \varphi(x)).
\end{equation*}\]
This in turn yields the following.







Theorem 2 (Recursion principle for well-founded relations) 
Let \(R\) be a well-founded relation on a class \(A\). For every function \(G : A \times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) there exists a unique function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F \mid_{\{x \mid xRa\}})  \text{ for all } a \in A.
\end{equation*}\]







Is there a way to systematically build the \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), the universe of all sets, “from below”?
We start with the empty set:
\[
V_0 = \emptyset
\]
Given \(V_\alpha\), the Power Set axiom requires the set of all subsets to exist, so we set
\[
V_{\alpha+1} = \mathcal{P}(V_{\alpha}).
\]
Finally, at limit stages we simply collect all sets we have obtained so far:
\[
V_ \lambda =  \bigcup_{\xi < \lambda} V_\xi \quad \text{for limit } \lambda
\]
What we really are doing here is to construct a function \(V: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) by ordinal recursion. Think \(V_\alpha = V(\alpha)\).
The following facts about the hierarchy are easily verified by transfinite induction:







Proposition 4  

Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.
\(\alpha < \beta\) implies \(V_\alpha \subset V_\beta\).
\(\alpha \subseteq V_\alpha\)





Remarkably, if we assume the axiom of Foundation, we reach all sets this way.







Theorem 3 
For every set \(x\) there exists an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(x \in V_\alpha\), that is, \[
    \mathop{\mathrm{V}}= \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha
\]











Remark 1. Recall that the notation \(\bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} \dots\) is really just a shortcut for the class obtained as \(\{ x \colon \exists \alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\dots\}\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(C\) be the class of all sets not in any \(V_\alpha\). Since \(\in\) is well-founded, if \(C\) is non-empty, it has a \(\in\)-minimal element \(x\). This implies that for all \(z \in x\), \(z \in \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha\). Define a function \(h\) by mapping each \(z\in x\) to the least \({}\alpha\) so that \(z \in V_\alpha\). Since \(x\) is a set, \(h[x]\) is a set of ordinals, by Replacement. This set of ordinals has a supremum, say \({}\gamma\). Then \(x \subseteq V_\gamma\) and therefore,
\[
x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\gamma) = V_{\gamma+1}.
\]
Hence \(C\) must be empty, and the theorem follows.











Definition 2 For any set \(x\) we define its rank as \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \text{ least } \alpha \text{ with } x \in V_{\alpha+1}.
\]











Exercise 1 Show that \[
\operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{ \operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x \}.
\]




We can split the question of “how large” \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is into two sub-questions:

How “long” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how many ordinals are there? Axioms for large cardinals attempt to extend this “length” as far as possible.
How “wide” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how large is the power set of a set? A rather “slim” universe is given by the constructible sets, which we will encounter soon.

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
The induction principle can be used to define functions by recursion. For example, addition on the natural numbers is given by
\[\begin{align*}
    x+0 \quad & =  x\\
    x+ (y+1) & =  (x + y)+1.
\end{align*}\]
In the case of ordinals, we have to consider the limit case, too.







Theorem 1 (Recursion on ordinals) 
If \(G : \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is a function, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that for all \(\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\),
\[
F(\alpha) = G(F\mid_{\alpha})
\]










NoteProof






Proof. The uniqueness of the function \(F\) follows by induction.
To show the existence of \(F\), we define the following:

Call \(h\) tame if \[\begin{equation*}
\exists \alpha \, (h: \alpha \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\wedge \forall \xi \in \alpha \; h(\xi) = G(h \mid_{\xi}))
\end{equation*}\]
Say \(h\) is compatible with \(g\) if \[\begin{equation*}
  \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom}(h) \cap \operatorname{Dom}(g) \; h(x) = g(x)
\end{equation*}\]

It follows by induction that any two tame functions are compatible.
This lets us define the desired \(F\) as
\[
F := \bigcup \{h \colon h\, \text{ tame}\}
\]
Then \(F\) is a function (otherwise there would be two incompatible tame functions), its domain is transitive, and satisfies the recursion condition (since it is the union of tame functions).
It remains to show that \(F\) is defined on all of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\). If \(D = \operatorname{Dom}(F) \neq \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\), then we would have \(D = \alpha\) for some ordinal \({}\alpha\). In particular \(D\) is a set therefore \(F = f\) is a set, for some tame \(f\). This \(f\) could be extended to a tame \(h = f \cup \{(\alpha,G(f \mid_{\alpha}))\}\), contradiction.




Note that we defined \(F\) explicitly as a union of all partial solutions to the recursion equation. (Of course, since \(F\) is a proper class, one has the translate the informal definition of \(F\) above into a formal expression.)
As with induction, we have the following variant of the recursion principle.







Proposition 3 (Recursion on ordinals, variant) 
If \(G, H: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) are functions and \(a\) is a set, then there exists a unique function \(F: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{align*}
    F(0) \quad & =  a\\
    F(\alpha+1) & =  G(\alpha,F(\alpha)) \\    
    F(\lambda) \quad & =  H(\lambda, \{F(\xi) \colon \xi<\lambda \}) \quad \text{for } \operatorname{Lim}(\lambda).
\end{align*}\]




We can establish a similar principle for a well-ordering \(<\) on a class \(A\). In case of a proper class, though, we have to require that for every \(a \in A\), the class of all predecessors of \(a\) \[\begin{equation*}
S(a,<): = \{x \in A\colon x < a \},
\end{equation*}\] is a set (if \(A\) is a set, this follows automatically by Separation). If this is the case, the recursion principle yields a function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F\mid_{S(a,<)}).
\end{equation*}\]

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
More generally, we can define induction and recursion on well-founded relations. We already encountered those in a previous chapter.







Definition 1 
A relation \(R\) on a class \(A\) is well-founded if it satisfies the minimality condition \[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Min}_R) \qquad  \emptyset \neq b \subset A \to \exists x \in b \; \forall y \in b \, (  \neg y R x)
\end{equation*}\] and the set condition \[\begin{equation*}
    \forall x \in A \; S(a,R):= \{x \colon x R a\} \text{ is a set}
\end{equation*}\]




If \(A\) is a set, the minimality condition is again automatically satisfied by Separation.
The set condition allows for taking the \(R\)-transitive closure of a set \(a \in A\): the smallest superset \(\operatorname{TC}_R(a)\) of \(a\) that is \(R\)-transitive:
\[ \forall x \in \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\; S(x,R) \subseteq  \operatorname{TC}_R(a)\]
This is done by recursion over the natural numbers. The following is an important example.







Example 1 (Transitive closure of a set) 
By the axiom of Foundation, \(\in\) is a well-founded relation on \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\). (The set condition is satisfied since \(S(a,\in)=a\).)
We can form the transitive closure, the smallest transitive superset, of a set \(a\) as
\[\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{TC}(a):&= a \cup \bigcup a \cup \bigcup \bigcup a \ldots
= \bigcup_{n< \omega} U^n(a), \quad \text{ where} \\
&U^0(a) = a, U^{n+1}(a) = \bigcup U^n(a).
\end{align*}\]
This is an example of definition by recursion along \(\mathbb{N}\).




We can use the existence of \(\operatorname{TC}_R\) as a set to strengthen the minimality condition to subclasses, similar to the case of the well-ordering of \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\):







Lemma 1 
For every non-empty class \(B \subseteq A\), there exists \(x \in B\) such that
\[
    \forall y \in B \;  \neg y R x
\]




To prove this lemma, simply pick any \(x \in B\), take its transitive \(R\)-closure, and intersect it with \(B\):
\[
    C = \operatorname{TC}_R(x) \cap B.
\]
\(C\) is a set, and by the minimality condition \((\operatorname{Min}_R)\) has an \(R\)-minimal element \(a\). \(a\) has to be minimal for \(B\), too, since otherwise there exists \(b \in B\) with \(b R a\). Since \(a \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), \(b \in \operatorname{TC}_R(x)\), and therefore \(b \in C\), contradicting the minimality of \(a\).
The lemma implies a corresponding induction principle for well-founded relations:
\[\begin{equation*}
    (\operatorname{Ind}_R) \qquad  \forall x \in A [ \forall y ( yRx \, \to \varphi(y)) \to \varphi(x)] \to \forall x \in A \, \varphi(x)).
\end{equation*}\]
This in turn yields the following.







Theorem 2 (Recursion principle for well-founded relations) 
Let \(R\) be a well-founded relation on a class \(A\). For every function \(G : A \times \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\longrightarrow  \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) there exists a unique function \(F: A \to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) such that \[\begin{equation*}
    F(a) = G(a,F \mid_{\{x \mid xRa\}})  \text{ for all } a \in A.
\end{equation*}\]

title: Induction and Recursion
text:
Is there a way to systematically build the \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), the universe of all sets, “from below”?
We start with the empty set:
\[
V_0 = \emptyset
\]
Given \(V_\alpha\), the Power Set axiom requires the set of all subsets to exist, so we set
\[
V_{\alpha+1} = \mathcal{P}(V_{\alpha}).
\]
Finally, at limit stages we simply collect all sets we have obtained so far:
\[
V_ \lambda =  \bigcup_{\xi < \lambda} V_\xi \quad \text{for limit } \lambda
\]
What we really are doing here is to construct a function \(V: \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\to \mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) by ordinal recursion. Think \(V_\alpha = V(\alpha)\).
The following facts about the hierarchy are easily verified by transfinite induction:







Proposition 4  

Each \(V_\alpha\) is transitive.
\(\alpha < \beta\) implies \(V_\alpha \subset V_\beta\).
\(\alpha \subseteq V_\alpha\)





Remarkably, if we assume the axiom of Foundation, we reach all sets this way.







Theorem 3 
For every set \(x\) there exists an ordinal \({}\alpha\) with \(x \in V_\alpha\), that is, \[
    \mathop{\mathrm{V}}= \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha
\]











Remark 1. Recall that the notation \(\bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} \dots\) is really just a shortcut for the class obtained as \(\{ x \colon \exists \alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}\dots\}\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(C\) be the class of all sets not in any \(V_\alpha\). Since \(\in\) is well-founded, if \(C\) is non-empty, it has a \(\in\)-minimal element \(x\). This implies that for all \(z \in x\), \(z \in \bigcup_{\alpha \in \mathop{\mathrm{Ord}}} V_\alpha\). Define a function \(h\) by mapping each \(z\in x\) to the least \({}\alpha\) so that \(z \in V_\alpha\). Since \(x\) is a set, \(h[x]\) is a set of ordinals, by Replacement. This set of ordinals has a supremum, say \({}\gamma\). Then \(x \subseteq V_\gamma\) and therefore,
\[
x \in \mathcal{P}(V_\gamma) = V_{\gamma+1}.
\]
Hence \(C\) must be empty, and the theorem follows.











Definition 2 For any set \(x\) we define its rank as \[
    \operatorname{rank}(x) = \text{ least } \alpha \text{ with } x \in V_{\alpha+1}.
\]











Exercise 1 Show that \[
\operatorname{rank}(x) = \sup\{ \operatorname{rank}(y)+1 \colon y \in x \}.
\]




We can split the question of “how large” \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\) is into two sub-questions:

How “long” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how many ordinals are there? Axioms for large cardinals attempt to extend this “length” as far as possible.
How “wide” is \(\mathop{\mathrm{V}}\), that is, how large is the power set of a set? A rather “slim” universe is given by the constructible sets, which we will encounter soon.

title: Finite Limits and Colimits
text:
Where we are going
Here is the definition we are aiming for.






NoteElementary topos (preview)



A category \(\mathcal{E}\) is an elementary topos if

\(\mathcal{E}\) has all finite limits;
\(\mathcal{E}\) has all finite colimits;
\(\mathcal{E}\) has exponentials \(B^A\) (it is cartesian closed);
\(\mathcal{E}\) has a subobject classifier \(1 \xrightarrow{\top} \Omega\).



Today is about (1) and (2). Next time we do (3) and (4). The category \(\mathcal{S}\) of abstract sets will then be a topos with some extra properties: \(1\) separates maps, there is a natural numbers object, and choice holds.
We have already met several pieces of (1) and (2) in Chapters 1–2: the terminal set \(1\), the initial set \(0\), binary sums \(A_0 + A_1\), and inverse images of parts. The point of today is that these are all instances of two general constructions, limits and colimits, and that a handful of special cases suffice to build all the others.
A remark on method. In \(\mathcal{S}\) we may test equations between maps on elements \(1 \to X\), since \(1\) separates. In a general topos this fails. So we will phrase everything with generalized elements \(x : T \to X\) for arbitrary \(T\). Every argument below then works in any category with the relevant structure.



Splittings and isomorphisms







Definition 1 (Retraction, section) For maps \(X \xrightarrow{i} Y \xrightarrow{r} X\) with \(ri = 1_X\), we call \(r\) a retraction (left inverse) of \(i\), and \(i\) a section (right inverse) of \(r\).











Proposition 1 If \(i\) has a retraction, then \(i\) is a monomorphism. Dually, if \(r\) has a section, then \(r\) is an epimorphism.










NoteProof






Proof. If \(ix_1 = ix_2\), then \(x_1 = (ri)x_1 = r(ix_1) = r(ix_2) = (ri)x_2 = x_2\). This is “dividing by \(i\) on the left”. The dual statement has the dual proof.




A mono with a retraction is called split. The converse of Proposition 1 is special to sets:

In \(\mathcal{S}\), every mono \(X \rightarrowtail Y\) with \(X \neq 0\) splits. Pick \(x_0 : 1 \to X\) and let \(X'\) be the complement of \(X\) in \(Y\), so \(Y = X + X'\). Define \(r\) by cases: \(r\) is \(1_X\) on \(X\) and constantly \(x_0\) on \(X'\).
In continuous settings this fails. The inclusion of the circle \(S^1 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2\) has no continuous retraction. It does have one into \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\), namely \(y \mapsto y/|y|\).

The proof for \(\mathcal{S}\) used complements. In a general topos, parts need not have complements. Toposes in which they always do are called Boolean. This is our first glimpse of how intuitionistic logic enters.







Definition 2 \(f : X \to Y\) is an isomorphism if there is \(g : Y \to X\) with \(gf = 1_X\) and \(fg = 1_Y\).











Proposition 2 If \(rf = 1_X\) and \(fs = 1_Y\), then \(r = s\). In particular, two-sided inverses are unique; we write \(f^{-1}\).










NoteProof






Proof. \(r = r1_Y = r(fs) = (rf)s = 1_Xs = s\).




In \(\mathcal{S}\), isomorphisms are exactly the bijections. Given bijective \(f\), define $g(y) = $ the unique \(x\) with \(fx = y\). Then \(gf\) and \(fg\) agree with the identities on elements, and \(1\) separates. No choice is needed, because \(g\) is uniquely determined.



Products







Definition 3 (Product) A product of objects \(A, B\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is an object \(P\) with maps \(A \xleftarrow{\pi_A} P \xrightarrow{\pi_B} B\) such that for every \(X\) and every pair \(f : X \to A\), \(g : X \to B\) there is a unique \(h : X \to P\) with \(\pi_A h = f\) and \(\pi_B h = g\).
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
& & A \\
& \overset{f}{\nearrow} & \big\uparrow{\scriptstyle \pi_A} \\
X & \xrightarrow{\;\;h\;=\;\langle f,g \rangle\;\;} & A \times B \\
& \underset{g}{\searrow} & \big\downarrow{\scriptstyle \pi_B} \\
& & B
\end{array}
\]




We write \(P = A\times B\) and \(h = \langle f,g \rangle\). Equivalently, composition with \(\pi_A, \pi_B\) is a bijection \[
\mathcal{C}(X, A\times B) \;\cong\; \mathcal{C}(X,A) \times \mathcal{C}(X,B).
\] So a map into a product is the same thing as a pair of maps. That is the operational content of a product, and it is what we use in practice.






NoteAxiom: Binary products



Any two sets \(A, B\) have a product \(A \times B\).


Computing with generalized elements. For \(x : T \to X\), \[
\langle f,g \rangle\,x = \langle fx,\, gx \rangle.
\] Both sides are maps \(T \to A\times B\) with projections \(fx\) and \(gx\). By the uniqueness clause they are equal. This is how “ordered pairs” are recovered without ever defining them.
Examples.

In \(\mathcal{S}\): the cartesian product with the usual projections.
In a poset viewed as a category: \(a \times b\) is the greatest lower bound \(a \wedge b\).
In \(\mathbf{Grp}\), \(\mathbf{Top}\), \(\mathbf{Vect}\): the direct product with the product structure.
In \(\mathcal{S}\) with \(2 = \{0,1\}\): a pair \(\varphi, \psi : X \to 2\) of characteristic maps is a single map \(\langle \varphi,\psi \rangle : X \to 2\times 2\). Composing with the truth table \(\& : 2 \times 2 \to 2\) gives the characteristic map of the intersection of the two parts. Logical operations are maps out of products of truth-value objects. This returns with \(\Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega\) in a general topos.

Graphs and diagonals. The graph of \(f : A \to B\) is \(\gamma_f = \langle 1_A, f \rangle : A \to A \times B\). Since \(\pi_A \gamma_f = 1_A\), the graph is a split mono, hence a part of \(A \times B\). A generalized element \(\langle x,y \rangle\) is a member of it iff \(y = fx\). The special case \(\delta_A = \langle 1_A, 1_A \rangle : A \to A\times A\) is the diagonal.

Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism







Proposition 3 If \((P, \pi_A, \pi_B)\) and \((P', \pi'_A, \pi'_B)\) are both products of \(A\) and \(B\), there is a unique isomorphism \(h : P \to P'\) with \(\pi'_A h = \pi_A\) and \(\pi'_B h = \pi_B\).










NoteProof






Proof. The universal property of \(P'\) gives \(h : P \to P'\) commuting with the projections. That of \(P\) gives \(k : P' \to P\). Now \(kh : P \to P\) satisfies \(\pi_A (kh) = \pi_A\) and \(\pi_B(kh) = \pi_B\). But \(1_P\) satisfies the same equations, so uniqueness forces \(kh = 1_P\). Symmetrically, \(hk = 1_{P'}\).




This argument uses nothing but “existence + uniqueness of induced maps”. It therefore applies verbatim to every universal construction below: equalizers, pullbacks, limits, and dually sums, coequalizers, pushouts. We will not repeat it. It is why we may say “the product” and why “equations” like \(1 \times A = A\) or \(A \times B = B \times A\) mean specified isomorphisms.
This is a point worth pausing on. In \(\mathsf{ZFC}\), \(A \times B\) is one particular set of Kuratowski pairs. Here, any object with the universal property is a product, and nothing we can say distinguishes between them.




Equalizers







Definition 4 (Equalizer) Given \(A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B\), an equalizer of \(f\) and \(g\) is a map \(e : E \to A\) such that

\(fe = ge\);
for every \(x : T \to A\) with \(fx = gx\) there is a unique \(\bar x : T \to E\) with \(e\bar x = x\).

\[
E \xrightarrow{\;e\;} A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B
\]











Proposition 4 Every equalizer is a monomorphism. Hence it is a part of \(A\), and for any \(x : T \to A\), \[
x \in e \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad fx = gx.
\]










NoteProof






Proof. Suppose \(e y_1 = e y_2 =: x\). Then \(fx = gx\), and both \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are factorizations of \(x\) through \(e\). By uniqueness, \(y_1 = y_2\). The membership statement is a restatement of clause 2.




So the equalizer is the categorical form of comprehension by an equation: \(\{a \in A : f(a) = g(a)\}\).
Examples.

The unit circle is the equalizer of \(\mathbb{R}^2 \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}\) given by \((x,y) \mapsto x^2+y^2\) and the constant map \(1\). This is Descartes’ idea: figures are cut out by equations.
In \(\mathbf{Grp}\), the kernel of \(\varphi: G \to H\) is the equalizer of \(\varphi\) and the trivial homomorphism.
The equalizer of the two projections \(\pi_0, \pi_1 : B \times B \rightrightarrows B\) is the diagonal \(\delta_B\).

The last example lets us build all equalizers from products and inverse images: the equalizer of \(f, g\) is the inverse image of the diagonal \(\delta_B\) along \(\langle f,g \rangle : A \to B\times B\) (L-R Exercise 3.32). Elementwise, \(\langle fx, gx \rangle \in \delta_B\) iff \(fx = gx\).



Pullbacks







Definition 5 (Pullback) Given \(A_0 \xrightarrow{f_0} B \xleftarrow{f_1} A_1\), a pullback (or fibered product) is an object \(P\) with maps \(\pi_0, \pi_1\) making the square commute, \[
\begin{CD}
P @>{\pi_1}>> A_1\\
@V{\pi_0}VV @VV{f_1}V\\
A_0 @>{f_0}>> B
\end{CD}
\] such that for all \(a_0 : T \to A_0\), \(a_1 : T\to A_1\) with \(f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\) there is a unique \(a : T \to P\) with \(\pi_0 a = a_0\) and \(\pi_1 a = a_1\). We write \(P = A_0 \times_B A_1\).




In \(\mathcal{S}\): \(A_0 \times_B A_1 = \{(a_0,a_1) \in A_0\times A_1 : f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\}\). This description already suggests how to construct pullbacks.







Proposition 5 If a category has binary products and equalizers, it has pullbacks.










NoteProof






Proof. Form \(A_0 \times A_1\) with projections \(p_0, p_1\), and let \(e : P \rightarrowtail A_0 \times A_1\) be the equalizer of \(f_0 p_0\) and \(f_1 p_1\). Set \(\pi_k = p_k e\). A pair \(a_0, a_1\) with \(f_0 a_0 = f_1 a_1\) is a map \(\langle a_0,a_1 \rangle : T \to A_0\times A_1\) equalizing \(f_0p_0\) and \(f_1p_1\). So it factors uniquely through \(e\).




Pullbacks are remarkably versatile. Many earlier constructions are special cases:







Data \(A_0 \xrightarrow{f_0} B \xleftarrow{f_1} A_1\)
Pullback




\(B = 1\) (so \(f_0, f_1\) are forced)
the product \(A_0 \times A_1\)


\(f_1 = j\) a mono (a part of \(B\))
the inverse image \(f_0^{-1}(j)\), a part of \(A_0\)


\(f_0, f_1\) both monos
the intersection of the two parts


\(f_1 = b : 1 \to B\) an element
the fiber of \(f_0\) over \(b\)


\(f_0 = f_1 = f : A \to B\)
the kernel pair of \(f\), i.e. \(\{(a,a') : fa = fa'\}\)



The second row needs one small fact. It will be used constantly once we have the subobject classifier.







Lemma 1 Monos are stable under pullback: in the square of Definition 5, if \(f_1\) is mono, then so is \(\pi_0\).










NoteProof






Proof. Let \(\pi_0 y = \pi_0 y'\). Then \(f_1 \pi_1 y = f_0 \pi_0 y = f_0 \pi_0 y' = f_1 \pi_1 y'\), so \(\pi_1 y = \pi_1 y'\) since \(f_1\) is mono. Now \(y\) and \(y'\) have the same two projections. By uniqueness in the pullback property, \(y = y'\).




Combining the first row with the construction of equalizers from products and inverse images gives the converse of Proposition 5:







Proposition 6 If a category has a terminal object and pullbacks, it has binary products and equalizers.







Finite limits in general
All of the above are instances of one notion. The input is a diagram: a family of objects with some maps between them. Following L-R, a diagram shape is a directed graph \(J \underset{c}{\overset{d}{\rightrightarrows}} I\) (vertices \(I\), edges \(J\), domain map \(d\), codomain map \(c\)). A diagram of that shape in \(\mathcal{C}\) consists of objects \(A_i\) (\(i \in I\)) and maps \(f_j : A_{d(j)} \to A_{c(j)}\) (\(j \in J\)). The shape is finite if \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.







Definition 6 (Limit) A cone over the diagram with vertex \(L\) is a family \(\pi_i : L \to A_i\) with \(f_j \pi_{d(j)} = \pi_{c(j)}\) for all \(j\). A limit is a cone that is universal: every cone \((a_i : T \to A_i)_i\) factors as \(a_i = \pi_i a\) through a unique \(a : T \to L\).




In words: a map \(T \to L\) is the same thing as a compatible family of maps \(T \to A_i\). In \(\mathcal{S}\), \(L\) is the set of compatible families of elements \((a_i)_{i\in I}\) with \(f_j(a_{d(j)}) = a_{c(j)}\).



Shape
Limit




empty graph
terminal object \(1\)


two vertices, no edges
binary product


\(\bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\)
equalizer


\(\bullet \to \bullet \leftarrow \bullet\)
pullback









NoteAxiom: Finite limits



\(\mathcal{S}\) has limits of all finite diagrams.


It is enough to check a few cases.







Theorem 1 If a category has finite products (including the empty product, i.e. a terminal object) and equalizers, then it has all finite limits.










NoteProof






Proof. (Sketch; this is Proposition 5 writ large.) Form the two products \(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\) and \(\prod_{j\in J} A_{c(j)}\) and two maps between them, specified by their components. Writing \(p_i\) for the projections of the first product and \(q_j\) for those of the second, define \[
\textstyle\prod_{i} A_i \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} \prod_{j} A_{c(j)},
\qquad
q_j\, u = p_{c(j)}, \qquad q_j\, v = f_j\, p_{d(j)} .
\] A family \((a_i)_i\), i.e. a map \(\langle a_i \rangle_i : T \to \prod_i A_i\), is equalized by \(u\) and \(v\) iff \(a_{c(j)} = f_j a_{d(j)}\) for every edge \(j\), i.e. iff it is a cone. So if \(e : L \rightarrowtail \prod_i A_i\) is the equalizer of \(u\) and \(v\), then \(\pi_i = p_i e\) is the limit cone.











Corollary 1 A category with a terminal object and pullbacks has all finite limits.




So for the topos axioms we can take “finite limits” to mean “\(1\) and pullbacks”, or “\(1\), binary products, and equalizers”. These are the forms we will actually check in examples.
Foundational aside. Compare this with \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). There, \(\{a \in A : f(a) = g(a)\}\) comes from Separation, and \(A \times B\) is built from Pairing, Union, Power Set, and Separation. Here, these constructions are axiomatized directly by what they do, and no internal membership structure of the objects is ever invoked.



Colimits by duality
Every category \(\mathcal{C}\) has an opposite \(\mathcal{C}^\mathrm{op}\): same objects, all arrows reversed. A colimit in \(\mathcal{C}\) is a limit in \(\mathcal{C}^\mathrm{op}\). So every definition and theorem above dualizes for free: reverse the arrows, swap “mono” and “epi”.








Shape
Limit
Colimit




empty
terminal \(1\)
initial \(0\)


two vertices
product \(A\times B\)
sum \(A + B\) (Ch. 2)


\(\bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\)
equalizer
coequalizer


\(\bullet\to\bullet\leftarrow\bullet\) / \(\bullet\leftarrow\bullet\to\bullet\)
pullback
pushout










Definition 7 (Coequalizer) Given \(A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B\), a coequalizer is \(q : B \to Q\) with \(qf = qg\) such that every \(h : B \to Z\) with \(hf = hg\) factors as \(h = \bar h q\) for a unique \(\bar h : Q \to Z\). \[
A \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} B \xrightarrow{\;q\;} Q
\]




Dually to Proposition 4, every coequalizer is an epimorphism.
In \(\mathcal{S}\). \(Q = B/{\sim}\), where \(\sim\) is the equivalence relation generated by \(f(a) \sim g(a)\) for \(a \in A\), and \(q\) is the quotient map. A map out of \(Q\) is a map out of \(B\) that respects the identifications. Equalizers are comprehension (cutting out by an equation); coequalizers are quotients (gluing by identifications).
Pushouts are the dual of pullbacks. In \(\mathcal{S}\), the pushout of \(B_0 \xleftarrow{f_0} A \xrightarrow{f_1} B_1\) is \((B_0 + B_1)/{\sim}\) with \(f_0(a) \sim f_1(a)\), i.e. \(B_0\) and \(B_1\) glued along \(A\). In \(\mathbf{Top}\), gluing two closed disks along their boundary circle gives the sphere \(S^2\).
By duality, from Theorem 1 and Corollary 1:







Theorem 2 A category has all finite colimits iff it has an initial object, binary sums, and coequalizers, iff it has an initial object and pushouts.










NoteAxiom: Finite colimits



\(\mathcal{S}\) has colimits of all finite diagrams.









Remark 1 (Finite colimits come for free in a topos). In Lawvere and Tierney’s original axiomatization, finite colimits were an explicit axiom. It was later shown that they follow from finite limits together with power objects (i.e. exponentials plus a subobject classifier). This is due to Mikkelsen, with a slick proof by Paré (1974) via the monadicity of the power-object functor. So axiom (2) in our preview is redundant. We keep it on the list because it is convenient, and because Lawvere–Rosebrugh assume the initial set and binary sums as axioms for \(\mathcal{S}\) long before power objects are available.




The duality between limits and colimits is a feature of the definitions, not a symmetry of \(\mathcal{S}\). For instance, \(0\) is a strict initial object: any map \(X \to 0\) is an isomorphism. The dual statement (every map \(1 \to X\) is an isomorphism) is plainly false. So \(\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{op}\) is a perfectly good category with finite limits and colimits, but it is not “like \(\mathcal{S}\)”. Strictness of \(0\), together with disjointness of sums, holds in every topos. Other asymmetries, such as “every epi splits” (the Axiom of Choice), are special to \(\mathcal{S}\) and will be among the extra axioms that single it out.



Summary

Finite limits = terminal object + pullbacks (equivalently: finite products + equalizers). They give us products, graphs, diagonals, equalizers (comprehension by equations), inverse images, intersections, fibers, and kernel pairs.
Finite colimits = initial object + pushouts (equivalently: finite sums + coequalizers). They give us sums and quotients. In a topos they follow from the other axioms.
Method. Every construction is specified by a universal property (existence + uniqueness of an induced map). This determines it up to unique isomorphism and is tested on generalized elements \(T \to X\).
Next time: exponentials \(B^A\) (maps as an object) and the subobject classifier \(\Omega\) (parts as maps). Together with today’s axioms, these give the full definition of an elementary topos.



Exercises







Exercise 1 Show from the universal property that \(B \times A \cong A \times B\) and \(1 \times A \cong A\). Which equation needs the uniqueness clause? (L-R 3.21, 3.22)











Exercise 2 Show that the equalizer of \(f, g : A \rightrightarrows B\) is the inverse image of the diagonal \(\delta_B\) along \(\langle f,g \rangle\). (L-R 3.32)











Exercise 3 (Pasting lemma) In a commutative diagram \[
\begin{CD}
X @>>> Y @>>> Z\\
@VVV @VVV @VVV\\
U @>>> V @>>> W
\end{CD}
\] suppose the right square is a pullback. Show that the left square is a pullback iff the outer rectangle is.











Exercise 4 Show that the kernel pair \(K \rightrightarrows A\) of \(f : A \to B\) (the pullback of \(f\) along itself) is, in \(\mathcal{S}\), the equivalence relation \(\{(a,a') : fa = fa'\}\). Then show that the coequalizer of the kernel pair is \(A \to f(A)\), the image of \(f\). (L-R 3.44)











Exercise 5 Let \(X\) be a set. Show that the slice category \(\mathcal{S}/X\) (objects: maps \(E \to X\); arrows: commuting triangles) has all finite limits. What is the terminal object? What is the product of \(E \to X\) and \(F \to X\)? (L-R 3.48)











Exercise 6 Show that \(\mathbf{Grp}\) has all finite limits. Does it have finite colimits? What is the sum of \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}\)? (L-R 3.47)

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Where We’re Going

This course compares three modern foundations of mathematics: set theory, category theory, type theory
Before any of that: a 19th-century story about rigor, completeness, and infinity
Today: Prologue – Bolzano (1817) \(\to\) Dedekind (1872) \(\to\) Cantor (1874)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
section: Gauss and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
text:
Gauss and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

THM: Every non-constant polynomial has a root over the complex numbers.
Gauss’s proofs (from 1799 on) quietly depend on the Intermediate Value Theorem

\[
f \text{ continuous},\ f(a)<0,\ f(b)>0 \ \implies\ f(c)=0 \text{ for some } c\in(a,b)
\]

IVT feels obvious: a curve can’t get from below the axis to above it without crossing. (Gauss and many others at the time thought so.)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Bolzano’s Insight (1817)


Bernard Bolzano was the first to realize importance of continuity in the proof of Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

He attempted a genuine proof of the IVT.
But he had no clear concept of the real numbers to work with.
His proof was not fully satisfactory — a rigorous treatment of continuity had to wait for Weierstrass (1874).








Bernard Bolzano
(1781–1848)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Completeness: An Ancient Intuition
Bolzano’s realization:
\[
\text{completeness of } \mathbb{R} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \text{absence of gaps}
\]

Ancient intuition: a line has no gaps
But then — what are the “parts” of a line?

To capture this, Bolzano introduced two principles:

the least upper bound principle
the nested interval property
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
How to Prove Completeness?

Bolzano could state completeness — but not prove it
Proving it requires first knowing what a real number is
That formalization of \(\mathbb{R}\) did not arrive until the 1870s

e.g. via Dedekind cuts
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Dedekind’s Breakthrough (1872)


Dedekind’s key move: stop presupposing what \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is.

A real number is a Dedekind cut \((L, U)\).


\((L,U)\) partitions \(\mathbb{Q}\): every element of \(L\) is less than every element of \(U\)
Completeness is now straightforward — union of left-sides of cuts defines a cut.








Richard Dedekind
(1831–1916)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Deeper Problem
Dedekind (1872) solved the problem “What is a real number?”
— but in doing so, he opened a deeper problem: the nature of infinity.

Reals are introduced as (pairs of) infinite sets of rationals
There seemed to be no way around this
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A New Kind of Object

Sets — and infinity — stop being background intuition.
They become mathematical objects in their own right
This shift is the seed of everything that follows in this course
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor (1874): Two Kinds of Infinity


Cantor showed that \(\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathbb{R}\) represent different types of infinity.
His first proof of the uncountability of \(\mathbb{R}\):

Take any sequence \((x_m)_{m \in \mathbb{N}}\) of distinct real numbers.
Construct nested intervals that exclude one \(x_m\) at a time.








Georg Cantor
(1845–1918)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor’s Construction
Build nested intervals
\[
a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < b_2 < b_1 < b_0
\]
such that
\[
\forall m\ \exists i \quad x_m \notin [a_i, b_i]
\]
(at each stage, shrink the interval just enough to exclude the next \(x_m\))
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Cantor’s Argument
By the nested interval property:
\[
\bigcap_i [a_i, b_i] \neq \emptyset
\]
Let \(x\) be a point in this intersection.

By construction, \(x \neq x_i\) for every \(i\).
So \((x_m)\) could not have enumerated all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
Hence \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable.


This only works because \(\mathbb{R}\) is complete — the nested interval property fails over \(\mathbb{Q}\).
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Bonus: Transcendental Numbers
The same construction gives more than uncountability:

The set of algebraic numbers is countable.
So the same nested-interval argument produces a real number not among the algebraic numbers

\[
\implies \text{transcendental numbers exist}
\]
— without ever exhibiting one!
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Not Everyone Was Convinced
Dedekind’s cuts and ideals, Cantor’s infinite sets — both rely on purely existential proofs:

they show an object exists, without showing how to construct or compute it.
this was a genuinely new style of mathematics in the 1870s–80s.

Not everyone welcomed it.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Kronecker’s Critique








Leopold Kronecker
(1823–1891)


Leopold Kronecker, one of the leading algebraists of the day, objected on principle.

1870: points out that the accumulation point in the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem cannot be constructed by elementary operations from the rational numbers.
1882: publicly attacked Dedekind’s ideals — used to prove unique factorization exists but the proof does not tell you how to compute it.
Combated Cantor’s transfinite sets as well.


“Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk.” — attributed to Kronecker: “God made the integers; all else is the work of man.”
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
A Debate Ensues

Dedekind replied in 1888 with a fully set-theoretic theory of the natural numbers (“Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?”, includes his definition of an infinite set).
The “early round” of the debate ended in victory for the infinitary side.

Hurwitz, Minkowski, Hilbert, Volterra, Peano, Hadamard, Klein all sided with Dedekind and Cantor.

Arbitrary functions, infinite sets, and existential proofs become the mainstream of analysis and algebra.

Kronecker’s constructivist objection doesn’t disappear — it resurfaces in Brouwer’s intuitionism, decades later.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Logicism


Gottlob Frege pursued an even more ambitious foundation: reduce all of arithmetic to pure logic.

Basic mathematical concepts should be definable in purely logical terms
Basic mathematical truths should be derivable from purely logical laws
Central logical law (the comprehension principle): for any well-defined property \(p\), there is a set \[
\{x : p(x)\}
\]
Frege built his Grundgesetze der Arithmetik (1893, 1903) on exactly this idea.








Gottlob Frege
(1848–1925)
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Logicism
Frege needed the comprehension principle to define the natural numbers in a purely logical way.

Frege (as later Russell and Whitehead) realized that natural numbers are logical attributes that belong to concepts, not to things.
“There are four horses in the barn” should be thought of as four objects fall under the concept “horse in barn”.
If \(f\) is a concept, we can then define “at least two objects fall under \(f\)” as \[
2_m(f) := \exists x \exists y \: [ x \neq y \: \wedge f(x) \: \wedge \: f(y)]
\] and can define the number \(2\) as \(2() := 2_m() \: \wedge \ \neg 3_m()\).

For this definition to work, Frege needed the comprehension principle - every concept determines a class containing exactly the objects falling under it.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Russell’s Paradox (1901–02)
Around 1901, Bertrand Russell (and, independently, Zermelo) found that comprehension is inconsistent.
Let \[
R = \{\, x : x \notin x \,\}
\]

If \(R \in R\), then by definition \(R \notin R\)
If \(R \notin R\), then by definition \(R \in R\)

Either way, contradiction. The very principle underlying Frege’s logic — and “naive” set theory generally — collapses.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Letter to Frege, 16 June 1902



“Let \(w\) be the predicate: to be a predicate that cannot be predicated of itself. Can \(w\) be predicated of itself? From each answer its opposite follows. […] Likewise there is no class (as a totality) of those classes which, each taken as a totality, do not belong to themselves.”
— Bertrand Russell, letter to Gottlob Frege








Bertrand Russell
(1872–1970)


Russell had been reading Frege’s Grundgesetze closely — and found the one crack in its foundation.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
Frege’s Reply, 22 June 1902

“Your discovery of the contradiction caused me the greatest surprise and, I would almost say, consternation, since it has shaken the basis on which I intended to build arithmetic. […] It is all the more serious since, with the loss of my Rule V, not only the foundations of my arithmetic, but also the sole possible foundations of arithmetic, seem to vanish.”
— Gottlob Frege, letter to Bertrand Russell

Frege added a hasty appendix to Volume II of the Grundgesetze, already at the printer, acknowledging the disaster.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage

title: Foundations of Mathematics
text:
What now?
Other set theoretic paradoxes had emerged before Russell’s.

Burali-Forti paradox (Cantor, 1896): There cannot be a set of all ordinals.

But these were tied deeply to Cantor’s transfinite set theory, which many people still viewed as remote and suspect.
Russell’s antinomy struck right at the heart of the very foundation of all of mathematics: the efforts to define the natural numbers.
crumbs: 1 · Some History and Setting the Stage
